We also followed the instructions given by my father’s mother, Deborah, who raised me after my father, Tobiel, died and left me an orphan.
When I came of age, I married Anna, a relative of mine, and we had a son, whom I named Tobiah.
After I was taken captive to Nineveh in Assyria, all my relatives and people ate Gentile food,
but I refused to eat any such food.
And because I obeyed God with all my heart,
the Most High brought me to the attention of King Shalmaneser, who made me his purchasing agent.
As long as the king lived, I went frequently to Media to buy supplies. One time I left 750 pounds of silver in the care of my relative Gabael, the brother of Gabri.
When Shalmaneser died and his son Sennacherib became king, the roads to Media were difficult to travel.
During the reign of Shalmaneser, I was able to do many good deeds for my relatives and my people.
I shared my food with the hungry and clothed the naked. Whenever I saw the dead body of one of my people thrown outside the walls of Nineveh, I would bury it.

One time Sennacherib had to retreat from Judea because the King of heaven was punishing him for speaking blasphemous things. In his anger Sennacherib put to death many of the captives from Judea, but I stole the bodies and buried them secretly. When Sennacherib looked for the bodies, he could not find them.
One day someone from Nineveh told the king what I was doing. When I realized that the king knew all about me and wanted to put me to death, I became afraid and fled for my life.
All my property was taken from me and put in the royal treasury. All that was left to me was my wife, Anna, and my son, Tobiah.

But less than forty days later the king was murdered by two of his sons, who escaped into the mountains of Ararat. He was succeeded by his son Esarhaddon, who appointed my nephew Ahikar (my brother Hanael’s son) to be his chief accountant and administrator.

Ahikar put in a good word for me, and I was able to return to Nineveh. (Ahikar had been Sennacherib’s chief cup-bearer, guardian of the king’s seal, administrator, and treasurer. When Esarhaddon became king, he reappointed Ahikar to office. As I said, Ahikar was my nephew, and so he was a close relative.)
So when Esarhaddon became king, I returned home to live with my wife, Anna, and my son, Tobiah. It was Pentecost, the Festival of Harvest, and a fine dinner was prepared for me.

When I saw all the food laid out on the table, I said to Tobiah, “My dear son, go and find a poor, sincere worshiper from among the Israelite captives here in Nineveh. Bring him home to share this dinner, and we will wait until you come back.”
Tobiah had hardly left when he returned. “Father!” he exclaimed.
I hurried from the table without touching my food and found the body. I carried it back from the public square and put it in an outbuilding until I could bury it after sunset.
Then I returned to my own house, washed myself, and ate my meal in sorrow.
As I ate, I thought of the prophecy of Amos against Bethel:
At sunset I dug a grave and buried the dead man.
But my neighbors ridiculed me: “Will he never learn? He had to run away the last time he did such a thing, and here he is burying the dead again!”
That same night I washed myself and went to bed along the inside wall of the courtyard. Because it was a hot night, I left my face uncovered.

I did not know there were sparrows on the wall until their droppings fell into my eyes, causing cataracts. I went to the doctors to be healed, but the more they treated me with ointments, the worse my vision became. Finally, I was totally blind. I remained blind for four years. During this time my relatives grieved for me, and my nephew Ahikar took care of me for two years until he went to Elymais in Persia.
My wife, Anna, supported us by making cloth.

Each time she delivered to her employers what she had made, they paid her. On a certain day in late winter, she finished a piece of work and took it to her employers. When they paid her in full for the cloth, they also gave her a young goat from their herd.
As soon as she returned home, the goat began to bleat. I called out to her, “Where did you get that goat? You didn’t steal it, did you? Give it back to its owners, for we cannot eat stolen food.”

She replied, “It was given to me as a bonus over and above what I earned.” But I did not believe her. I became angry and told her to take the goat back. She answered, “And you’re supposed to be a man of charity and righteous deeds! Now your true character is coming out!”
I was struck with grief over my actions. I groaned and wept, and in my sadness I began to pray.
“You are just, O Lord,
Remember me, Lord,
and disobeyed your commandments.
I admit the justice of your many judgments;
Now deal with me as you please.
On the very same day, at Ecbatana in Media, Sarah, the daughter of Raguel, was insulted by one of her father’s servant girls.

Sarah had been married to seven husbands, each of whom had been killed by the evil demon Asmodeus before any of the marriages had been consummated. The servant said to her, “You are the one who kills your husbands. You have already had seven husbands and no children from any of them.
Why do you punish us? Because your husbands died? Go with them! We never want to see a son or daughter of yours!”

Sarah was in deep anguish because of these insults. She went upstairs in tears, intending to hang herself. But she thought about it again and said, “People would reproach my father and say, ‘Your only beloved daughter killed herself because of her troubles.’ And I would bring my father in his old age down to his grave in sorrow. It is better for me not to hang myself but to pray to the Lord to let me die. Then I won’t have to hear these insults anymore.”
So she spread out her hands at the window and prayed:
To you, O Lord, I turn my face
Command that I be allowed to die,
You know, O Master, that I am innocent
I have disgraced neither my name
At that very moment, the prayers of both Sarah and Tobit were heard in the glorious presence of God.

Raphael was sent to answer their prayers for healing. He was going to heal Tobit’s eyes so that he might once again see God’s light. He also would arrange the marriage of Sarah, the daughter of Raguel, to Tobiah son of Tobit and would free Sarah from the demon Asmodeus. For Tobiah, more than anyone else who wanted her, was entitled to marry her. Tobit returned from the courtyard into his house at the same moment that Sarah came down from the upper room.
That same day Tobit remembered the money he had entrusted to Gabael’s care at Rages in Media.
He said to himself, “Since I have prayed for death, why shouldn’t I tell my son, Tobiah, about this money before I die?”

So Tobit called for Tobiah and said to him, “My son, give me a proper burial when I die. Honor your mother and care for her as long as she lives. Do what will please her and do nothing to make her sad.
Remember, my dear son, that she went through many dangers for you while you were still in her womb. When she dies, bury her beside me in the same plot.
“Remember the Lord every day of your life. Never sin deliberately or break his commandments. As long as you live, do what is right and never take part in wrongdoing.
For those who live in the truth will succeed in all they do. To those who live righteous lives,
give generously from your possessions. But don’t give a gift grudgingly. If you do not ignore the poor, God will not ignore you.
Let your giving be in proportion to your possessions. If you have great wealth, give a generous amount. If you have few possessions, give from that little.
In this way you will store up a great treasure for a time of need.
For giving to people in need frees people from death and keeps them from going down into darkness.
Giving to charity is a pleasing sacrifice to the Most High.

“My dear son, be on your guard against all sexual immorality. It is important that you take a wife from your own tribe. Do not marry a foreign woman, for we are descendants of the prophets. My son, remember the example of Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, our ancestors who took wives from among their relatives. They were blessed by the lives of their children, whose descendants will inherit their land.

Be like them, my son; love your relatives. Do not proudly think you are better than your relatives, and do not hesitate to take a wife from your own tribe. Pride is the source of ruin and confusion. Idleness will result in famine.

“Pay your workers each day; don’t make them wait until the next day to receive their wages. If you serve God, you will be rewarded. Watch yourself, my son, in everything you do, and be disciplined in all your conduct.
Don’t do to others what you would hate to have them do to you. Don’t drink too much wine or let drunkenness become a way of life.
Give food to the hungry and clothing to the poor. Don’t hesitate to give away your surplus to people in need.
Place bread on the tombs of the just, but give nothing to sinners.
“Seek the counsel of every wise person, and do not reject useful advice.

Bless the Lord God at every opportunity. Ask him to keep you on a straight path so that you will be successful in everything you do. The nations don’t understand these things. It is the Lord who gives them good counsel, but if the Lord decides otherwise, he can bring them down to the grave. So now remember these commands, my son, and never let them be erased from your heart.
“Now, my son, I want to tell you that I have left 750 pounds of silver in the care of Gabael son of Gabri at Rages in Media.
Do not be anxious, my son, that we have become poor. You will have great wealth if you fear God, run from every sin, and do what is right in the sight of the Lord your God.”
Then Tobiah said to his father, “I will do everything you have told me.

But how will I get your money from him, since I do not know him and he does not know me? What proof should I give him of my identity to convince him to give me the money? I do not even know the roads to Media.”

Tobit told him, “He and I made two copies of a written agreement. We tore one of them in half, and each of us kept one of the halves. I put the other copy with the money. Twenty years have passed since I deposited that money. So find a reliable man to accompany you, my son. We will pay him for his time when you get back. Now go and reclaim this money from Gabael.”
Tobiah went out to find someone who knew the roads to Media and would accompany him there. He found Raphael standing outside, but Tobiah did not know that he was an angel of God.
Tobiah asked him, “Who are you, young man?”

“Yes,” Raphael answered. “I have gone there often and know all the roads. I used to stay with our relative Gabael in Rages. We will first have to travel to Ecbatana, which is on the plain east of here. Then it is two more long days to get to Rages, which is in the mountains.”
Tobiah said to him, “Wait for me, young man, while I go in and tell my father. I need someone to accompany me to Rages, and I will pay you to guide me.”
Raphael replied, “I am at your service, but don’t be too long.”
Tobiah went in and told his father, “I have found a fellow Israelite who will go with me.”
When Raphael came in, Tobit immediately greeted him. Raphael replied, “And may all be well with you.”
Tobit inquired, “Tell me, brother, to what tribe and family do you belong?”
“Why do you need to know my tribe?” replied Raphael.
Raphael answered, “I am Azariah, son of the great Hananiah, one of your relatives.”

Tobit said, “Welcome, my brother. Do not be insulted because I wanted to know your tribe and family. You are a relative of mine, of good and noble stock. I knew Hananiah and Nathan, the two sons of the great Shemeliah. They used to make the pilgrimage to Jerusalem with me, and we would worship together. They did not turn away from keeping the law of Moses. Your relatives are good people, and you come from a good family. Again, welcome!”
He added, “I will pay you a silver coin for each day of your trip as well as all your expenses.
I will also pay you a bonus if you both return safely.”

Tobit said, “May God bless you, brother.” Then he called Tobiah and said to him, “My son, prepare whatever is necessary for the trip. May God in heaven protect both of you as you travel and bring you back to me safely. May his angel guard your way.”
Tobiah’s mother began to weep. She said to Tobit, “Why have you sent my son away? Isn’t he the one we depend on?
Why do you want more money if it costs us the life of our son?
Can’t we be satisfied with the life the Lord has given us?”
Tobit said to her, “Don’t worry. Our child is leaving in good health, and he will return the same way. You will see for yourself that he will be safe. Say no more. Do not fear for them, dear wife.
A good angel will go with him. His mission will be successful, and he will return in good health.”
So she stopped weeping.
The young man and the angel left together,
and Tobiah’s dog followed them. They traveled until dusk and then spent the night beside the Tigris River.
When Tobiah went down to wash his feet in the river, a large fish jumped from the water and tried to swallow his foot. As Tobiah cried out,
the angel shouted, “Catch the fish and hang on to it!” Tobiah grabbed the fish and pulled it up on the bank.
Then the angel told him, “Cut open the fish, and save its heart, liver, and gall. Throw away the intestines. The heart, liver, and gall make good medicines.”
Tobiah did as the angel told him. Then he roasted the fish, ate some of it, and preserved the rest of it with salt.
Then the young man asked the angel, “Brother Azariah, what medicine can be made from the fish’s heart, liver, and even the gall?”
He replied, “If you burn the heart and liver and blow the smoke on a man or woman who is tormented by a demon or an evil spirit, the spirit will leave and never return.
As for the gall, you can use it to anoint the eyes of a person who has cataracts. Then, if you blow on the eyes, they will be healed.”
When they had entered Media and were getting close to Ecbatana,
Raphael spoke to the young man and said, “Brother Tobiah.”

He has no male heir, and Sarah is his only daughter. Since you are the only eligible relative, you have the right to marry her and gain her inheritance. The young woman is sensible, courageous, and very beautiful, and her father is a good man.”

He continued: “You have the legal right to marry her. So, listen to me, brother. I will speak to the young woman’s father tonight so that you can take her as your bride. When we return from Rages, we will celebrate the marriage. Raguel cannot keep her from you or promise her to another man, for that would be punishable by death according to the law of Moses. Raguel knows that you—above all others—are entitled to marry his daughter. So listen to me, brother. This very night we will arrange for you to marry her. And when we return from Rages, we will take her back with us to your house.”

But Tobiah said to Raphael, “Brother Azariah, I have heard that this woman has already been married seven times and that each husband died on his wedding night in the bridal chamber when he approached her. I have heard that it was a demon that killed them.

The demon doesn’t harm her, but it kills anyone who wants to come near her. So I am afraid. I am my father’s only son, and my death would bring my mother and father to their graves. Then there would be no son to bury them.”

Raphael said to him, “Remember your father’s command to take a wife from your own tribe. Now listen to me, brother, and say no more about this demon. Take her as your wife. I know that she will marry you tonight.
When you enter the bridal chamber, take the fish’s liver and heart and lay them on the burning incense. The demon will smell the smoke and flee, never to return.

Then, when you are about to go to bed with her, both of you must first stand up and pray. Ask the Lord of heaven to give you mercy and deliverance. Don’t be afraid. Sarah was set apart for you from all eternity. You will rescue her and she will go with you. I have no doubt that you will have children by her, and they will be very dear to you. So don’t worry!”
When Tobiah heard Raphael’s words and realized that Sarah was his relative on his father’s side of the family, he fell deeply in love with her and his heart was set on her.

When they reached Ecbatana, Tobiah said to Raphael, “Brother Azariah, take me straight to our brother Raguel.” So they arrived at Raguel’s house, where they found him seated by the courtyard door. They greeted Raguel, and he replied, “Greetings to you also, brothers. Welcome, and good health to you.” Then Raguel brought them into the house
and said to his wife, Edna, “This young man looks a lot like my relative Tobit!”
Then Edna asked them, “Where are you from, brothers?”
She asked them, “Do you know our relative Tobit?”
They answered, “He is alive and well.” Then Tobiah added, “He is my father!”
Raguel jumped up, kissed him, and wept.
Then he said, “Bless you, child. You are the son of a good and noble man. What an unfortunate calamity that such a righteous and charitable man became blind!” He embraced Tobiah and wept.
His wife, Edna, also wept for Tobit, and even their daughter, Sarah, began to weep.
They showed the visitors a warm welcome by preparing a young ram from the flock for a meal.

Raguel overheard the question, so he said to the young man, “Eat, drink, and be happy. No man is more entitled to my daughter than you. Indeed, I have no right to give her to anyone else since you are my closest relative. But, my son, let me explain the true situation to you.

I have given her to seven husbands from our family, and each of them died on his wedding night when he approached her. But don’t be discouraged, my son. Eat and drink, for the Lord will make it work out for both of you.”

Then Raguel called for his daughter, Sarah. When she came, he took her by the hand and gave away the bride to Tobiah, saying, “Here she is. Take her to be your wife according to the law of Moses. Take her to your father safely. And may the God of heaven prosper your journey with peace.”

Then Raguel called the young woman’s mother and told her to bring him a scroll. On it he wrote out the marriage contract, stating that he was giving Sarah to Tobiah as his wife according to the law of Moses.
Then they began to eat and drink.
Then Raguel said to Edna, “Dear wife, prepare the bedroom, and take our daughter there.”
So Edna went and made the bed as she was told. She took Sarah there and began to weep for her. Then she wiped away her tears and said,
“Be brave, daughter. May the Lord of heaven grant you joy in the place of your sorrow. Be brave, my child.” Then she left.
After they had feasted, Tobiah wanted to go to bed with his bride. So the young woman’s parents took him to the bedroom.
Remembering Raphael’s words, Tobiah took the fish’s liver and heart out of his bag, and he put them on burning incense.
The odor of the fish repelled the demon, and it fled through the air to Upper Egypt. (But Raphael followed him there and completely subdued him.)
When the parents had left and shut the bedroom door, Tobiah got up from the bed and said to Sarah, “Stand up, dear wife. We must pray to our Lord and ask him to grant us mercy and deliverance.
So she got up, and they began to pray, asking God for deliverance. Tobiah said,
You made Adam, and then you made his wife, Eve,
I do not take this woman as my wife
They both said, “Amen, Amen.”
Then they went to bed and slept together.
He said, “Perhaps the man will die, so we will bury him before we are criticized and ridiculed.”
When they had dug the grave, Raguel went back to his wife at the house and said to her,
“Send one of your servant girls to see if Tobiah is still alive. If he is dead, we can bury him before it is daylight so that no one will know.”
So they sent one of the servants, who took a lighted lamp into the bedroom. She found them safe and sound, sleeping together.
So the servant came out and told the parents, “He is alive. Nothing is wrong.”
Then they blessed the God of heaven. Raguel said,
May you be praised because you have given me joy.
We praise you for having mercy
Then Raguel commanded his servants to fill up the grave before dawn.
Raguel asked his wife to prepare many loaves of bread. He also slaughtered two cows and four young rams in preparation for a feast.
And he said to Tobiah, “You must stay here with me for fourteen days, eating and drinking and cheering up my daughter, for she has been depressed.

Take half of what I own, and return safely to your father. The other half will be yours when my wife and I die. Be encouraged, my son. I am your father and Edna is your mother, and all of us—including your wife—belong to you forever. Be encouraged, my son.”
Then Tobiah said to Raphael,

“Brother Azariah, take four household servants and two camels with you, and go to Rages. Go to Gabael, give him this portion of the written agreement, and get the money from him. Invite him to return with you to my wedding feast.
You know that my father is counting the days until we return, and if I stay one day more than necessary, he will be very worried.
You know that Raguel made an oath, obligating me to stay; I cannot violate his oath.”

So Raphael took the four servants and two camels and went to Rages in Media, where he stayed overnight with Gabael. Raphael gave him Tobit’s portion of the written agreement. Then Raphael told Gabael that Tobit’s son, Tobiah, had married, and he invited Gabael to the wedding feast. So Gabael got up and counted out the money bags, each properly sealed, and loaded them on to camels.

In the morning they both got up early and went to the wedding celebration. When they came to Raguel’s house, they found Tobiah sitting at the table. He stood up and greeted Gabael. Then Gabael began to weep, and he blessed Tobiah with these words: “You are the good and honorable son of a good and honorable man, who also is just and charitable. May the Lord grant the blessings of heaven to you and your wife and to your wife’s father and mother. Praise God, for I see that Tobiah looks a lot like my relative Tobit.”
Tobit had calculated the number of days it would take Tobiah to reach Rages and return again. He counted the days, and when his son did not return,
he said, “What can be detaining him? Do you think Gabael has died and there is no one to give Tobiah the money?”
Tobit began to worry.
His wife, Anna, said, “My child has died and is no longer alive.” She began to weep and mourn for her son:
“How terrible! Oh, my son, you are the light of my eyes. Why did I let you take that journey?”

But Tobit said to her, “Be quiet and stop worrying, my dear wife. Our son is safe. Probably something unexpected has happened. The man we sent with him is a trustworthy relative. Don’t grieve for Tobiah. He will be here soon.”

She answered him, “You be quiet! Stop trying to deceive me. My child has died.” Every day she would rush out and look down the road Tobiah had taken. No one could persuade her to do otherwise. When the sun set, she would go inside to mourn and weep all night long, never getting any sleep.
But Raguel said, “Don’t go; stay with me, my son. I will send messengers to your father to tell him about you.”
But Tobiah responded, “No! I beg you to send me back to my father!”
So Raguel let Tobiah leave with his wife, Sarah. He also gave Tobiah half of all his property: his male and female servants, cattle and sheep, donkeys and camels, clothing, money, and utensils.

As he sent them off, he embraced Tobiah and said to him, “Farewell, my son. Travel safely. May the Lord of heaven give you and your wife many good things. May my eyes see my grandchildren before I die.”

Then he kissed his daughter, Sarah, and said to her, “My daughter, honor your father-in-law and mother-in-law because now they are your parents, just as we are. Go in peace, Daughter. As long as I live, may I hear that you are doing well.” And then he let them go.

Then Edna said to Tobiah, “My child and my beloved brother, may the Lord of heaven bring you home safely. And may I live long enough to see my grandchildren. In the sight of the Lord, I entrust my daughter, Sarah, to you. Don’t ever do anything to make her sad. Go in peace, my son. From now on I am your mother and Sarah is your beloved wife. May we all have prosperous lives.” Then she tenderly kissed them both and sent them on their way.

And Tobiah left Raguel with great joy, praising the Lord of heaven and earth, the King of all, because he had given him a successful journey. Before leaving, he told Raguel and Edna, “May I fulfill the Lord’s command to honor you all the days of my life.”
When they came to Kaserin, which is near Nineveh, Raphael said to Tobiah,
“You know that your father is old and blind.
Therefore, let us go ahead of your wife to get the house ready before the others arrive.”
So they went on ahead, and Tobiah’s dog followed them. As they traveled together, Raphael reminded Tobiah, “Make sure you’re ready to use the gall of the fish.”
Anna sat looking down the road for her son, as she had been doing every day.
When she saw them coming, she said to her husband, “Look, your son is coming, along with the man who went with him!”
(Raphael had said to Tobiah, “I know that your father’s eyes will be healed.
Anoint his eyes with the fish gall you carry. This will cause the cataracts to fall off, and your father will regain his sight and see the light.”)
Anna ran to her son, embraced him, and said, “Now that I have seen you, my child, I can die in peace.” And she wept.
Despite his blindness, Tobit stood up and, hurrying to meet his son, stumbled through the courtyard door. Tobiah approached him
with the fish gall in his hand. He took hold of his father, blew into his eyes, and said, “Don’t be afraid, Father.”
Then Tobiah took the medicine and put it on his father’s eyes,
causing him some pain. Using both of his hands, Tobiah pulled the cataracts from Tobit’s eyes. Embracing Tobiah,
Tobit wept and said, “I can see you, my son; you are the light of my eyes!” Then he said,
Though he afflicted me,

Then Tobit, rejoicing and praising God, went out to meet his daughter-in-law at the gate of Nineveh. The people of Nineveh were amazed to see him walking along, fully restored and with no one leading him by the hand.

Tobiah told them all that God had been merciful to his father and restored his sight. When Tobit met Sarah, the wife of his son, Tobiah, he blessed her by saying, “Come in, my daughter. Praise God, who has brought you to us, my daughter. Blessed be your father’s household, and blessed be my son, Tobiah, and you, my daughter. Come into your home now. May you have health, blessings, and joy.”
Ahikar and his nephew Nadab came to join in the celebration with Tobit.
When the wedding festivities ended, Tobit said to Tobiah, “My son, take care of paying the wages of the man who traveled with you, and give him a bonus as well.”
Tobiah replied, “How much should I pay him, Father? How about half of the possessions I brought back with me?
He brought me back safely to you, he healed my wife, he brought the money back with me, and he healed you. How much extra shall I give him as a bonus?”
Tobit said, “My son, he deserves to receive half of all he has brought back.”
So Tobiah said to Raphael, “For your wages, accept half of everything you brought back. Now go in peace.”

Then Raphael took the two men aside privately and said, “Praise God, and tell everyone about the good things he has done for you. Sing praises to his name. Honor God by telling everyone his words. Don’t hold back from telling about him.
While it is good to hide the secret of a king, it is also good to reveal and praise the works of God.
Prayer made with true sincerity is good, and charitable acts done with justice are better than wealth gotten by unjust means. It is better to give to the poor than to store up treasures of gold.
For charitable giving saves us from death and cleanses us from sin. Those who give charitably will be satisfied.
Those who do evil and commit sin are their own worst enemies.
“Now I will tell you the truth, hiding nothing from you. I already hinted at it when I said, ‘While it is good to hide the secret of a king, it is also good to reveal and praise the works of God.’
When you prayed, Tobit, and when Sarah prayed, it was I who brought your prayer into the presence of the glorious Lord. And I was there whenever you buried the dead.
When you left your dinner to bury a dead man, I was sent to test you.
At the same time, God sent me to heal you and your daughter-in-law.
I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand ready and enter the glorious presence of the Lord.”
Tobit and Tobiah were greatly shaken. They fell with their faces to the ground.
But Raphael said to them, “Do not be afraid; peace be with you. Praise God forever.
When I was with you, I was there by the will of God. Praise him each and every day. Sing his praises.
(By the way, if you thought I ate and drank with you, it was only imaginary—a vision.)
Praise the Lord of the earth, and publicly acknowledge God. See, I am ascending to the one who sent me. Write down all the things that have happened to you.” Then he ascended to heaven.
They stood up and saw him no more.
Then they kept blessing God and singing his praises, and they openly acknowledged God for the wonderful things that happened when God’s angel appeared to them.
Then Tobit said:
He both punishes and shows mercy.
Praise him before the Gentiles, children of Israel.
yet he has shown you his greatness even there.
Although he punished you for your sins,
If you turn to him with all your heart and all your soul
Now see what he has done for you,
Let everyone speak of his majesty
O Jerusalem, the holy city,
Acknowledge the Lord, for he is good.
A bright light will shine to the ends of the earth.
All who speak harshly against you will be cursed,
Go and rejoice for the children of the righteous,
Blessed are all who love you
O my soul, praise the Lord, the great King,
for Jerusalem will be built as his eternal house.
The main streets of Jerusalem will be paved
The gates of Jerusalem will sing hymns of joy,
So ended Tobit’s praise.

Tobit died in peace at the age of 112 years and was buried with honor in Nineveh. He was 62 years old when he went blind. After he was healed, he lived in prosperity, giving money to the poor, continually praising God and acknowledging his majesty.
When Tobit was on his deathbed, he sent for his son, Tobiah, and gave him this command: “My son, take your children,

and go to Media. For I believe the message that God has spoken by Nahum concerning Nineveh’s destruction. All the things Nahum said will come upon Assyria and Nineveh. Everything that was spoken by the prophets God sent to Israel will happen. None of their words will fail; all will come true at the right time. So it will be safer in Media than in Assyria and Babylon, for I know and believe that whatever God has said will happen. Not a single word of the prophets’ messages will fail. All of our fellow Israelites will be scattered from the good land, Israel, and taken into captivity. The whole land of Israel will become desolate, including Samaria and Jerusalem. And the Temple of God will be burned to the ground for a while.

“But God will again have mercy on them and will bring his people back to the land of Israel. They will rebuild the Temple of God, though it won’t be like the first one. This will be the situation until the time comes for God’s promise to be fulfilled. Then the people of Israel will return from captivity to Jerusalem and rebuild it with splendor. And the Temple of God will be built in it, even as the prophets of Israel said.
Then all the nations of the earth will turn from their ways and will truly worship God. All of them will abandon their idols, which led them into error,

and they will praise the eternal God in righteousness. All the Israelites who are rescued in those days and who truly acknowledge God will go to Jerusalem. They will live safely forever in the land of Abraham, which will be handed over to them. Those who truly love God will rejoice, and those who practice sin and injustice will disappear from the earth.

As soon as your mother dies and you have buried her beside me in the tomb, leave this city without delay. For I see that there is great injustice here; this city is full of treacherous and shameless people.
So now, my children, see what happens to those who are charitable. And see what happens to those who are unjust—they die!
When Tobiah’s mother died, Tobiah buried her beside his father. Then he and his wife returned to Media and lived in Ecbatana with Raguel, his father-in-law.

Respecting the old age of his parents-in-law, he took care of them until they died. He buried them in Ecbatana of Media, and he inherited the property and possessions of Raguel, along with that of his father, Tobit.
Then Tobiah died and was buried with honor at the age of 117.

But before he died, he not only heard about the destruction of Nineveh but witnessed it as well. He saw its captives being taken to Media by King Cyaxares. Tobiah praised God for all that he had done to the people of Nineveh and Assyria. Before he died, he rejoiced over the destruction of Nineveh, and he praised the Lord God who lives forever and ever.
It was the twelfth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled over the Assyrians in the great city of Nineveh. At the same time, Arphaxad ruled over the Medes in Ecbatana.
Arphaxad built walls around Ecbatana with huge stones 4-1/2 feet thick and 9 feet long. These walls were 105 feet high and 75 feet thick.
He also made towers that were 150 feet high and 90 feet wide at the foundation.
He built the gateways of the city 105 feet high and 60 feet wide to allow his armies to march out in force, division by division.
In those days King Nebuchadnezzar fought against King Arphaxad on the great plain near the borders of Ragau.

Nebuchadnezzar was joined by people from the hill country, from along the Euphrates, the Tigris, and the Hydaspes, and from the plain where Arioch ruled over the Elymeans. In this way, many nations joined forces with the Babylonians.

Then Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, sent a message to everyone in Persia and to all who lived in the west. The message went to those in Cilicia, Damascus, and the region of Lebanon and the Anti-Lebanon Mountains, and to all the people on the seacoast.
The message also went to the people of Carmel, Gilead, Upper Galilee, the great plain of Esdraelon,

the towns of Samaria, and to everyone who lived west of the Jordan River. This included Jerusalem, Bethany, Chelous, and Kadesh. The message went as far as the border of Egypt to Tahpanhes, Rameses, and the whole land of Goshen.
It even went beyond Tanis and Memphis to the entire land of Egypt as far as the border of Ethiopia.

But everyone throughout the region chose to disregard the summons from Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, refusing to join him in war. They were not afraid of him; after all, he was just one man. So they dishonored him by sending back his messengers with a negative response.

Then King Nebuchadnezzar became angry. He swore by his throne and kingdom that he would seek revenge on the whole territory of Cilicia and Damascus and Syria. He vowed to kill all the people of Moab, Ammon, Judea, and Egypt as far as the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea.
In the seventeenth year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar led his forces against King Arphaxad and defeated him in battle, overpowering Arphaxad’s entire army, including all his horsemen and chariots.
He took possession of all the towns and then conquered Ecbatana, capturing its towers, plundering its marketplaces, and reducing its glory to ruins.
He captured Arphaxad in the mountains of Ragau and killed him with spears, thus destroying him once and for all.
Then Nebuchadnezzar returned to Nineveh with his entire army, a vast number of troops. There he and his army rested and feasted for 120 days.

In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, on a certain day in midspring, word went out from the palace of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, that he would seek revenge on the whole region, just as he had said.
He called all his advisers and governors and told them about his secret plan. And when he told them that the people throughout the region had refused to help him,
they decided that everyone who had disobeyed his command should be destroyed.
After the council had finished making its plan, Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, gave these orders to Holofernes, his commander who was second in power only to himself:
“This is what the great king, the lord of the whole earth, says: Prepare for battle, and take with you 120,000 brave foot soldiers and 12,000 horsemen.
March out against all the lands to the west, for they disregarded my orders.
Tell them to prepare to submit to my authority, for in my rage I am marching against them. I will cover the whole earth with my armies, and my troops will plunder it.
Their wounded will fill their valleys and ravines. Their dead will be thrown into the rivers, causing them to overflow.
I will lead them captive to the ends of the earth.
Go! Seize all their territory for me. All must surrender to you, and you are to hold them for me until I can punish them.
Show no mercy to those who resist. Slaughter and plunder them throughout the region.
For as I live, and by the power of my kingdom, I have spoken. I will accomplish all this by my own power.
Be careful, Holofernes, not to neglect any of your master’s commands. Carry them out exactly as I have ordered you, and do so immediately.”
So Holofernes left the king and called together all the commanders, generals, and officers of the Assyrian army.
He arranged the 120,000 select troops by divisions, as the king had ordered him to do, together with 12,000 archers on horseback.
He organized them in battle formation.
He secured a vast number of camels, donkeys, and mules for carrying baggage, and innumerable sheep, oxen, and goats for food.
Everyone received plenty of rations and a large amount of gold and silver from the royal palace.
Then Holofernes personally led his army ahead of King Nebuchadnezzar and overran the entire region to the west with chariots and horsemen and select troops.
After them followed a huge force of all sorts of people—like a swarm of locusts and the dust of the earth, too many to count.
They marched for three days from Nineveh to the plain of Bectileth, and they camped near Bectileth by the mountain to the north of Upper Cilicia.
From there Holofernes took his whole army—the foot soldiers, horsemen, and chariots—and went up to the hill country.
He devastated the region of Lydia and carried away all the Rassisites and the Ishmaelites on the border of the desert south of the country of the Chelleans.
Then he marched along the Euphrates, crossed Mesopotamia, and destroyed all the fortified towns along Abron Brook as far as the sea.
He seized control of the territory of Cilicia and killed everyone who resisted him. Then he went to the southern borders of Japheth, across from Arabia.
He surrounded all the Midianites, burned their tents, and plundered their sheepfolds.

Then he went to the plain of Damascus during the wheat harvest. He burned their fields, destroyed their flocks and herds, plundered their towns, ravaged their lands, and slaughtered all their young men with the sword.

All the people who lived along the seacoast were terrified—those who lived in Sidon and Tyre and those in Sur, Ocina, and Jamnia. Those who lived in Azotus and Ashkelon were seized with terrible panic.
These people sent messengers to Holofernes with this petition for peace:
“We, the servants of Nebuchadnezzar, the great king, fall humbly before you. Do with us whatever you will.
See, all we have is at your disposal—our buildings, our land, our wheat fields, our flocks and herds, and our sheepfolds and their surrounding tents. Do with them as you please.
The people of our towns will all be your slaves. Come and deal with us and all we own as you see fit.”
The messengers went to Holofernes and told him all this.
Then Holofernes went down to the seacoast with his army, stationed garrisons in all the fortified towns, and drafted the best men there as reserve troops.
All the people along the coast and in the surrounding areas welcomed him, wearing garlands, dancing, and playing tambourines.

But Holofernes demolished all their shrines and cut down their sacred groves. For King Nebuchadnezzar had commanded him to destroy all the gods of the land so that he alone might be served as a god in the nations conquered by Holofernes.
Then he came to the plain of Esdraelon, near Dothan, a village facing the great ridge of Judea.
He camped between Geba and Scythopolis, and he stayed there for a whole month to collect all the provisions his army needed.
The Israelites throughout Judea heard that Holofernes, the commander serving Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, had plundered all the other nations and destroyed their temples.
As he approached, they became terrified for Jerusalem and for the Temple of the Lord their God,

for they had only recently returned from captivity. (All the people of Judea had recently resettled the city and rededicated the sacred vessels and the altar and the Temple, all of which had been defiled.)
So the Israelites in Judea sent word to every district of Samaria and to Kona, Beth-horon, Belmain, Jericho, Choba, Aesora, and the Salem Valley.
They occupied all the high hilltops and fortified the villages there. They also stored up food to prepare for war, for their fields had recently been harvested.
Joakim, the high priest, was in Jerusalem at the time and wrote to the people of Bethulia and Betomesthaim, towns facing Esdraelon across the plain near Dothan.

He told them to guard the mountain passes, for it was only through these passes that Judea could be invaded. It would be easy to stop any forces trying to enter because the passage was narrow, wide enough for only two soldiers to pass at a time.
The Israelites did as they had been ordered by the high priest Joakim and the high council of all the people of Israel, which was in session at Jerusalem.
All the people cried out earnestly to God and humbled themselves by intense fasting.
All the men, their wives, their children, and every resident foreigner (both hired workers and slaves) put on sackcloth to show they were in mourning. They even put sackcloth on their livestock.
And all the Israelite men, women, and children living in Jerusalem lay face down in front of the Temple, and with ashes on their heads, they spread out their sackcloth before the Lord.

They even draped the altar with sackcloth. They cried out together, earnestly asking the God of Israel not to allow their infants to be carried off, their wives to be taken captive, their towns to be destroyed, and the sanctuary to be desecrated. They knew the Gentiles around them would be overjoyed at their defeat.
The Lord heard their prayers and acknowledged their distress—for the people fasted many days throughout Judea and in Jerusalem before the sanctuary of the Lord Almighty.
Joakim the high priest and all the priests who ministered before the Lord wore sackcloth as they offered the people’s daily burnt offerings, offerings to fulfill vows, and freewill offerings.
With ashes on their turbans, they earnestly called on the Lord, asking him to look kindly on the people of Israel.

Holofernes, the commander of the Assyrian army, was told that the people of Israel had prepared for battle by closing the mountain passes, fortifying all the high hilltops, and placing obstructions in the plains.
Holofernes was very angry at this and called together all the princes of Moab, the commanders of Ammon, and all the governors of the coastlands.

He asked them, “Tell me, you Canaanites, who are these people that occupy the hill country? What towns do they live in? How large is their army? What is the source of their power and strength? Who is the king that leads their army?
Why is it that, of all the nations in this western region, they are the only ones who refuse to surrender to me?”
Then Achior, leader of the Ammonites, answered, “My lord, if you wish, I will tell you the truth about these people who live in the hills nearby. I will not lie.
The ancestors of these people were Chaldeans.
For a time they settled in Mesopotamia because they refused to worship the gods their ancestors had worshiped in Chaldea.

Since they had abandoned their ancestors’ ways and worshiped the God of heaven, the God they had come to know, their neighbors expelled them from the presence of their gods. So they fled to Mesopotamia, where they lived for a long time.
Then their God commanded them to leave that place and go to the land of Canaan. They settled there and acquired great wealth in gold, silver, and livestock.
“When a famine spread over the land of Canaan, they went down to Egypt and lived there as long as there was food. They became such a great multitude that their race could not be counted,
so the king of Egypt became hostile toward them. He exploited them by making them slaves who produced bricks for him.
They cried out to their God, who punished all of Egypt with incurable plagues. So the Egyptians drove them out of their sight.
Then God dried up the Red Sea before them,
and he led them forward to Sinai and Kadesh-barnea. They drove out all the people living in the desert
and settled in the land of the Amorites. With great force they destroyed all the inhabitants of Heshbon. Then they crossed over the Jordan River and took control of all the hill country.
They drove out the Canaanites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Shechemites, and all the Girgashites. Then the Israelites lived there a long time.
“As long as they did not sin against their God, they prospered, for the God who is with them hates sin.
But when they disobeyed him, they were defeated in many battles and were taken captive to foreign lands. The Temple of their God was demolished, and their towns were taken by their enemies.

But now they have returned to their God and have come back from the places where they were scattered. Some of them have occupied Jerusalem, the site of their Temple, while others settled in the unoccupied hill country.
“So now, master and lord, we must find out if these people have sinned against their God. If so, we can go up and defeat them.
But if they are not guilty, my lord, you would do better to leave them alone and move on. For their Lord and God will protect them, and we would become the laughingstock of the whole world.”

When Achior had finished his talk, all the people standing around the tent began to disagree with him. Holofernes’ officers, together with the people from the coastal area and from Moab, insisted that Achior should be killed.
“Why should we be afraid of the Israelites?” they said. “They are weak and powerless, incapable of withstanding any sort of attack.
Let’s go ahead! Your great army, master Holofernes, will swallow them up!”
When the uproar made by the men outside the council died down, Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, spoke to Achior in the presence of all the foreigners and Moabites.

He said, “Achior, who do you think you are—you and the other mercenaries of Ephraim? Who are you to tell us like some prophet not to make war against the people of Israel? Do you think their God will defend them? What god is there except Nebuchadnezzar? He will send his forces to wipe them from the face of the earth! Their God will not rescue them.
We, the king’s servants, will destroy them as if they were but one man. They could never resist the force of our horsemen.

We will burn them completely. Their mountains will be drunk with their blood, and their plains will be filled with their dead. Not a single trace of them will survive our attack; they will all die. So says King Nebuchadnezzar, lord of the whole earth, for he has spoken, and he makes no empty threats.
“As for you, Achior, you Ammonite mercenary, you have spoken these words rashly. You will not see my face again until I take revenge on these people who came out of Egypt.
When I return, the swords of my soldiers and the spears of my servants will pierce your sides, and you will fall among their wounded.
Now my slaves are going to take you into the hill country and leave you in one of the towns near the mountain passes.
You will not die until you are destroyed along with these people.
If you really believe in your heart that they will not be conquered, don’t look so sad! But I have spoken, and none of my words will fail to come true.”
Then Holofernes commanded his personal slaves to seize Achior and take him away to Bethulia, where they would hand him over to the Israelites.
So the slaves led him out of the camp into the plain. From there they went up into the hill country and came to the springs below Bethulia.

When the men of the town saw them, they picked up their weapons and ran from the town to the top of the hill. All the slingers prevented Holofernes’ slaves from coming up because they kept slinging stones at them.
So the slaves took shelter below the hill. Then they tied Achior, left him lying at the foot of the hill, and returned to their master.
The Israelites came down from their town and found Achior. After untying him, they brought him into Bethulia, where he could speak to the leaders of their town.
The leaders in those days were Uzziah son of Micah (of the tribe of Simeon), Chabris son of Gothoniel, and Charmis son of Melchiel.

They called together all the elders of the town, and all the young men and women hurried to the assembly as well. Achior stood in the middle of all the people, and Uzziah questioned him about what had happened.

Achior answered by telling them what had taken place at Holofernes’ council. He told them everything he had said to the Assyrian leaders and how Holofernes had bragged about what he would do to the people of Israel.
Then all the people fell down and worshiped God. They cried out,
“O Lord God of heaven, see their pride, and be merciful to our humble race. Show your kindness to those who are dedicated to you.”
Then they reassured Achior and praised him warmly.
Uzziah took him from the assembly to his own house and gave a banquet for the elders. All that night they called on the God of Israel for help.

The next day Holofernes ordered his whole army and all the reserve troops who had joined him to break camp and march against Bethulia. He told them to take over the mountain passes as the first step in their attack on the Israelites.
The army began to march that very day; it numbered at 148,000 foot soldiers and 12,000 horsemen, not counting the baggage carts and the soldiers handling the supplies.
They set up camp in the valley near Bethulia beside the spring. They covered the whole land from Dothan to Balbaim and from Bethulia to Cyamon, which faces Esdraelon.
When the Israelites saw this huge army, they were terrified and said to each other, “They will strip the whole land clean. The mountains, valleys, and hills cannot bear their weight.”
Yet they all took up their weapons and lit fires on their towers, where they remained on guard all night.
On the second day Holofernes led all his horsemen out in full view of the Israelites in Bethulia.

He scouted out the slopes leading up to the town and located the springs that supplied their water. So he took control of these springs and set guards of soldiers over them. Then he returned to his army.
Then all the leaders of the Edomites and the Moabites and the commanders of the coastal area came to him and said,
“Listen to what we have to say, our master, and your army will suffer no casualties.
These Israelites do not have to rely on their spears, for they live in safety in the high mountains.
Therefore, master, you do not have to fight against them in the normal way, and you will not lose a single man of your army.
Simply stay in your camp and keep all your forces with you. Let your men keep control of the spring of water at the foot of the mountain,

for this is where all the people of Bethulia get their water. Eventually their thirst will force them to surrender their town. Meanwhile, we and our people will go up to the tops of the nearest mountains. We will camp there to keep watch and to prevent anyone from leaving the town.
All the men, women, and children will waste away from thirst, and you won’t even need to attack them. Their bodies will be scattered about in the streets outside their houses.
Thus, you will pay them back for their defiance and for refusing to receive you peaceably.”
This suggestion pleased Holofernes and all his officers, and he gave orders to do as they had said.
So the army of the Ammonites moved forward along with five thousand Assyrians. They set up camp in the valley and seized the Israelites’ water sources and springs.

Meanwhile, the Edomites and Ammonites went up and camped in the hill country opposite Dothan. They sent some of their men southeast toward Acraba, near Chusi, which is beside Mochmur Brook. The rest of the Assyrian army camped in the plain. Their tents and supply wagons spread out in great numbers, and they covered the entire area.
The Israelites lost their courage and cried out to the Lord their God for help. All their enemies had surrounded them, and there was no way of escape.
The whole Assyrian army, including their foot soldiers, chariots, and horsemen, surrounded them for thirty-four days. Eventually, all the water jars of every house in Bethulia became empty.
Their cisterns were going dry, and no one had enough water to drink, for their water was rationed.
The children wasted away, and the women and young men, faint from thirst, were collapsing in the streets of the town and in the gateways. No one had any strength left.
Then all the people—including the young men, the women, and the children—gathered around Uzziah and the rulers of the town. They shouted at the elders,
“Let God judge between you and us! We are suffering because you wouldn’t make peace with the Assyrians.
Now we have no one to help us. God has handed us over to them, thirsty and helpless.
Call them immediately, and surrender the whole town as a prize to the army of Holofernes,

for it would be better for us to be captured by them. We will be forced to become their slaves, but at least our lives will be spared. And we won’t have to see our infants dying before our eyes or see our wives and children taking their last breath.
We call on heaven and earth and God to be our witnesses. The Lord of our ancestors is punishing us for our sins and the sins of our ancestors. Do what we have asked for today!”
Then the entire assembly began to weep, and they cried out to the Lord God with a loud voice.
But Uzziah said to them, “Take heart, my brothers and sisters. Let’s hold out for five more days. By then the Lord our God will show us his mercy again, for he will not completely forsake us.
But if no help comes during that time, I will do as you say.”

Then he dismissed the people to their various quarters. The men returned to their stations on the walls and towers of the town. The women and children went home. And everyone in the town was miserable and discouraged.

Now Judith heard about what had happened. She was the daughter of Merari son of Ox, son of Joseph, son of Oziel, son of Elkiah, son of Ananias, son of Gideon, son of Raphain, son of Ahitub, son of Elijah, son of Hilkiah, son of Eliab, son of Nathanael, son of Salamiel, son of Sarasadai, son of Israel.
Her husband, Manasseh, who was from the same tribe and family, had died several years earlier during the barley harvest.

As he supervised the workers who were binding sheaves of grain in the field, he was overcome by the burning heat and was confined to his bed. He died in Bethulia, his hometown, and was buried with his ancestors in the field between Dothan and Balamon.
Judith had remained a widow for three years and four months.
She stayed at home, where she set up a room for herself on the roof of her house. She wore sackcloth around her waist and dressed in widow’s clothing.
She fasted every day except on the day before the Sabbath, the Sabbath itself, the day before the new moon, the festival of the new moon, and all the joyful festivals of Israel.
She was a beautiful woman, very lovely in appearance. Her husband, Manasseh, had left her gold and silver, male and female servants, herds, and cultivated land, and she managed the entire estate.
No one spoke a bad word about her, for she was devout and feared God.

Judith heard how the people, who were fainting because they had no water, had spoken against Uzziah, the ruler. And she heard all that Uzziah had promised them, even that he had sworn to surrender the town to the Assyrians after five days.
So she sent her maid, who was in charge of all she owned, to summon Uzziah and Chabris and Charmis, the elders of the town.

When the elders came to Judith, she said, “Listen to me, rulers of the people of Bethulia! What you have said to the people today is wrong. You have bound yourselves by an oath to God, promising to surrender the town to our enemies unless the Lord helps us within a certain number of days.
Who are you to test God? Who are you to set yourselves above him?
You are testing the Lord Almighty, but you will never learn anything!

If you cannot discover the depths of the human heart or understand the thoughts of the human mind, how can you search out God, who made these things? How can you grasp his mind or comprehend his thoughts? No, my brothers, do not make the Lord our God angry.
For if he doesn’t choose to help us within these five days, he still has the power to protect us for as long as he pleases. Or he could decide to destroy us in the presence of our enemies.
Do not try to control the plans of the Lord our God, for God is not like a human being, to be manipulated. He is not like a mere mortal, who can be persuaded.
Therefore, while we wait for him to rescue us, let us call on him for help. He will hear us, if it pleases him.
“In these days there are no tribes, families, clans, or towns among us that worship gods they themselves have made, as was done before.
That was why God allowed our ancestors to be killed, plundered, and humiliated by our enemies.
But now we worship no other gods but him, and so we hope that he will not abandon us or any of our people.
For if we are captured, all Judea will be captured, and our Temple will be plundered. God will make us pay for its desecration with our very lives.

Our relatives will be slaughtered, our land will be taken over, and our inheritance will be destroyed—and all this in the presence of the Gentiles, to whom we will be slaves. We will be disgraced before these masters.
For our slavery will not bring us into their favor; rather, the Lord our God will make our slavery shameful.
“Therefore, fellow Israelites, let us be an example to our relatives, for their lives depend on us. And so does the Temple—even the holy places and the altar.
In spite of everything, we should thank the Lord our God, who is testing us, just as he tested our ancestors.
Remember how he tested Abraham and Isaac. And remember what happened to Jacob in Syrian Mesopotamia while he was taking care of the sheep of Laban, his mother’s brother.
The Lord tried them with fire to test their hearts. But he is not punishing us. He punishes those who are close to him in order to warn them.”
Then Uzziah said to her, “Everything you have said was spoken with a good heart, and there is no one who can disagree with your words.
Today is not the first time you have shown your wisdom, for the people have recognized your understanding and integrity from the time you were a small girl.
But the people were so thirsty that they forced us to make this promise, and they made us take an oath that cannot be broken.
Now, since you are a devout woman, pray for us, that the Lord may send rain to fill our cisterns. Then we will no longer die of thirst.”
Then Judith said to them, “Listen to me. I am about to do something that will be remembered by all our descendants.
Tonight, stand by the gate, where I will leave with my maid. Within five days—the period after which you have promised to surrender the town to our enemies—the Lord will rescue Israel through me.
But don’t try to find out what I am doing, for I will not tell you until I have done it.”
Uzziah and the rulers said to her, “Go in peace. May the Lord God go before you and take revenge on our enemies.”
Then they left her room and returned to their quarters.

Then Judith fell face down on the ground, put ashes on her head, and removed her clothing, leaving only the sackcloth she was wearing. At the very time the evening incense was being offered in the Temple of God in Jerusalem, Judith cried out to the Lord with a loud voice. She said,

“O Lord God of my ancestor Simeon, you gave Simeon a sword to take revenge on the foreigners who had defiled a virgin by stripping off her clothes, exposing her thighs to put her to shame, and raping her. You said, ‘Such a thing must not be done.’ Yet they did it.

So you allowed their rulers to be killed and their bed to be stained with blood, for it was covered with the shame of their deceitful deed. You struck down slaves along with princes and killed even the princes on their thrones.

You let their wives be captured and their daughters be taken into captivity, and you gave all their possessions to be divided among your beloved children. Your children burned with zeal for you and abhorred the stain on their sister, so they called on you for help. Listen to me and answer me, O God, my God, for I am a widow.
You made the things of the past, and you designed everything that now exists and everything that is to come. What you planned has all happened.
Everything you decided on has taken place just as you said it would. For all your ways are prepared in advance, and you make your judgments with knowledge of what will happen in the future.

“Here now are the Assyrians, a great force, who take pride in their horses and riders. They boast in the strength of their foot soldiers and trust in shield and spear, bow and sling. They do not know that you are the Lord who crushes armies.

Your name is the Lord. Break their strength by your might. Subdue their power in your anger. For they intend to defile your sanctuary, to pollute the Temple, where your glorious name resides, and to break off the horns of your altar with their powerful swords.
Look at their pride. Send your fury on their heads. Give strength to a widow’s hand to do what I plan.
When I trick them with my words, strike down the slave with the ruler and the ruler with his servant. Break their pride by the hand of a woman.

“For your strength does not depend on numbers nor your might on the powerful. But you are the God of the humble, helper of the oppressed, supporter of the weak, protector of the forsaken, deliverer of those without hope.
Please, please, O God of my ancestor, God of Israel’s heritage, Lord of heaven and earth, Creator of the seas, King of your whole creation—hear my prayer!

Help my deceitful tongue to wound and bruise those who have planned cruel things against your covenant, against your holy dwelling place on top of Mount Zion, and against this land that your children possess.
Show your whole nation and every tribe that you are God, the God of all power and might. You are the only one who protects the people of Israel!”
When Judith finished pleading to the God of Israel,
she got up from where she was lying face down before the Lord. She called her maid and went down into her house, where she lived on Sabbaths and festival days.

Then she took off her sackcloth and the clothes that showed she was a widow in mourning. She took a bath, anointed herself with the finest lotion, braided her hair, put a tiara on her head, and dressed in her most beautiful clothing—things she had often worn when her husband, Manasseh, was still alive.
Then she put sandals on her feet and put on anklets, bracelets, rings, and earrings. She made herself very beautiful to catch the attention of any man who might see her.

She gave her maid a wineskin filled with wine and a flask of oil to carry. She also filled a bag with roasted grain, dried fig cakes, and fine bread, and she filled a sack with her dishes and gave them to the maid to carry.
Then they went to the town gate of Bethulia, where Uzziah and the elders of the town, Chabris and Charmis, were waiting.
They were astonished when they saw her so transformed, and they greatly admired her beauty. They said to her,
“May the God of our ancestors bring you favor and fulfill your plans, bringing glory to the Israelites and exaltation to Jerusalem.”
“Order the town gate to be opened, and I will go out and do what you have just said.” So they ordered the young men to open the gate for her.
Then Judith went out, accompanied by her maid. The men of the town watched her while she went down the mountain and passed through the valley. Then they lost sight of her.
As Judith and her maid went straight through the valley, an Assyrian patrol met her
and took her into custody. They asked her, “To what people do you belong? Where are you coming from? Where are you going?”
I want to see your commander, Holofernes, so I can tell him their secrets and show him a way to take the hill country without losing a single life.”
When the men heard her words and saw her face—for she was incredibly beautiful—they said to her,
“You have saved your life by choosing to surrender to our lord. Go to his tent immediately. Some of us will escort you to him.
Don’t be afraid when you tell him what you just told us, for he will treat you well.”
Then they chose a hundred men to accompany her and her maid, and they brought them to the tent of Holofernes.
The whole camp was very excited, for news of her arrival spread from tent to tent. They came and gathered around her as she stood outside the tent of Holofernes, waiting to be invited in.

They were amazed at her beauty and admired the Israelites, judging them by her. They said to one another, “Who can look down on the Jews when they have such beautiful women? We must destroy them all, for any that escape could captivate the whole world.”
Then Holofernes’ guards and servants came out and led her into the tent.
Holofernes was resting on his bed under a purple canopy that was decorated with gold, emeralds, and other precious stones.
When they told him about her, he came to the front of the tent, accompanied by servants with silver lamps.
And when Holofernes and his servants saw Judith, they were all amazed at the beauty of her face. She showed honor by bowing low before him, but his slaves lifted her to her feet.
Then Holofernes said to Judith, “Take courage and don’t be afraid. I have never hurt anyone who was willing to serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of all the earth.
If your people from the hill country had not resisted me, I would never have attacked them. They have brought this on themselves.
But tell me why you fled from them and came over to us. In any event, you have come to safety. Take courage! You will live tonight and ever after.
No one will hurt you. In fact, everyone will treat you well, just as they treat all the servants of my lord, King Nebuchadnezzar.”
Judith replied, “I am your servant. Please let me speak to you, and I will not lie to you.
If you follow my advice, God will accomplish great things through you, and you will achieve your goals.

For I swear this by Nebuchadnezzar, king of all the earth, and by his great power, which he has given you to bring order to every living being. And because of you, not only people serve him, but even the wild animals, the livestock, and the birds live under Nebuchadnezzar’s rule.

We have all heard of your wisdom and skill, and everyone throughout the whole world knows that you alone are the most capable man in the whole kingdom, the most knowledgeable and brilliant in military strategy.
“We have heard about what Achior said at your council meeting, for the people of Bethulia spared him, and he told them what he told you.
Lord and master, do not disregard what he said, for it is true. Indeed, our nation cannot be punished, nor can the sword conquer the people if they have not sinned against their God.
“But as it is now, my lord will not be defeated by them. Death will surely fall on them, for they have been overtaken by sin and provoked the anger of their God.
Since their food supply is depleted and their water is almost gone, they have planned to kill their livestock and eat all the parts that God has forbidden them to eat.

And they have decided to eat the first part of the grain harvest and the tithes of the wine and oil, which they had dedicated and set aside for the priests in Jerusalem who minister in the presence of our God. It is not lawful for any of the people to even touch these things.
But the elders of our town have sent men to Jerusalem (where they have been doing the same thing) to get permission from the high council of elders there.
When they get this permission and act upon it, on that very day they will be handed over to you to be destroyed.
“When I, your slave, learned all this, I fled from them. God has sent me to accomplish with you things that will astonish everyone in the world who hears about them.

I revere and serve the God of heaven night and day. So, my lord, I would like to remain with you, but every night I must go out into the valley and pray to God. He will let me know when my people have committed their sins.
Then I will come and tell you so that you may go out with your whole army, and not one of the Israelites will be able to stand against you.

Then I will guide you through Judea until you reach Jerusalem, where you will be enthroned. You will round up the people like sheep without a shepherd, and no dog will so much as bark at you. I was sent to tell you all this, which has been shown to me before it even happens.”
Judith’s words pleased Holofernes and all his servants. They were amazed at her wisdom and said,
“No other woman on earth looks so beautiful or speaks so wisely!”
Then Holofernes said to her, “God has done well to send you ahead of the others. This strengthens our hands to bring destruction on those who have insulted my lord.
You are as wise as you are beautiful. If you do as you have said, your God will be my God, and you will live in the palace of King Nebuchadnezzar and be famous throughout the whole world.”
Holofernes commanded his servants to bring Judith inside the tent, where his silver dinnerware was set on a table with some of his own delicacies and his own wine.
But Judith said, “I cannot eat and drink these things without sinning. But I have enough to eat from the supply I brought with me.”
Holofernes said to her, “If your supply runs out, where can we get you more? For none of your people are here.”
Judith replied, “As surely as you live, my lord, I will not use up my supplies before the Lord uses me to carry out what he has planned.”
Then the servants of Holofernes took her to her own tent. She slept until midnight and then got up about two o’clock in the morning.
She sent a message to Holofernes asking permission to be allowed to go out and pray.
Holofernes commanded his personal bodyguards not to stop her. She was at the camp three days, and each night she went out to the valley of Bethulia and bathed at the spring.
After bathing, she asked the Lord, the God of Israel, to show her how to achieve victory for his people.
When she had purified herself, she returned and stayed in the tent all day until she ate her evening meal.
On the fourth day Holofernes held a private banquet for his personal staff. He did not invite any of his officers.
He said to Bagoas, the eunuch in charge of his personal affairs, “Persuade the Hebrew woman to join us, for I want her to eat and drink with us.
It would be a shame to let such a beautiful woman go without sleeping with her. If we fail to seduce her, she will laugh at us.”

So Bagoas went out to see Judith and said, “Would this lovely woman come to my lord as his guest of honor? Please come and enjoy our wine, and you will be treated like one of the Assyrian women who serve in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar.”
Judith replied, “Who am I to refuse my lord? I will do whatever he wants me to do, and it will be a joy to me until my dying day.”
So she dressed herself in all her beautiful clothing and feminine finery. Her maid went ahead and spread before Holofernes the lambskins Bagoas had provided for Judith’s bed and dining couch.
When Judith went in and lay down, Holofernes’ heart burned with passion, for he had been waiting for a chance to seduce her ever since he first saw her.
So Holofernes said to her, “Please, enjoy yourself! Have a drink!”
Judith said, “I will gladly drink, my lord, because today is the best day of my life.”
Then she took the food and drink her maid had prepared and ate and drank with him.
Holofernes was so pleased with her that he drank a great quantity of wine, much more than he had ever drunk before.
When evening came, Holofernes’ slaves left quickly. Bagoas closed the tent from the outside and sent the attendants away. They went to their beds, for they were all weary from the long banquet.
Judith was left alone in the tent with Holofernes, who had collapsed on his bed in a drunken stupor.

Judith told her maid to stand outside Holofernes’ sleeping quarters and wait for her to come out, as she had done on the other days, for Judith said she would be going out for her prayers. (She had told Bagoas the same thing.)
So now everyone had left, and she was alone in the tent.
Now is the time to help your people and to carry out my plan to destroy the enemies who have attacked us.”
She went up to the bedpost near Holofernes’ head and took down his sword that hung there.
She came close to his bed, took hold of his hair, and said, “Make me strong today, Lord God of Israel!”
Then she struck his neck twice with all her might and cut off his head.
Next she rolled his body off the bed and pulled the canopy down from the posts. Then she quickly went out and gave Holofernes’ head to her maid,
who put it in her food bag. Then the two of them left camp together, as they usually did when they went to pray.

From a distance Judith called out to the guards at the gates, “Please, open the gate! Open! God, our God, is still with us. He has shown his power in Israel and his strength against our enemies on this very day!”
When the people of the town heard her voice, they hurried down to the town gate and summoned the elders of the town.

The leaders and the rest of the people all ran to the gate, for it seemed unbelievable that she had returned. They opened the gate and welcomed the two women. Then they lit a fire for light and gathered around them.
With a loud voice, Judith said to them, “Praise God! Praise him! Praise God, who has not withdrawn his mercy from the people of Israel. He has helped me destroy our enemies this very night!”

Then she pulled the head out of the bag and showed it to them. “Look,” she said. “This is the head of Holofernes, the commander of the Assyrian army. Here is the canopy beneath which he lay drunk. The Lord has struck him down by the hand of a woman!
The Lord protected me in this mission, and as the Lord lives, I swear that it was my beauty that seduced him to his destruction. But he committed no sin with me so as to disgrace and shame me.”
All the people were completely amazed. They bowed down and worshiped God, saying with one voice, “We bless you, our God, for on this day you have humiliated the enemies of your people.”

Then Uzziah said to Judith, “Daughter, may you be blessed by the Most High God above all women on earth. Praise to the Lord God, who created the heavens and the earth, who has guided you to cut off the head of the leader of our enemies.
Those who acknowledge the power of God will forever find hope in him.

May God give you honor forever, and may he reward you with blessings, for you did not think about your own life when our nation was brought to its knees. You prevented our ruin by walking in the straight path of our God.”
Then Judith said to them, “Listen to me, brothers and sisters. Take this head and hang it on the battlements of your wall.

When morning comes and the sun is up, every able-bodied man should go out of the town with his weapons. Appoint a leader over them, as if you were going down to the plain to attack the Assyrian scouts—only don’t really go.
The scouts will grab their weapons and run into the camp and wake up the officers. They will all rush to the tent of Holofernes, but when they cannot find him, they will panic and flee before you.
Then you and all who live within the borders of Israel will chase them and cut them down in their tracks.
But before you do all this, bring Achior the Ammonite to identify this man who despised the people of Israel and who thought he was sending Achior to his death by sending him to us.”
So they called Achior, who was staying in the home of Uzziah. When he came and saw one of the men holding Holofernes’ head, he fell to the ground in a faint.
When they revived him, he threw himself at Judith’s feet and honored her. He said, “May you be blessed by every family of Judah! In every nation, those who hear your name will be afraid.
How in the world did you do this?”
When she finished, the people cheered, rejoicing throughout the town.
When Achior saw all that the God of Israel had done, he became a firm believer in God. So he was circumcised and joined the people of Israel, remaining so to this day.
As soon as it was dawn, the people of Bethulia hung Holofernes’ head on the wall. Then they all took their weapons and went in companies to the mountain passes.
When the Assyrians saw them, they sent word to their commanders, who reported the news to the generals and captains and all their other officers.
The officers went to Holofernes’ tent and said to the man in charge of Holofernes’ personal affairs, “Wake up our lord, for those slaves are so bold they are attacking us—but we will destroy them!”
Bagoas went inside and knocked at the inner entrance of the tent, for he thought Holofernes was sleeping with Judith.
But when no one answered, he opened it and went into the bedchamber and found Holofernes’ dead body lying on the floor with his head cut off.
Bagoas cried out in anguish, wept, moaned, shouted, and tore his clothes.
Then he ran to the tent where Judith had stayed. When he saw that she was gone, he ran out to the people and shouted,
“Those slaves have tricked us! A single Hebrew woman has disgraced the whole house of King Nebuchadnezzar. Look, Holofernes is lying dead on the ground, and his head is missing!”
When the leaders of the Assyrian army heard this, they tore their clothing in terror and distress, and their loud cries and shouts rang throughout the camp.
When the men in the tents heard about it, they were astonished at what had happened.
Panic-stricken, they didn’t wait for each other but rushed out and fled across the plain and through the hill country on any available road or path.
Those who were camped in the hills around Bethulia also fled. Then all the Israelite soldiers charged after them.
Uzziah sent messengers to Betomasthaim, Bebai, Choba, Kola, and all the territory of Israel to tell what had happened and to urge everyone to pursue and destroy the enemy.
