When the Israelites heard it, they joined together to fight the enemy, cutting them down all the way to Choba. Those in Jerusalem and in all the hill country also came, for they were told what had happened in the enemy camp. The men of Gilead and Galilee repeatedly attacked the enemy from the flank and slaughtered them, pursuing them even to the borders of Damascus.
The people of Bethulia plundered the Assyrian camp and carried off great riches.

And when the other Israelites returned from the slaughter, they took what remained. There was such a huge amount of plunder that even the villages and towns in the hill country and in the plain received much of it.
Then Joakim the high priest and the high council of the Israelites in Jerusalem came to see the good things that the Lord had done for Israel. They also wanted to see Judith and congratulate her.
When they met her, they all blessed her and said to her, “You are the glory of Jerusalem; all Israel boasts about you! You are the great pride of our nation!
You have done all this with your own hand. You have done a great thing for Israel, and God is well pleased with it. May the Almighty Lord bless you forever!” And all the people said, “Amen.”

The people plundered the Assyrian camp for thirty days. They gave Holofernes’ tent and all his silver dinnerware, his beds, his bowls, and his furniture to Judith. She loaded her mules, hitched up her carts, and piled up all the plunder.
All the women of Israel hurried to see her and bless her. They danced in her honor, and Judith gave them ivy-covered wands.
Then the women crowned themselves with olive wreaths. Judith led all the women in a dance procession, and the men of Israel followed, carrying their weapons, wearing garlands, and singing hymns.
With all Israel surrounding her, Judith sang a song of thanksgiving. And all the people joined in her song of praise.
This is Judith’s song:
For the Lord is a God who crushes warfare.
Assyria came down from the mountains of the north.
They boasted that they would set my land on fire,
But the Lord Almighty has defeated them
Their mighty leader was not struck down by young men,
She put away her widow’s clothing
and fastened her hair with a tiara.
and a glimpse of her sandal aroused him.
The Persians trembled at her boldness,
Then my oppressed people shouted a war cry.
Sons of slave girls pierced the enemy
I will sing a new song to my God:
May all your creatures serve you,
The mountains and oceans will shake in your presence,
Sweet-smelling sacrifices are a small thing to you.
Destruction is certain for the nations that rise up against my people!
Eventually the entire group arrived at Jerusalem, where they worshiped God. As soon as the people were purified, they offered burnt offerings, freewill offerings, and gifts.
Judith dedicated to God all the possessions of Holofernes she had been given, and she gave the canopy from his sleeping quarters as an offering to fulfill a vow.
For three months the people enjoyed the festivities in Jerusalem before the Temple. And Judith was with them the whole time.
After these events, the people all went home. Judith returned to Bethulia and lived on her estate, and she was esteemed throughout the country for the rest of her life.
Many men wanted to marry her, but she never gave herself to another man after the death of her husband, Manasseh.

She became more and more famous through the years. She grew old in her husband’s house, reaching the age of 105. She set her maid free, and then she died in Bethulia. She was buried in a cave beside her husband, Manasseh,
and all Israel mourned for seven days. Before she died she distributed her property to all of her relatives and to Manasseh’s relatives.
No one troubled the Israelites during Judith’s lifetime or for a long time afterward.
But after Xerxes’ anger had subsided, he began thinking about Vashti and what she had done and the decree he had made.
So his personal attendants suggested, “Let us search the empire to find beautiful young virgins for the king.

Let the king appoint agents in each province to bring these beautiful young women into the royal harem at the fortress of Susa. Hegai, the king’s eunuch in charge of the harem, will see that they are all given beauty treatments.
After that, the young woman who most pleases the king will be made queen instead of Vashti.” This advice was very appealing to the king, so he put the plan into effect.
At that time there was a Jewish man in the fortress of Susa whose name was Mordecai son of Jair. He was from the tribe of Benjamin and was a descendant of Kish and Shimei.
His family had been among those who, with King Jehoiachin of Judah, had been exiled from Jerusalem to Babylon by King Nebuchadnezzar.
This man had a very beautiful and lovely young cousin, Hadassah, who was also called Esther. When her father and mother died, Mordecai adopted her into his family and raised her as his own daughter.
As a result of the king’s decree, Esther, along with many other young women, was brought to the king’s harem at the fortress of Susa and placed in Hegai’s care.

Hegai was very impressed with Esther and treated her kindly. He quickly ordered a special menu for her and provided her with beauty treatments. He also assigned her seven maids specially chosen from the king’s palace, and he moved her and her maids into the best place in the harem.
Esther had not told anyone of her nationality and family background, because Mordecai had directed her not to do so.
Every day Mordecai would take a walk near the courtyard of the harem to find out about Esther and what was happening to her.

Before each young woman was taken to the king’s bed, she was given the prescribed twelve months of beauty treatments—six months with oil of myrrh, followed by six months with special perfumes and ointments.
When it was time for her to go to the king’s palace, she was given her choice of whatever clothing or jewelry she wanted to take from the harem.

That evening she was taken to the king’s private rooms, and the next morning she was brought to the second harem, where the king’s wives lived. There she would be under the care of Shaashgaz, the king’s eunuch in charge of the concubines. She would never go to the king again unless he had especially enjoyed her and requested her by name.

Esther was the daughter of Abihail, who was Mordecai’s uncle. (Mordecai had adopted his younger cousin Esther.) When it was Esther’s turn to go to the king, she accepted the advice of Hegai, the eunuch in charge of the harem. She asked for nothing except what he suggested, and she was admired by everyone who saw her.
Esther was taken to King Xerxes at the royal palace in early winter of the seventh year of his reign.
And the king loved Esther more than any of the other young women. He was so delighted with her that he set the royal crown on her head and declared her queen instead of Vashti.
To celebrate the occasion, he gave a great banquet in Esther’s honor for all his nobles and officials, declaring a public holiday for the provinces and giving generous gifts to everyone.
Even after all the young women had been transferred to the second harem and Mordecai had become a palace official,
Esther continued to keep her family background and nationality a secret. She was still following Mordecai’s directions, just as she did when she lived in his home.

One day as Mordecai was on duty at the king’s gate, two of the king’s eunuchs, Bigthana and Teresh—who were guards at the door of the king’s private quarters—became angry at King Xerxes and plotted to assassinate him.
But Mordecai heard about the plot and gave the information to Queen Esther. She then told the king about it and gave Mordecai credit for the report.
When an investigation was made and Mordecai’s story was found to be true, the two men were impaled on a sharpened pole. This was all recorded in The Book of the History of King Xerxes’ Reign.
That night the king had trouble sleeping, so he ordered an attendant to bring the book of the history of his reign so it could be read to him.

In those records he discovered an account of how Mordecai had exposed the plot of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the eunuchs who guarded the door to the king’s private quarters. They had plotted to assassinate King Xerxes.
“What reward or recognition did we ever give Mordecai for this?” the king asked.
“Who is that in the outer court?” the king inquired. As it happened, Haman had just arrived in the outer court of the palace to ask the king to impale Mordecai on the pole he had prepared.
So the attendants replied to the king, “Haman is out in the court.”
So Haman came in, and the king said, “What should I do to honor a man who truly pleases me?”
So he replied, “If the king wishes to honor someone,
he should bring out one of the king’s own royal robes, as well as a horse that the king himself has ridden—one with a royal emblem on its head.

Let the robes and the horse be handed over to one of the king’s most noble officials. And let him see that the man whom the king wishes to honor is dressed in the king’s robes and led through the city square on the king’s horse. Have the official shout as they go, ‘This is what the king does for someone he wishes to honor!’”
“Excellent!” the king said to Haman. “Quick! Take the robes and my horse, and do just as you have said for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the gate of the palace. Leave out nothing you have suggested!”
So Haman took the robes and put them on Mordecai, placed him on the king’s own horse, and led him through the city square, shouting, “This is what the king does for someone he wishes to honor!”
Afterward Mordecai returned to the palace gate, but Haman hurried home dejected and completely humiliated.

When Haman told his wife, Zeresh, and all his friends what had happened, his wise advisers and his wife said, “Since Mordecai—this man who has humiliated you—is of Jewish birth, you will never succeed in your plans against him. It will be fatal to continue opposing him.”
While they were still talking, the king’s eunuchs arrived and quickly took Haman to the banquet Esther had prepared.
So the king and Haman went to Queen Esther’s banquet.

On this second occasion, while they were drinking wine, the king again said to Esther, “Tell me what you want, Queen Esther. What is your request? I will give it to you, even if it is half the kingdom!”
Queen Esther replied, “If I have found favor with the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my request, I ask that my life and the lives of my people will be spared.

For my people and I have been sold to those who would kill, slaughter, and annihilate us. If we had merely been sold as slaves, I could remain quiet, for that would be too trivial a matter to warrant disturbing the king.”
“Who would do such a thing?” King Xerxes demanded. “Who would be so presumptuous as to touch you?”
Esther replied, “This wicked Haman is our adversary and our enemy.” Haman grew pale with fright before the king and queen.
Then the king jumped to his feet in a rage and went out into the palace garden.
In despair he fell on the couch where Queen Esther was reclining, just as the king was returning from the palace garden.

Then Harbona, one of the king’s eunuchs, said, “Haman has set up a sharpened pole that stands seventy-five feet tall in his own courtyard. He intended to use it to impale Mordecai, the man who saved the king from assassination.”
So they impaled Haman on the pole he had set up for Mordecai, and the king’s anger subsided.

So on March 7 the two decrees of the king were put into effect. On that day, the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them, but quite the opposite happened. It was the Jews who overpowered their enemies.
The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the king’s provinces to attack anyone who tried to harm them. But no one could make a stand against them, for everyone was afraid of them.
And all the nobles of the provinces, the highest officers, the governors, and the royal officials helped the Jews for fear of Mordecai.
For Mordecai had been promoted in the king’s palace, and his fame spread throughout all the provinces as he became more and more powerful.
So the Jews went ahead on the appointed day and struck down their enemies with the sword. They killed and annihilated their enemies and did as they pleased with those who hated them.
In the fortress of Susa itself, the Jews killed 500 men.
They also killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha—
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. But they did not take any plunder.
That very day, when the king was informed of the number of people killed in the fortress of Susa,

he called for Queen Esther. He said, “The Jews have killed 500 men in the fortress of Susa alone, as well as Haman’s ten sons. If they have done that here, what has happened in the rest of the provinces? But now, what more do you want? It will be granted to you; tell me and I will do it.”
Esther responded, “If it please the king, give the Jews in Susa permission to do again tomorrow as they have done today, and let the bodies of Haman’s ten sons be impaled on a pole.”
So the king agreed, and the decree was announced in Susa. And they impaled the bodies of Haman’s ten sons.
Then the Jews at Susa gathered together on March 8 and killed 300 more men, and again they took no plunder.

Meanwhile, the other Jews throughout the king’s provinces had gathered together to defend their lives. They gained relief from all their enemies, killing 75,000 of those who hated them. But they did not take any plunder.
This was done throughout the provinces on March 7, and on March 8 they rested, celebrating their victory with a day of feasting and gladness.
(The Jews at Susa killed their enemies on March 7 and again on March 8, then rested on March 9, making that their day of feasting and gladness.)
So to this day, rural Jews living in remote villages celebrate an annual festival and holiday on the appointed day in late winter, when they rejoice and send gifts of food to each other.
Mordecai recorded these events and sent letters to the Jews near and far, throughout all the provinces of King Xerxes,
calling on them to celebrate an annual festival on these two days.

He told them to celebrate these days with feasting and gladness and by giving gifts of food to each other and presents to the poor. This would commemorate a time when the Jews gained relief from their enemies, when their sorrow was turned into gladness and their mourning into joy.
So the Jews accepted Mordecai’s proposal and adopted this annual custom.
Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews, had plotted to crush and destroy them on the date determined by casting lots (the lots were called purim).
But when Esther came before the king, he issued a decree causing Haman’s evil plot to backfire, and Haman and his sons were impaled on a sharpened pole.
That is why this celebration is called Purim, because it is the ancient word for casting lots.

the Jews throughout the realm agreed to inaugurate this tradition and to pass it on to their descendants and to all who became Jews. They declared they would never fail to celebrate these two prescribed days at the appointed time each year.

These days would be remembered and kept from generation to generation and celebrated by every family throughout the provinces and cities of the empire. This Festival of Purim would never cease to be celebrated among the Jews, nor would the memory of what happened ever die out among their descendants.
Then Queen Esther, the daughter of Abihail, along with Mordecai the Jew, wrote another letter putting the queen’s full authority behind Mordecai’s letter to establish the Festival of Purim.
Letters wishing peace and security were sent to the Jews throughout the 127 provinces of the empire of Xerxes.

These letters established the Festival of Purim—an annual celebration of these days at the appointed time, decreed by both Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther. (The people decided to observe this festival, just as they had decided for themselves and their descendants to establish the times of fasting and mourning.)
So the command of Esther confirmed the practices of Purim, and it was all written down in the records.
Love justice, you rulers of the earth.
for he is found by those who trust him,
Dishonest thinking separates people from God.
Wisdom will not enter an evil person,
Someone with a disciplined, holy spirit will flee from deceit,
Wisdom is a spirit that is kind to humanity,
The Spirit of the Lord fills the whole world;
Therefore, those who speak unjustly cannot escape notice.
The thoughts of the ungodly will be carefully examined;
His jealous ear hears all things;
So be sure you don’t engage in pointless grumbling,
Do not court death by living a life of error;
God did not make death,
He created all things so that they could exist,
for righteousness is immortal.
But the wicked invite death by their deeds and words.
The wicked have reached this irrational conclusion:
We are born by chance,
When that spark is extinguished, it will leave the body in ashes;
In time even our name will be forgotten,
For our days are but the passing of a shadow,
“Come, then, let’s enjoy the good things around us
Let’s take our fill of costly wines and perfumes;
Let’s crown ourselves with rosebuds before they wilt;
let’s stop in every meadow for joyous play.
“Let’s oppress the righteous poor man
Let’s consider our might to be right,
Let’s lie in wait for righteous people,
They claim to know God
They tell us our thoughts are sinful;
They are not like other people;
They regard us as insignificant
Let’s see then if their words are true;
If the righteous are the children of God,
Let’s insult and torture them;
Let’s condemn them to a most shameful death,
They reasoned this way, but they were deceived,
They did not know the secret plan of God.
For God created people to be immortal;
But because of the envy of the Devil,
But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God,
In the eyes of the foolish, the righteous appear to die;
They seem to be on their way to destruction,
And though they appear to suffer punishment,
The righteous may suffer a little in this life,
He has tried them like gold purified by fire
In their time of judgment, the righteous will shine;
They will govern nations and rule over people,
Those who trust in the Lord will understand truth,
But the wicked will be punished as their thoughts deserve,
Those who reject wisdom and instruction are miserable;
Their wives are foolish,
God blesses the childless woman who remains pure,
God also blesses the eunuch whose hands have done no wrong,
For everyone knows that good labor yields good fruit,
But the children of adulterers will not reach maturity;
Even if they live long, they will not be esteemed;
And if they die young, they will have no hope
for harsh is the end of a wicked generation.
It is better to be childless
When virtue is present, people imitate it,
The numerous offspring of the ungodly will not thrive;
They may flourish for a time,
The young branches will be broken off,
For children who are born of sinful relationships
But the righteous, though they may die young,
Honor is not gained merely by a long life,
but understanding comes with gray hair,
Once such a man pleased God and was loved by him.
He was taken away so evil could not undermine his judgment
For fascination with wickedness obscures what is truly good,
He was made perfect in his few short years,
Since his soul pleased the Lord,
Yet the people saw this and did not understand it;
The righteous who have died
The unjust will see the end of the wise,
The unjust will see them and despise them,
They will become dishonored corpses;
They will be filled with dread when their sins are recounted,
Then the righteous will stand up with great confidence
Those who see the righteous will tremble with terrible fear
They will speak to each other with words of repentance.
“These are the people we once derided!
Look, now they are regarded as children of God.
We were the ones who strayed from the truth.
We took all the paths of wickedness and destruction
“But how has our pride helped us?
All those things have passed away like a shadow
They have vanished like a ship passing through the waves,
They are like a bird flying through the air,
They are like an arrow shot at a target.
So it is with us; we die almost as soon as we are born.
The hope of the wicked is like thistledown blown by the wind
But the righteous will live forever,

It is also the same for the blacksmith who sits by the anvil,
It is also the same for the potter, who sits at his work,
He fashions the clay with his hands
All these people rely on their hands,
Without them a city could not be inhabited,
Yet they are not chosen for the council of the people
But they sustain the structure of society,
How different it is for the one who devotes himself
He is careful to remember the sayings of the famous,
He searches out the hidden meanings of proverbs
His services are employed by the great,
He determines to rise early
If it pleases the great Lord,
The Lord will direct his counsel and his knowledge
He will display the wisdom he has gained
Many will praise his understanding,
Nations will declare his wisdom,
If he lives long, he will leave a name that surpasses a thousand;
I, Sirach, have yet more on my mind to express,
Listen to me, my faithful children, and blossom
Give off fragrance like frankincense,
Give glory to his name;
“All the works of the Lord are very good,
You must not say, ‘What is this?’ or ‘Why is that?’—
When he commands, his will is carried out entirely,
He sees what everyone does,
He sees everything throughout all eternity,
You must not say, ‘What is this?’ or ‘Why is that?’—
“The Lord’s blessing overflows like a river
His anger drives out the nations
To the faithful, his journey is smooth,
From the beginning, good things were created for good people,
The basic necessities of life
All these things are good for the godly,
“Some winds are created for vengeance,
Fire, hail, famine, and disease—
So also the fangs of wild animals, scorpions, and serpents,
These things delight in doing the Lord’s bidding,
I, Sirach, have been sure of all this from the beginning;
All the works of the Lord are good,
No one can say, “This is not as good as that,”
So now sing praise with all your heart and voice,
Hard work was created for everyone,
They are filled with thoughts and fears of the heart
From the one who sits on a glorious throne
from the one who wears a purple robe and a crown
And when such people rest in bed,
They get little or no rest,
The instant they reach safety, they wake up
For all creatures, both human and animal—
come death and bloodshed, quarrels and war,
All these were created for the wicked,
All that is from the earth returns to the earth,
All bribery and injustice will be blotted out,
The riches of the unjust will dry up like a seasonal brook
A generous person will rejoice,
The children of sinners put forth few branches.
The reeds growing along any riverbank
But kindness is like a garden of blessings,
Wealth and wages can make life sweet,
A person’s name is established through children and through building a city,
Wine and music cheer the heart,
The flute and the harp make a sweet melody,
The eye seeks grace and beauty,
A friend or companion is always welcome,
Family and friends are for times of trouble,
Gold and silver give a person security,
Wealth and strength make a person confident,
The fear of the Lord is like a garden of blessing;
My child, do not live like a beggar,
When people must depend on another for food,
For the shameless, begging is sweet in the mouth,
O death, how bitter is the reminder of you
O death, how welcome your sentence is
Do not fear the sentence of death.
This sentence is from the Lord to everyone.
The children of sinners are detestable,
The inheritance of sinners’ children will perish,
Children will blame their ungodly father,
How terrible it will be for you ungodly,
When you were born, you were born under a curse;
All things from the earth return to the earth;
Physical death brings grief,
Be careful of your reputation, for it will live on after you.
The actual life span of a good person is limited,
My children, be true to your upbringing and be at peace,
Better are those who hide their foolishness
Therefore, show respect for what I say,
Be ashamed of sexual immorality before your father or mother
of a crime before a judge or official;
of dishonest dealings before a partner or friend;
Be ashamed of breaking an oath or covenant
of receiving or giving ungraciously;
of looking at a prostitute;
of taking away someone’s inheritance or gift;
Be ashamed of making advances toward a man’s servant girl;
Be ashamed of reprimanding friends,
Be ashamed of repeating what you have heard
Then you will display a proper sense of shame
Don’t sin to maintain your dignity,
of the law of the Most High and of his covenant;
of sharing expenses with partners and fellow travelers;
of using accurate scales and weights;
of making profit from trade;
Bolting the door is wise when you have an untrustworthy wife.
Keep careful records of your deposits,
Do not be ashamed to correct the ignorant and foolish
A daughter causes her father unspoken anxiety,
While she is a virgin, her father worries that she may be seduced
Keep strict watch over a headstrong daughter,
Don’t let her display her beauty to any man,
For as from clothes comes the moth,
The wickedness of a man is better than the goodness of a woman.
I will now recall the works of the Lord
The sun shines down on all things,
Not even the holy ones were empowered by the Lord
He searches out the watery depths and the human heart,
He discloses the past and the future
No thought escapes his notice,
He has set in order the glorious works of his wisdom,
How desirable are all the Lord’s works,
All these things live and remain forever,
All things come in pairs, one opposite the other,
Each adds to the good things of another.
The clear firmament of the sky is the pride of the higher realms.
The rising sun testifies
At noon it parches the land.
A person must tend a furnace to get any heat,
Great is the Lord who made it,
He created the moon to mark the seasons.
The moon sets apart the days for festivals.
The month is named after the moon.
The glory of the stars makes the heavens beautiful;
They stand in their appointed places, just as the Holy One has ordered them,
Look at the rainbow, and praise him who made it;
It spans the heavens with its glorious arc.
By his command he sends snowstorms
The storehouses of heaven are opened at his command as well,
By his greatness he gives the clouds their strength,
At his sight the mountains shake,
The noise of his thunder causes the earth to recoil,
The eye admires the beauty of snow’s whiteness,
The Most High pours frost upon the earth like salt,
The cold north wind blows,
The Most High levels the mountains, burns up the wilderness,
Then a cloud soon heals everything,
By his design the Most High calmed the watery depths
When those who sail on the sea tell of its dangers,
The sea contains strange and amazing creatures,
It is by the Most High that each messenger reaches his destination,
We could say more but could never say enough.
Where can we find the ability to praise him?
The Lord is awesome and very great,
Glorify the Lord as much as you can,
Who has seen him and can describe him?
Many things greater than these lie hidden from us,
The Lord has made all things,
Let us now praise famous men,
The Lord has created great glory,
There were those who ruled in their kingdoms;
Some led the people by advising them
Some composed musical tunes
Others were rich and powerful,
All these men gained glory in their generations;
Some of them have left behind a famous name,
But others are not remembered at all;
But these were godly men,
Their wealth will remain in the family,
Their children have kept the covenants,
Their line of descendants will continue forever,
Their bodies are buried in peace,
The people tell about their wisdom,
Enoch pleased the Lord and was taken up to heaven
Noah was found perfect and righteous.
Everlasting covenants were made with him
Abraham was the great father of many nations,
He obeyed the law of the Most High
Therefore, the Lord promised him with an oath
He gave Isaac the same assurance
He confirmed Jacob’s position by blessing him,
From Jacob’s descendants the Lord brought forth a godly man,
The Lord made Moses’ glory equal to that of the holy ones.
With his words Moses put a stop to the miracles of others,
Because of Moses’ faithfulness and meekness, the Lord set him apart as holy,
The Lord allowed him to hear his voice
The Lord exalted Aaron, a holy man like Moses.
The Lord made an everlasting covenant with Aaron,
He clothed him with majestic attire
The Lord encircled Aaron’s attire with pomegranates,
He gave Aaron a sacred garment of gold, blue, and purple,
with twisted scarlet, the work of an artisan.
The Lord also gave Aaron a gold crown to put over his turban.
Before Aaron’s time none of these beautiful things existed,
Aaron’s sacrifices were to be completely consumed with fire,
Moses ordained Aaron
The Lord chose Aaron out of all the living
The Lord entrusted Aaron with his commandments
Strangers conspired against Aaron
The Lord saw their actions and was displeased,
He increased Aaron’s glory
For the priests eat the sacrifices of the Lord,
But Aaron did not receive any of the land as an inheritance.
Phinehas son of Eleazar ranks third in glory
Therefore, the Lord made a covenant of peace with him.
In the covenant that was given to David,
May the Lord grant you wisdom of mind
Joshua was mighty in war.
How glorious he was when he raised his arm
Before Joshua’s time, who ever stood so firmly?
Wasn’t he the one through whom the sun stood still
He called upon the Most High, the Mighty One,
Joshua overwhelmed that nation in battle.
and he showed his allegiance in the days of Moses.
These two alone were spared
The Lord gave strength to Caleb,
He did this so the Israelites might see
Let us also consider all the judges with their respective names,
May their bones, wherever they lie, give life to others,
Samuel was beloved by his Lord,
By the law of the Lord he judged the people,
His faithfulness proved that he was a prophet,
He called upon the Lord, the Mighty One,
Then the Lord thundered from heaven
Samuel conquered the leaders of Tyre
Before he died he proclaimed
Even after Samuel died, he prophesied,
Then Nathan came along
As the fat is set aside in preparing a peace offering,
He played with lions, as though they were young goats,
When David was young, did he not kill a giant
David called upon the Lord Most High,
They glorified him for the tens of thousands he had conquered
David annihilated his enemies on every side.
In all that he did David gave thanks,
David stationed singers before the altar
He gave fitting dignity to the festivals
The Lord removed David’s sins
After David, a wise son came along
Solomon reigned in an age of peace
O Solomon, how wise you were when you were young!
Your understanding spread throughout the earth;
Your fame spread to distant islands,
Your answers astounded the nations,
In the name of the Lord God,
But you brought in women to sleep with
You stained your honor
You caused the kingdom to be divided.
But the Lord will never cease to be merciful
Solomon died
Their sins piled up more and more
For they explored every kind of evil
Then Elijah the prophet arose like a fire,
He brought a famine upon Israel,
By the word of the Lord he held back the rain
How glorious your amazing deeds made you, Elijah!
You raised a corpse from death
You brought down kings to destruction
You heard rebuke at Mount Sinai
You anointed kings to mete out retribution
You were taken up in a whirlwind of fire,
The Scriptures say that you are to come at the appointed time
Blessed are they who saw you
When Elijah was enveloped in the whirlwind,
Nothing was too difficult for him,
During his lifetime, Elisha performed wonders,
Despite all this the people did not repent.
Some of them did what was right,
Hezekiah fortified his city
During Hezekiah’s reign Sennacherib invaded the country.
The hearts of the people were shaken, and their hands trembled.
But they called upon the Lord, who is merciful,
The Lord attacked the army of the Assyrians,
For Hezekiah did what pleased the Lord
During Isaiah’s time the sun went backward,
Empowered by the Spirit, he saw the future
He showed what would happen until the end of time
The memories of Josiah are like blended incense
He did the right thing by reforming the people
He kept his heart directed toward the Lord,
Except for David, Hezekiah, and Josiah,
They gave their power to others
These nations burned Jerusalem, the chosen city of the sanctuary.
For they had mistreated Jeremiah,
Ezekiel saw the vision of glory,
For the Lord remembered his enemies and sent a storm,
May the bones of the twelve prophets
How will we praise Zerubbabel?
and so was Jeshua son of Jehozadak.
Nehemiah is often remembered
No one on earth has ever been created who was comparable to Enoch,
Nor has anyone like Joseph ever been born.
Shem and Seth were honored among people,
Simon the high priest, the son of Onias,
He laid the foundations for the high double walls,
During Simon’s time a water cistern was dug,
He devised a plan to save his people from destruction
How glorious Simon was when the people would surround him
He shone like the morning star among the clouds,
He was like the sun when it shines on the Temple of the Most High,
He was like roses in the springtime,
Simon was like fire and incense in the censer,
He was like an olive tree weighed down with fruit,
When he put on his glorious robe
When he received the sacrifices from the priests
All the sons of Aaron in their glory
When Simon finished the service at the altar,
Simon would reach out to receive the cup
Then the sons of Aaron would shout
Then all the people would quickly
Then the singers would praise him with their voices,
The people of the Lord Most High would offer
Then Simon would come down and raise his hands
The people would bow down again to worship
Now bless the God of all,
May he grant us joyfulness of heart,
May he confirm his mercy toward us
There are two nations my soul abhors
those who live in Edom and Philistia
I, Jeshua son of Eleazar
Blessed are those who ponder these things,
For if they put them into practice, they will be equal to any task,
I give thanks to you, O Lord and King,
for you have been my protector and helper.
you have been my helper and rescued me.
You rescued me from the choking flames that surrounded me,
from deep in the belly of Hades,
My soul was approaching death;
My enemies surrounded me on every side,
Then I remembered your mercy, O Lord,
I called out in prayer from the earth.
I cried, “Lord, you are my Father.
I will praise your name continually
You saved me from destruction
When I was still young, before I had traveled much,
At the Temple I prayed to receive her,
My heart delighted in wisdom
I made some effort to listen and received wisdom.
I have advanced in wisdom;
For I have determined to live according to wisdom.
My soul has fought to possess wisdom,
I directed my soul toward wisdom,
My heart was stirred to seek her;
The Lord has rewarded me with things to say,
Draw near to me, you unlearned,
Why do you complain of lacking these things,
I have declared,
Submit your neck to wisdom’s yoke,
See with your own eyes how I have not worked hard
Acquire instruction with a large sum of silver,
May your soul rejoice in the Lord’s mercy,
Do your work before the assigned time,
These are the words that Baruch son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, son of Zedekiah, son of Hasadiah, son of Hilkiah, wrote in Babylon.
He wrote it on the seventh day of the month during the fifth year after the Babylonians captured Jerusalem and destroyed it by fire.
Baruch read this book to Jehoiachin son of Jehoiakim, the king of Judah, and to all the people who came to hear it.
He also read it to the nobles, the princes of Judah, the elders, and everyone else, from the least to the greatest, who lived in Babylon by the Sud River.
When the people heard what Baruch wrote, they wept, fasted, and prayed to the Lord.
Then they collected all the money they could afford to give
and sent it to Jerusalem to the high priest, Jehoiakim son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum, and to the other priests, and to all the Jews who were still with them in Jerusalem.

At about this time in early summer, Baruch recovered the silver utensils that had been looted from the Temple, in order to return them to the land of Judah. Zedekiah son of Josiah, the king of Judah, had made these silver utensils
after Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, had deported Jehoiachin, the princes, the skilled workers, the nobles, and other people from Jerusalem and had taken them as captives to Babylon.
They sent this message to the people in Jerusalem:
Pray for the health of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon and for his son Belshazzar so that their days on earth may last as long as heaven itself lasts.
And pray that the Lord will give us strength and wisdom as we live under the protective shadow of King Nebuchadnezzar and his son Belshazzar. May we serve them for a long time and win their favor.
Also, pray to the Lord our God for us, for we have sinned against him, and even to this day the anger of the Lord has not turned away from us.
Finally, we send you this book to read aloud as your confession in the Lord’s Temple during the special feasts and sacred festivals.
“This is what you will say: Lord, you are in the right, and our faces are covered with shame. This is true of us all, including the people of Judah and Jerusalem,
our kings, our rulers, our priests, our prophets, and our ancestors.
We have sinned before the Lord.
We have not obeyed him, nor have we listened to the voice of the Lord our God, nor kept the commandments that the Lord gave us.
From the day the Lord brought our ancestors out of Egypt until today, we have disobeyed the Lord our God. We have acted thoughtlessly and have not listened to his voice.
So to this day we have experienced many disasters as well as the curses spoken by the Lord when his servant Moses brought our ancestors out of Egypt into a land flowing with milk and honey.
Despite all the warnings of the prophets he sent us, we have not listened to the voice of the Lord our God.
We have each followed the inclinations of our own wicked heart, serving other gods and doing evil in the sight of the Lord our God.
“As a result, the Lord has carried out his threat on our kings, our rulers, and each person of Israel and Judah.
As it is written in the law of Moses, the atrocities we experienced in Jerusalem have never before been witnessed under heaven.
Some people even ate the flesh of their own sons and daughters.
God allowed us to be captured by the kingdoms around us. Our land became a desert, and we were scorned by the surrounding nations where the Lord has scattered us.
Instead of being exalted, we were humiliated because we sinned against the Lord our God by not obeying what he said.
“Even now the Lord our God is in the right, and our faces are covered with shame, just like our ancestors.
All the disasters that the Lord threatened have happened to us.
Yet we have not renounced our wicked thoughts to win back the favor of the Lord our God.
The Lord has kept the disasters ready for just the right moment and then allowed them to fall on us. But we deserved them, for the Lord is just in all that he has commanded us to do.
We have not listened to his voice, nor have we obeyed the commandments he gave us.
“O Lord God of Israel, you brought your people out of Egypt with amazing power, miraculous signs and wonders, and overwhelming terror. Because of this, you have brought lasting honor to your name.
Now we acknowledge that we have sinned by being ungodly and doing wrong; we have disobeyed all your commands, O Lord our God.
But please let your anger turn away from us, for we are but a small group among the nations where you have scattered us.
Hear our prayers and petitions, O Lord. Deliver us for your own sake, and grant us favor with those who have taken us as captives.
Then the whole world will know that you are the Lord our God, for Israel and his descendants bear your name.
Look down upon us from your holy dwelling place, O Lord; think of us and hear us.
Open your eyes and look at us. Those who are dead, whose spirits have been taken from their bodies, cannot give glory and recognition to the Lord.

But the person who is deeply sorrowful, who walks bowed down, who is feeble and has failing eyes, and who has spiritual hunger—such a person gives glory to the Lord and acknowledges his righteousness.
“It is not because of the merits of our ancestors or kings that we pour out our prayers and beg your mercy, O Lord our God,
for you have punished us because of your anger and indignation with us. You revealed this through your servants the prophets, who told us,
‘This message is from the Lord: If you work hard and serve the king of Babylon, you will remain in the land I promised to your ancestors.
But if you do not listen to the voice of the Lord and do not serve the king of Babylon,

I will remove all happy and joyful voices from the towns of Judah and from those surrounding Jerusalem. I will silence the voice of the bridegroom and the bride, and the land will become a desert with no people living in it.’

“But we did not listen to your command that we should serve the king of Babylon. As a result, you carried out what you had threatened through your servants the prophets. The bones of our rulers and our ancestors have been scattered from their tombs, as you said.
Indeed, they have been thrown out into the heat of the day and the frost of the night. People have died in severe pain by famine, by sword, and by plague.
Because of the wickedness of the people of Israel and Judah, you have humbled your Temple and left it as it is today.
“And yet, O Lord our God, you have dealt with us according to your kindness and great mercy.
Everything has happened exactly as you warned us when you commanded your servant Moses to write your law in the presence of the people of Israel.
This law says, ‘If you do not obey my voice, this great multitude will be turned into a very small number among the nations where I will scatter them.
But I know they will not listen to me, for they are stubborn. In their exile they will finally come to their senses,
and then they will realize that I am the Lord their God. I will give them an understanding heart and an attentive ear.
Then they will praise me in the land of their captivity and will recall my name.
Remembering the sins of their ancestors, they will turn away from their own wickedness and stubborn ways.
Then I will bring them back again to the land that I promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and they will rule over it. Their numbers will not grow smaller, for I will increase their population.
I will make an everlasting covenant with them to be their God, and they will be my people. I will never again remove my people Israel out of the land that I have given them.’
“And now, O Lord Almighty, God of Israel, our souls are in pain. With troubled spirits, we cry out to you.
Listen, O Lord, and have mercy on us who have sinned against you.
You will reign forever, but we will remain dead forever.

O Lord Almighty, God of Israel, hear the prayer of those who have died in Israel and of their children, who have sinned against you. They failed to listen to the voice of the Lord their God, and so disaster fell upon us.
Do not dwell on the sins of our ancestors, but for now think only of your power and your name.
You are the Lord our God, and we will praise you, O Lord.
For you have caused us to fear you so that we will call upon your name. We praise you in our captivity, for we have turned from the evil of our ancestors, who sinned against you.
Look at us today in our land of exile, where you have scattered us to be reproached, cursed, and punished for all the sins of our ancestors who deserted you, O Lord our God.”
Listen, O Israel, to the commandments of life;
How did it happen, O Israel,
You are defiled with the dead;
It is because you have abandoned the fountain of wisdom.
If you had walked in the way of God,
Learn where understanding resides,
Who has discovered wisdom’s dwelling place?
Where are the leaders of the nations?
and entertain themselves with birds?
Where are the careful craftsmen of silver?
They have vanished into the place of the dead,
Generations have seen the light of day
They do not know the path,
Wisdom has not been heard of in Canaan;
The descendants of Hagar search after worldly wisdom,
O Israel, how great is the world God created;
It is great and has no end;
In it were born giants,
Yet God did not choose them,
And because they did not have wisdom,
Who has gone up into heaven and seized wisdom?
Who has sailed across the sea and found her?
No one can know the way to wisdom
But God, who knows all, knows her;
He sends forth the light, and it speeds away.
The stars shine joyfully in their appointed places.
When he calls to them, they reply: “Here we are!”
This is our God,
He who holds all knowledge
Then wisdom came to earth
Wisdom is the book of God’s commandments,
Come back, O Jacob, and take hold of wisdom;
Do not give your honor to another,
We rejoice, O Israel,
Take courage, my people,
It was not for your destruction
You angered your Creator
You have forgotten the eternal God, who brought you up,
For Jerusalem saw the wrath of God that came upon you,
for I have seen my sons and daughters being taken captive.
I nourished them with joy,
Let no one rejoice over me, a widow
They have not heeded his laws
Let those who live near Zion come
For he brought a distant nation against them,
They carried away the widow’s beloved sons
“But as for my part, what help can I give you?
Only he who allowed you to suffer these disasters
Go your way, my children, go your way,
I have taken off the robe of peace
“Take courage, my children, and cry out to God.
For I have put my hope in the Eternal One to save you.
Although I sent you away with mourning and weeping,
For as those who live near Zion have seen your captivity,
My children, endure patiently the punishment
My tender children have walked rough paths,
“Take courage, my children, and cry out to God,
Just you chose to stray from God,
For he who allowed you to suffer these disasters
Take courage, O Jerusalem,
Misery will come to those who have harmed you
Misery will come to the cities that enslaved your children,
Just as they rejoiced at your fall
I will rob them of their pride in their great numbers,
Fire from the Eternal One will fall on them for many days,
Look to the east, O Jerusalem,
Look! The children you sent away are now returning,
O Jerusalem, take off the garment of your sadness and pain.
Wrap the cloak of God’s righteousness around you,
For God will reveal your splendor
God will give you a name that will last forever:
Arise, Jerusalem! Go to a high point
Although they left you on foot,
For God has ordered the leveling of every high mountain
The forests and every fragrant tree
For God will lead Israel with joy,
This is a copy of the letter that Jeremiah sent to those who were to be taken to Babylon as captives by the king of the Babylonians. Jeremiah gave them the message that God had given him.
You will have to spend many years in Babylon—as much as seven generations. After that captivity, I, the Lord, will bring you home in peace.
In Babylon you will see gods of silver, gold, and wood—gods that are carried about on people’s shoulders and that cause other nations to fear.
Be careful that you do not imitate these pagan acts, and do not become fearful of pagan gods.
When you see crowds carrying the images in a procession and worshiping them, you must say in your hearts, ‘O Lord, we must worship you alone.’
For my angel is with you, and he will watch over your lives.
“The pagan gods are overlaid with gold and silver, and their tongues are polished by woodcarvers, but they are fake and cannot speak.
The people make gold crowns for their gods as if they were dressing up a girl who loves fancy clothing.
Sometimes the priests steal the gold and silver for themselves
or give it to the temple prostitutes. They put clothes on these gods of gold, silver, and wood as if they were human.
Yet these gods, dressed in purple robes, cannot protect themselves from tarnish or decay.
Even the temple dust needs to be cleaned from their faces.
One god holds a scepter, like a district judge, yet it is powerless to condemn an offender to death.
Another holds a sword or an ax in its hand but cannot protect itself from war or thieves. Therefore, it is evident that they are not gods, so do not fear them.
“Just as a pot becomes worthless when it is broken,
so these gods are worthless as they sit in their temples. Their eyes are full of dust kicked up by the feet of those who enter the temple.
A person who is awaiting execution for offending the king must be securely locked up. In the same way, the priests must secure their temples with bars and locks, lest their gods be taken by thieves.
The priests light more lamps than they themselves would ever need, but their gods cannot see the light.
The gods are like the wooden beams in the temple, for termites eat out their hearts from within. Even their garments are devoured, but the gods do not even notice.
Their faces are black from the smoke that rises in the temple.
Bats, swallows, and other birds perch on their bodies and heads, and so do cats.
All this is evidence that they are not gods, so do not fear them.
“They may be adorned with gold, but unless someone cleans off the tarnish, they will not shine. And they felt nothing when they were being molded.
Even though they cost much money, there is no spirit in them.
Because they cannot walk, they must be carried on people’s shoulders, which proves how worthless they are. People who worship them are put to shame,
for if these idols topple over, their worshipers must stand them up again. And even when they are set upright, they cannot move. Offering gifts to them is like offering gifts to the dead.

Everything offered as a sacrifice to these idols is taken by the priests for their own use. The wives of the priests take their share of the food, storing it for later use, but they never give even part of it to the poor or the helpless.
Even women who are ceremonially unclean because of menstruation or childbirth handle the sacrifices. Thus you can see that they are not gods; do not fear them.
“How can they even be called gods? They allow women to place offerings before these idols made of silver, gold, and wood!
The priests sit in their temples with torn clothing, with heads and beards shaved, and with their heads uncovered!
The priests moan and shriek before their gods as if they were wailing for a dead person at a funeral.
The priests even take the clothing of the idols to give to their wives and children.
And whether these gods are treated well or poorly, they cannot repay in kind. They don’t have the power to appoint a king or to depose him.
Likewise, they cannot give wealth or money to anyone. If someone makes a vow to them and does not keep it, these idols cannot hold that person accountable.
They cannot prevent a person from dying or protect the weak from the strong.
They cannot restore sight to the blind or rescue a person in distress.
They cannot show concern for widows or help orphans.
These wooden idols that are overlaid with gold and silver are as powerless as a block of stone from a mountain quarry! Anyone who worships idols will be put to shame.
So how can anyone claim, or even think, that such idols are gods?
“Even the Babylonians themselves dishonor them. When they find a person who cannot speak, they present him to Bel, asking him for the gift of speech, as though Bel understands them!
Yet the people fail to understand the contradiction, for they have no common sense. So they do not abandon these gods.
Women sit in their roped-off area along the passageways, burning grain as incense.
And when one of them is selected by a man to sleep with him, she mocks the women next to her who are less attractive and were not selected.
Everything that takes place around these idols is false. So how can anyone claim, or even think, that these idols are gods?
“Made by carvers and goldsmiths, these idols can be only what the artisans want them to be.
And the very craftsmen who make them don’t live very long themselves. So how can the things made by mortals be gods?
The only legacy they leave is lies and disgrace.
If war comes or a disaster occurs, the priests discuss where they can hide with their gods.
How can anyone think these idols are gods when they cannot even save themselves from war or disaster?

Considering that they are only wood covered with gold or silver, it will become obvious that they are not gods; every nation and king will realize that they are merely human creations without any divine power in them.
Don’t the people realize that these idols are not gods?
“These idols cannot appoint a king or send rain to people.
They cannot regulate their own affairs or vindicate someone who has been wronged. They are as useless as crows that fly across the sky.
If fire breaks out in the temple of these gods made of wood and covered with gold or silver, their priests run to safety, but the gods burn up like the temple beams.
They cannot stop an enemy king and his armies.
So why should anyone say, or even think, that they are gods?
Those who steal the gold and silver and clothing of the idols are not stopped, for the gods are helpless.

Therefore, it is better to be a king who shows his courage, or even a kitchen pot that is used by its owner, than to be one of these false gods. It is even better to be a door that protects a house or a wooden pillar in a palace than to be one of these false gods.
The sun, moon, and stars shine brightly, fulfilling the purpose for which God made them.
Lightning flashes across the sky and is seen by many people. The winds blow in every land.
The clouds obey God’s orders to float over all the earth.
Fire falls from the sky and burns up mountainsides and woods, just as it is commanded to do. But idols cannot compare to such glory or power.
So no one should think or say these idols are gods, for they cannot decide a case or do any good to anyone.
Since you know then that these idols are not gods, do not fear them.
“They can neither curse kings nor bless them.
They cannot produce signs in the heavens for nations to see. They neither shine like the sun nor give light like the moon.
Wild animals are better off than idols because they can flee to shelter and take care of themselves.
No one can produce evidence that they are gods, so do not fear them.
“These wooden gods, overlaid with silver and gold, are as powerless as a scarecrow in a cucumber patch.
They are no better than a thornbush in a garden—which birds perch on anyway! These wooden gods, overlaid with gold and silver, are like a corpse thrown out into the darkness.

The purple robes and silk garments rot as they hang upon the idols, so you can tell that these idols are not gods. In the end they themselves will be destroyed as well and will become a disgrace to their country.
Therefore, it is better to be an upright person who has no idols; such a person will never be in danger of disgrace.”
Alexander the Macedonian, the son of Philip, was king of Greece. Alexander marched from the land of Greece and conquered Darius, king of the Persians and Medes, and became king in his place.
He fought in many campaigns, captured many fortresses, and put the local kings to death.
He campaigned throughout the known world, plundering the nations, and all the nations of the world submitted to him. Alexander’s heart was filled with pride,
for he had gathered a powerful and mighty army and now ruled many nations and kingdoms, all of which paid him a tribute tax.
But after all his great conquests, Alexander became very sick and was confined to his bed. When he knew he was dying,
he called for his close friends—noblemen who had grown up with him—and he divided his kingdom among them while he was still alive.
At his death, Alexander had reigned for twelve years.
Each of his close friends took over the region assigned to him,
and each one crowned himself after Alexander’s death. They and their descendants ruled for many years, spreading evil throughout the earth.
Antiochus Epiphanes, son of King Antiochus, was a sinful descendant of these rulers. He had been a hostage in Rome before rising to the throne in the one hundred thirty-seventh year of Greek rule.

In those days there were some ungodly Jews who tried to lead many astray. They said, “Let’s make an agreement with the Gentiles around us, for since we separated ourselves from them, disaster has followed after disaster.”
Many thought this was good advice,
so they went to the king, who authorized them to introduce Gentile practices.
In Jerusalem they built an education complex for promoting Greek culture, as was customarily done among the Gentiles.
They hid the fact that they were circumcised, abandoned their holy covenant with God, and joined with the Gentiles, becoming slaves to evil.
Once Antiochus Epiphanes consolidated his power, he decided to make himself king of Egypt as well so that he might rule over two kingdoms.
He invaded Egypt with a massive army—chariots, elephants, and horsemen—and a large fleet.
He attacked Ptolemy Philometor, king of Egypt, who turned and fled in terror, leaving behind many casualties.
Antiochus captured the fortified cities of Egypt and plundered the entire land.
After conquering Egypt in the one hundred forty-third year of Greek rule, Antiochus returned to Israel
with his powerful force and marched into Jerusalem. He arrogantly entered the Temple sanctuary and carried away the gold incense altar, the lampstand for light and all its accessories,

the table of the Bread of the Presence, the cups used for making drink offerings, the bowls, the gold incense burners, the curtain, the crowns, and the gold decoration that was on the front of the Temple. He stripped the Temple of everything of value.
He took the silver and gold and the precious vessels as well as all the hidden treasures he could find.
When he had gathered everything of value, he returned to his own country. He had murdered many people and arrogantly bragged about it.
Throughout Israel, people mourned deeply,
and the rulers and elders grieved.
Every bridegroom began to lament,
The land trembled for its residents,
Two years later King Antiochus sent his chief tax collector to the towns of Judea, and he arrived at Jerusalem with a massive force.
He deceived the people by speaking peaceful words, thus gaining their trust. But suddenly he attacked the city and killed many of the Israelites.
He plundered the city, set it on fire, and tore down its houses and walls.
He took women and children captive and carried away their livestock.
He rebuilt and fortified the City of David with a great wall and strong towers, and it became their citadel.
He manned and strengthened the fortifications with sinful and wicked men.
They stored up weapons and provisions and collected there the wealth he and his men plundered from Jerusalem. And so they became a perpetual threat to Israel.
The citadel became an ambush for the Temple,
They murdered the innocent all around the sanctuary;
Because of them the residents of Jerusalem fled,
Her Temple became as barren as a desert;
Her dishonor was as great as her former glory;
King Antiochus issued a proclamation that his entire kingdom should be united as one people
and that each nation should renounce its own customs.
The Gentiles accepted this command of the king, and many Israelites also willingly followed his religion. They offered sacrifices to idols and no longer observed the Sabbath.
The king sent messengers with letters to Jerusalem and to all the towns of Judea, ordering the people to follow the foreign customs of his kingdom.
He banned burnt offerings, sacrifices, and drink offerings in the Temple, and he prohibited keeping the Sabbath and celebrating religious festivals.
He defiled the Temple and the priests.
He ordered altars, temples, and idols to be built and pigs and other ceremonially unclean animals to be sacrificed.
Their sons were not to be circumcised, and they were to practice all kinds of unclean and vile customs
so that they would forget to keep the law of Moses.
Anyone who failed to obey the king’s command would be put to death.
Antiochus sent this command to his whole kingdom. He appointed officers to enforce his policies, and he commanded all the towns of Judea to take turns offering pagan sacrifices.
Many of the people who abandoned the law of Moses joined in these sacrifices and committed evil deeds.
They forced the faithful Israelites to hide in any possible place of refuge.

On December 6 in the one hundred forty-fifth year of Greek rule, the king and his forces set up a sacrilegious object causing desecration on top of the altar for burnt offerings, and they built pagan altars in the surrounding Judean towns.
They burned incense and offered sacrifices at the doors of the houses and in the streets.
Whenever a copy of the Book of the Law was found, it was torn up and burned.
By the king’s decree, they put to death anyone found with a copy of the Book of the Covenant or anyone discovered following the law of Moses.
Each month they punished any Israelites who were caught remaining in the towns,
for on the twenty-fifth day of each month they offered sacrifices on the pagan altar that stood on top of the altar of burnt offering.
By order of the king, women who had their sons circumcised were put to death
with their babies hung around their necks. And all their families and everyone else who took part in the circumcisions were killed with them.
Yet there were many Israelites who refused to eat unclean food
and who welcomed death rather than be defiled by food, profaning the holy covenant.
So a time of great trouble had come upon Israel.
In those days Mattathias son of John, son of Simeon, a priest in the line of Joarib, had left Jerusalem to make his home in the town of Modein.
He had five sons: John, who was known as Gaddi;
Simon, who was called Thassi;
Judas, who was called Maccabeus;
Eleazar, who was called Avaran; and Jonathan, who was called Apphus.
When Mattathias saw the sacrilegious acts done in Judea and Jerusalem,
he said,
Her Temple is like a man who has lost his honor;
the glorious vessels have been carried into exile.
What nation has not taken its share of her realm?
All her ornaments have been taken away.
Look at our sanctuary and see how our beauty
What is left to live for?”
To show their grief, Mattathias and his sons tore their clothing, dressed themselves in sackcloth, and mourned deeply.
Officers of the king arrived in Modein to force the people to abandon Judaism and to offer pagan sacrifices.
Many of the Israelites went along with these men, but Mattathias and his sons refused to go near the pagan altar.
In response, the king’s officers said to Mattathias, “You are an honored leader and an important man in this town. Your sons and brothers follow you.

Therefore, be the first in your town to obey the king’s command, just as all the Gentiles and the people of Judea and those living in Jerusalem have done. Then you and your sons will be counted among the king’s favored leaders and be made rich with gold, silver, and many gifts.”
But Mattathias loudly replied, “Even if every nation in the kingdom obeys the king, yielding to his decrees and forsaking their own ancestral religion,
I and my sons and my brothers will still follow the covenant of our ancestors.
Heaven forbid that we should abandon the law of Moses and the commandments!
We will never obey the orders of the king, nor will we stray from our religion—either to the right or to the left.”
As he finished speaking, a certain Jew came forward to offer sacrifices on the pagan altar in the town of Modein, according to the king’s regulations.
When Mattathias saw this, he burned with passion. Then driven by righteous fury, he ran at the man and slaughtered him on the altar.
At the same time, he killed the officer the king had sent to enforce the pagan sacrifices, and he pulled down the altar.
In his zeal for the law of Moses, he showed the spirit Phinehas had shown against Zimri son of Salu.
Mattathias then went through the town, shouting loudly, “Everyone who is zealous for the law of Moses and wants to obey the covenant, follow me!”
Then he and his sons escaped into the hills, leaving behind everything they owned.
Many who were committed to righteousness and justice retreated into the wilderness and lived there
with their children, their wives, and their livestock because their troubles had become so difficult to bear.
The king’s officers and soldiers in Jerusalem, in the City of David, heard about these Jews who had defied the king’s commands and gone into hiding in the wilderness.
Soldiers were sent after them, and when they found them, they set up camp across from them and prepared to attack them on the Sabbath.
But first the soldiers said to them, “Enough of this! Come forward and obey the king’s command, and you will live.”
But the Jews replied, “We will not come forward, nor will we desecrate the Sabbath by obeying the king’s orders.”
Without hesitation the soldiers attacked,
but the Jews offered no resistance, refusing to throw stones at them or even to barricade their hideouts.
They said, “Let us all die in innocence. Heaven and earth will witness to the fact that you are killing us unjustly.”
So the foreigners attacked them on the Sabbath, and they were killed, together with their wives, their children, and their livestock. A thousand people died that day.
When Mattathias and his friends heard this news, they mourned deeply.
They said to one another, “If we all do as our fellow Israelites have done and refuse to fight the Gentiles for our lives and beliefs, they will quickly wipe us off the face of the earth.”
So that day they decided, “If anyone attacks us on the Sabbath day, we will fight them. We will not die in our hiding places as our fellow Israelites did.”
They were joined at that time by a group of Hasideans, strong Israelite warriors who were deeply committed to the law of Moses.
And all those who fled from persecution joined them, giving them added support.
They formed an organized army and in their anger killed guilty and ungodly Jews. The survivors fled to the Gentiles for safety.
Mattathias and his friends went around and tore down the pagan altars,
and they forcibly circumcised any boys in the hill country of Israel who had not been circumcised.
They hunted down the arrogant and were successful in their fight.
They rescued the law of Moses from the control of the Gentiles and their kings, and they never gave in to those who were guilty.
As the time of Mattathias’ death drew near, he said to his sons, “Pride and scorn have become rampant; it is a time of violence and fury.
Therefore, my sons, be zealous for the law of Moses and give your lives for the covenant of your ancestors.
If you remember the deeds our ancestors did for each of their generations, you will receive great honor and everlasting fame.
Wasn’t Abraham found faithful when he was tested? And wasn’t he declared to be righteous?
Joseph kept the law through trying times, and he became master over Egypt.
As a reward for his zeal, our ancestor Phinehas was granted a covenant that his descendants would be priests for all time.
For fulfilling his duty, Joshua became a judge in Israel.
For giving a positive report to the people, Caleb received an inheritance in the land.
For showing mercy, David received the promise that his descendants would rule for all time.
Because of his zeal for the law of Moses, Elijah was taken up into heaven.
Because they had faith, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were rescued from the flames.
Because he was innocent, Daniel was delivered from the lions’ jaws.
“Take notice how, in every generation, all who trust in God are strong.
Do not fear the threats of sinners, for their glory will turn to dung and worms.
Today they are exalted, but tomorrow they cannot be found, because they will return to dust, and their planning will come to nothing.
Therefore, my sons, be courageous and strong in keeping the law of Moses, for by obeying it you will gain glory.
“Your brother Simon is a wise man, so listen to him always, for he will take my place.
Let Judas Maccabeus, who has always been valiant and strong, be the leader of your army and direct the war against the Gentiles.
Gather together all who observe the law of Moses, and avenge the wrong of your people.
Pay back the Gentiles in full, and always obey the law of Moses.”
Mattathias blessed his sons, and then he died
in the one hundred forty-sixth year of Greek rule. He was buried in the tomb of his ancestors in Modein, and all Israel mourned deeply for him.
Judas, who was called Maccabeus, took the place of his father, Mattathias.
His brothers and all who had joined his father helped him, and they gladly fought for Israel.
Judas brought great honor to his people.
He was like a lion in his actions,
He hunted down the wicked and pursued them,
The wicked fled in fear,
he bitterly angered many kings.
He went throughout the towns of Judea and destroyed the wicked,
He was famous even to the ends of the earth,
Apollonius gathered a large army of Gentiles and Samaritans to attack Israel.
When Judas heard this, he went out to meet him, and he defeated and killed him. Many were wounded and fell, and the survivors fled.
Judas plundered their belongings, including the sword of Apollonius, which he used the rest of his life.
When Seron, commander of the Syrian forces, heard that Judas had formed a large army of faithful men,
he said, “I will make a reputation for myself and become famous in my kingdom by crushing Judas and his followers, who have scorned the king’s command.”
So Seron organized his troops, a large number of wicked men who sought vengeance on the Israelites.
They marched as far as Beth-horon, where Judas went out to meet him with only a few men.
When the Israelites saw the advancing army, they said to Judas, “How can so few of us fight against an army that is so large and strong? And we are weak, for we have eaten nothing today.”
Judas replied, “It is easy for many to be overpowered by a few, for it makes no difference in God’s sight whether we are saved by few or many.
Success in battle depends not on the size of the army but on strength that comes from God.
This arrogant and wicked army has come to destroy us, our wives, and our children and to take our belongings.
But we will fight for our lives and our laws,
and the Lord himself will crush them as we watch. So don’t be afraid of them.”
As soon as Judas had finished speaking, he and his troops suddenly charged Seron and his army and overpowered them.
They pursued them from Beth-horon down to the plain; there they killed eight hundred soldiers, and the rest fled into Philistia.
Then the Gentiles in the area feared Judas and his brothers.
Even the king heard of his reputation, and all the Gentiles talked about his battles.
When King Antiochus Epiphanes heard these reports, he became angry. He formed a very strong army from the forces of his entire kingdom.
Opening his treasury, he paid his troops a year’s wages and told them to be ready for anything.
In this way he exhausted the money in his treasury. Antiochus realized that his tax revenues were small because he had antagonized and impoverished the people when he abolished the ancient laws.
He feared that he would not have enough money for all his expenses and for the gifts he liked to give. (He gave more lavishly than any of the kings who had preceded him.)
He was very perplexed about this, so he decided to go to Persia to collect a large tax fund from those regions.
So King Antiochus left Lysias, a nobleman of the royal family, to oversee the affairs of the kingdom—from the Euphrates River to the border of Egypt.
Lysias was also supposed to take care of the king’s son Antiochus until he returned.
The king gave Lysias half his soldiers and all his elephants and gave him orders concerning the people of Judea and Jerusalem.
Lysias was instructed to attack them in order to crush the strength of Israel and to wipe out the people left in Jerusalem. He was to erase even the memory of them from that place.
He was instructed to settle foreigners in their territory and redistribute the land to them.

Then the king took the other half of the army and left Antioch, his capital city, in the one hundred forty-seventh year of Greek rule. He crossed the Euphrates River and went through the upper provinces.
Lysias chose Ptolemy Macron son of Dorymenes along with Nicanor and Gorgias, all capable men who were among the king’s favored leaders,
and sent them with forty thousand foot soldiers and seven thousand horsemen to destroy the land of Judea, as the king had ordered.
So the powerful army marched out and set up camp in the plain near Emmaus.

When the merchants of the surrounding area heard about it, they brought chains and large amounts of silver and gold to the camp to buy as slaves any Israelites who might be captured. Then forces from Syria and Philistia joined the army in its camp.
Judas and his brothers saw that the situation was desperate, for the army had camped in their territory. They also knew that the king had given orders to completely destroy the Israelites.
They said to each other, “Let us fight for our people and for our Temple; let us rescue them from ruin.”
Then they assembled the people for battle and prayed for God’s mercy and compassion.
Jerusalem was abandoned like a wilderness;
The Israelites assembled at Mizpah near Jerusalem, since it was a traditional place of prayer for them.
That day they fasted and dressed in sackcloth. They also put ashes on their heads and tore their clothes in grief.
And in contrast to the Gentiles, who search for answers from the idols of their gods, the Israelites opened the Book of the Law to find guidance.
They brought out the priestly garments, the gifts that represented the first portion of the harvest, and the tithes, and they summoned the Nazirites, who had completed their vows.
They cried loudly to heaven, “What can we do with these Nazirites? Where can we take them to fulfill the law of Moses?
For your Temple is torn down and defiled. Your priests mourn in humiliation.
The Gentiles have gathered together to destroy us. You know what their intentions are.
How can we stand against them if you do not help us?”
Then they sounded the trumpets and loudly cried out.
After this, Judas appointed officers over the people to command groups of one thousand, one hundred, fifty, and ten.

(He told those who were building houses and those soon to be married, as well as those who were planting vineyards and those who were afraid, that they should go home, just as the law of Moses instructed.)
Then the army moved out and set up a new camp on the south side of Emmaus.
Judas said, “Prepare yourselves and be brave. Be ready early in the morning to fight these Gentiles, for they want to destroy us and our Temple.
It is better for us to die in battle than to see the ruin of our nation and our Temple.
May God’s will be done.”
Gorgias took a detachment of five thousand foot soldiers and a thousand select horsemen and moved out of the camp by night.
Their plan was for the men of the citadel in Jerusalem to guide them to the camp of the Jews, and then they would launch a surprise attack.
But Judas heard of their plan, so he and his soldiers prepared to attack the king’s forces in Emmaus
while the army was divided.
When Gorgias reached Judas’s camp that night, he found no one there, so he began looking for them in the hills, saying, “They ran away from us.”
Daybreak found Judas on the plain with three thousand men, but they lacked the armor and swords they needed.
They saw that the camp of the Gentiles was well fortified, with men wearing body armor and horsemen patrolling it. These were trained soldiers.
But Judas told his soldiers, “Don’t be frightened by their numbers. Don’t flinch at their attack.
Remember how our ancestors were saved at the Red Sea when Pharaoh pursued them with his army.
Now let us call upon God with the hope that he will think of us, remembering his covenant with our ancestors, and that he will destroy this army facing us today.
Then all the Gentiles will know that there is one who redeems and rescues Israel.”
The foreigners looked up and saw Judas’s army advancing against them,
so they rushed out of the camp to engage them in battle. The trumpet sounded for Judas’s army,
and they began fighting. The Gentiles were routed and fled across the plain,
and their rear guard was destroyed. Judas and his army chased them as far as Gazara and even to Azotus and Jamnia and the plains of Idumea. The enemy lost about three thousand men.
Judas stopped the pursuit and returned with his men.
He said to the people, “Forget the plunder. We have another battle to face.
Gorgias and his detachment are in the hills nearby. First stand firm against our enemies and crush them. Then you may take as much plunder as you want.”
While Judas was still speaking, the enemy was spotted coming out of the hills.
But Gorgias saw that the soldiers he left in Emmaus had fled, and the smoke rising from his camp showed that Judas’s men had set fire to it.
When Gorgias’s troops saw this, they were terrified. Then they saw Judas and his army in battle formation on the plain,
so they all fled into Philistia.
Then Judas turned back to plunder the camp. He and his men carried away a great amount of gold and silver, blue and purple silks, and other valuables.
On the way home they sang hymns of praise to God, singing, “He is good, and his faithful love endures forever.”
So Israel experienced great deliverance that day.
The Gentiles who escaped reported to Lysias all that had happened.
He was shocked and upset when he heard about it, because things had not turned out as he had planned for Israel, and he had failed to fulfill the king’s command.
So the next year Lysias gathered sixty thousand select troops and five thousand horsemen in order to subdue the Jews.
This army marched into Idumea and set up camp in Beth-zur, where Judas faced them with ten thousand men.

When Judas saw their military might, he prayed, “Blessed are you, O Savior of Israel, for you stopped the giant warrior by your servant David and handed over the Philistine camp to Jonathan son of Saul and his armor bearer.
Now let this army be surrounded by your people Israel, and let their many soldiers and horsemen become confused.
Strike them with fear, and undermine their confidence in their own strength. Give them fear for their own destruction.
Let those who love you strike them down with swords so that your followers may praise you with hymns.”
The opposing forces engaged in hand-to-hand combat, and five thousand men of the army of Lysias were killed.

Lysias saw his men in retreat, and he also saw that Judas’s followers were very bold and ready to live or die bravely. So he withdrew to Antioch to recruit mercenary soldiers; then he planned to return to Judea with an even larger army.
