Judas and his brothers said, “Our enemies have been utterly defeated. Now let us go up to purify the Temple and dedicate it.”
So all the army was assembled, and they went up to Mount Zion.
There they saw the empty sanctuary, the desecrated altar, the gates burned down, the weeds growing in the courtyards as in a forest or on a hill, and the priests’ rooms next to the Temple in ruins.
They tore their garments and mourned deeply, putting ashes on their heads
and falling face down on the ground. When the trumpets gave the signal, the people cried out to God.
Then Judas sent troops to attack the defenders of the citadel while he purified the Temple.
He chose blameless priests, who were devoted to the law of Moses.
They cleansed the sanctuary, and the stones that had been defiled were carried away to an unclean place.
They discussed what should be done about the altar of burnt offering, for it had been defiled.
Someone suggested that it be torn down so it would not become a lasting shame to them, for the Gentiles had defiled it. So they pulled the altar down
and put the stones in a suitable place on the Temple hill until a prophet could come someday and tell them what to do with them.
Then they took uncut stones, as required in the law of Moses, and built a new altar like the old one.
They restored the sanctuary and all the things inside the Temple. Finally, they sanctified the Temple and its courtyards.
They made new sacred vessels and took into the Temple the lampstand, the altar of incense, and the table for the Bread of the Presence.
They burned incense on the altar and lit the lamps on the lampstand, which gave light in the Temple.
Then they set the Bread of the Presence on the table, hung up the curtains, and finished all the work they had set out to do.
On December 14 in the one hundred forty-eighth year of Greek rule, they arose early in the morning
and offered sacrifices on the new altar of burnt offering, as the law of Moses directed.
On the day of the month that the Gentiles regularly defiled it, the altar was dedicated anew with songs, harps, lutes, and cymbals.
And all the people fell face down in adoration and blessed God, who had given them success.
For eight days they celebrated the dedication of the altar, and they joyfully offered burnt offerings, praise, and thanksgiving for their deliverance.
They adorned the front of the Temple with gold crowns and shields, and they repaired the gates and restored the priests’ rooms, furnishing them with doors.
The people were very joyful because the disgrace caused by the Gentiles had been removed.
Judas and his brothers and all Israel decreed that the dedication of the altar should be celebrated every year with joy and gladness for eight days, beginning on December 14.
They then built high walls and fortified towers around Mount Zion to stop the Gentiles from attacking and destroying it as they did before.
Judas assigned a garrison to guard Mount Zion, and he fortified Beth-zur, so that the people would have a defense against Idumea.
When the surrounding Gentile peoples heard that the altar and sanctuary had been restored, they became very angry.
Determined to destroy all of Jacob’s descendants living among them, they began to persecute and kill the people.

Judas fought against Esau’s descendants at Akrabattene in Idumea because they were attacking the Israelites there. The Idumeans were thoroughly humiliated in defeat and were stripped of their valuables and weapons.
Judas also avenged the evil deeds of the sons of Baean, who constantly threatened travelers by ambushing them along the roads.
Judas chased them into their fortified towers and surrounded them. Then, calling a curse down on them, he set the towers on fire and burned them down with everyone inside.
Next, Judas crossed over to attack the Ammonites and found a strong and numerous army under the command of Timothy.
After fighting many battles with them, he routed them and cut them to pieces.
He captured the town of Jazer and its nearby villages. Then he returned to Judea.
Now the Gentiles in Gilead banded together against the Israelites in their area and plotted to destroy them. But these Israelites fled to the fortress of Dathema.
From there they sent this letter to Judas and his brothers:
They are preparing to come and capture the fortress where we have taken refuge. Timothy is the leader of their army.
Please come at once and rescue us from them, for many of us have already been killed or wounded.
All our fellow Israelites in the land of Tob are dead. Their wives and children have been taken captive, and their goods have been confiscated. The enemy has killed almost a thousand men there.”
While this letter was being read, other messengers came from Galilee with their clothes torn. They had similar news:
“Everyone in Ptolemais, Tyre, and Sidon has joined with the Gentiles of Galilee to destroy us.”
When Judas and the people heard these reports, they held a large meeting to decide how to help their fellow Israelites who were being attacked by their enemies.
Judas said to his brother Simon, “Choose your men and rescue your fellow Israelites in Galilee; Jonathan and I will go to Gilead.”
He left Joseph son of Zechariah and Azariah, a leader of the people, to guard Judea with the rest of the army.
He gave them these instructions: “Take charge of these people, but do not begin fighting the Gentiles until we return.”
Three thousand men were assigned to accompany Simon into Galilee, and Judas led eight thousand men into Gilead.
Simon invaded Galilee, and after fighting many battles, he completely crushed the Gentile forces there.
He chased them all the way to the gate of Ptolemais. Almost three thousand Gentiles were killed, and Simon captured all their belongings.
He led the Jews who were in Galilee and in Arbatta—together with their wives, children, and possessions—to Judea with great celebration.
Judas Maccabeus and his brother Jonathan crossed the Jordan River and marched for three days into the wilderness.
There they met the Nabateans, who received them peacefully. The Nabateans told them all that had been happening to the Israelites in Gilead.
They related that many had been trapped in Bozrah, Bosor, Alema, Chaspho, Maked, and Karnaim (all of which were large and fortified cities).
They said that Jews were also being held captive in the other towns of Gilead. The enemy planned to attack these towns the next day, and then they would capture and destroy all the Jews at once.
Judas and his army quickly marched back by the wilderness road to Bozrah and captured that town. They killed every male by the sword, carried away all their goods, and burned the town.
They left Bozrah by night and marched until they came to the fortress of Dathema.
At dawn they saw a great number of soldiers carrying ladders and battering rams to attack the fortress and capture the Jews.
Judas saw that the fight had just begun and that the battle cry of the people was going up to heaven with trumpet blasts and shouts.
He shouted to his army, “Fight today for your fellow Israelites!”
Then Judas’s men advanced from behind the enemy in three companies while sounding trumpets and crying aloud in prayer.
When the men of Timothy’s army realized it was Maccabeus, they fled from him. Judas’s army inflicted a crushing defeat, killing about eight thousand men that day.
Judas then turned to Alema, assaulted and captured it, killed all the males, carried away all the goods, and burned it.
From there he marched on and captured Chaspho, Maked, Bosor, and the rest of the towns of Gilead.
Following his defeat, Timothy assembled another army and set up camp just across the streambed from Raphon.
Judas sent scouts to survey the enemy camp, and they returned to report, “All the Gentiles from the region have gathered to form a great army under Timothy’s command;
they have also hired Arab reinforcements. They are camped on the opposite side of the streambed, ready to fight you.” So Judas went forward to attack them.
As Judas approached, Timothy said to his officers, “If Judas comes to the streambed and crosses it, we will not be able to resist him; he will certainly get the better of us.
But if his courage fails and he sets up camp on the other side, we will cross over and crush him.”
When Judas came near the stream, he stationed the officers of the army on the bank, ordering them, “Don’t let anyone stay behind to set up camp. Send everyone into battle.”
Judas himself led the charge across the streambed, and his entire army followed. They routed the Gentile forces, who fled to the temple area in Karnaim, discarding their weapons as they ran.
But Judas captured Karnaim and burned out the temple area with everyone in it. So Karnaim was subdued, and all resistance against Judas ceased.
Then Judas gathered together all the Israelites who were in Gilead, from the least to the greatest—with their wives, children, and possessions—and he led this large company back to Judea.
Along the way they came to Ephron, a large city that was strongly fortified. They could not go around it, either to the right or left, so they had to go through it.
But the people in the city shut themselves in and barricaded the gates with stones.

Judas sent them a message of peace, saying, “Let us pass through your territory to get to our own. No one will harm you. We will only pass through on foot.” But they refused to open the gates for him.
So Judas issued orders for all his troops to set up where they were.
His army prepared for battle and attacked the city all that day and through the night until the city fell to them.
Judas and his men killed every male by the sword, carried away their possessions, and completely destroyed the city. Then they marched through the city over the bodies of the dead.
They crossed the Jordan River to the great plain near Beth-shan.
Judas hurried the stragglers and encouraged the people all the way until they reached Judea.
Then with joy and gladness they climbed Mount Zion, where they offered burnt offerings, for none of them had been killed and all had returned safely.
Now while Judas and Jonathan were in Gilead and their brother Simon was in Galilee outside Ptolemais,
Joseph son of Zechariah and Azariah, commanders of the soldiers in Judea, heard of the victories and the battles that had been fought.
They said, “Let’s also make a name for ourselves by fighting the Gentiles around us.”
So Joseph gave orders to his troops, and they marched against Jamnia.
Gorgias and his men came out of the town to fight them.
Joseph and Azariah were routed, and they were chased all the way to the borders of Judea. About two thousand Israelites were killed that day.
This great defeat took place because they did not listen to Judas and his brothers. They thought they would do brave deeds themselves,
but they were not from the family through whom deliverance was to come to Israel.
Valiant Judas and his brothers, however, were greatly honored by all Israel, and their fame spread among the Gentiles.
People rallied around and cheered for them.

Judas and his brothers marched out and attacked the descendants of Esau in the land to the south. They captured Hebron and its surrounding towns, destroying their fortifications and burning down their perimeter towers.
As Judas and his army headed for Philistia, they passed through Marisa.
That day some priests were killed in battle, for they had foolishly decided to make a name for themselves in battle.
Judas turned and marched to Azotus in Philistia. He tore down their altars, burned the statues of their gods, and carried away their possessions. Then he returned to Judea.
King Antiochus was passing through the upper provinces when he heard that the city of Elymais in Persia was famous for its rich stores of silver and gold.
The temple in this city was very rich, containing gold armor, shields, and weapons left there by Alexander the Macedonian, son of Philip, the first ruler of Greece.
Antiochus came and tried to capture the city and strip it of its wealth, but he did not succeed because its citizens had learned of his plans to attack.
They resisted him in battle, so he retreated and returned to Babylon greatly disappointed.
While Antiochus was still in Persia, someone told him that his armies had been defeated in Judea.

He was told that Lysias had attacked them with a strong force but had been defeated by the Jews. The Jews had now grown strong by capturing armor, war supplies, and stores of goods from the armies they destroyed.

Antiochus was told that the Jews had thrown down the sacrilegious object he had set up on the altar in Jerusalem, had surrounded the Temple with high walls as in the past, and had fortified Beth-zur, his town.
When the king heard this news, he was astounded and badly shaken. He became so sick with grief that he was confined to his bed, for things had not worked out as he had planned.
He lay there for many days, overcome with bitterness and constant grief, until finally he realized he was dying.
The king called for his favored leaders and said to them, “I can’t sleep, and my heart has been broken with worry.
At first I said to myself, ‘How could I have come to such distress and deep sorrow? I have been kind, and my people have always loved me.’
But now I remember the wrongs I committed in Jerusalem—how I seized all the vessels of gold and silver and ordered the slaughter of the people of Judea without just cause.
I know now that this is why these evils have fallen on me. Now I will die of great sorrow in a foreign land.”
King Antiochus then called for Philip, one of his favored leaders, and put him in command of all his kingdom.
He gave Philip the royal crown, his robe, and his signet ring, with the understanding that Philip would be guardian to his son Antiochus and train him to become king.
Antiochus Epiphanes died there in Persia in the one hundred forty-ninth year of Greek rule.
Now when Lysias learned that the king was dead, he went ahead and crowned the king’s son Antiochus as the new king. Lysias had raised him from childhood and gave him the title Eupator.
Meanwhile, the soldiers from the garrison in the Jerusalem citadel were harassing the Israelites near the sanctuary. They tried in every way they could to harm the Jews and strengthen the Gentiles.
Judas decided to destroy them, so he gathered all the people to besiege the citadel.
They joined together and attacked the citadel in the one hundred fiftieth year of Greek rule, using siege weapons and battering rams.
Some of the people in the citadel escaped from the siege, and some ungodly Israelites joined them.
They went to King Antiochus Eupator and said, “How long will you refuse to do justice and avenge the attacks on our people?
We were content to serve your father, doing all he ordered and obeying his commands.
But because of this, the other Israelites are angry with us and have besieged the citadel. They have killed as many of us as they could catch and have seized our inheritances.
They have opposed not only us but also people in all the surrounding territories.
Now they have besieged the citadel in Jerusalem and have fortified the Temple and the stronghold of Beth-zur.
Unless you act quickly, they will do worse things than these, and you will not be able to stop them.”
The king became angry when he heard this. He called together all his favored leaders, the commanders of his army, and the officers over his horsemen.
He also hired mercenaries from various places, including the Mediterranean islands.
His army numbered one hundred thousand foot soldiers, twenty thousand horsemen, and thirty-two elephants trained in warfare.

After marching through Idumea, they came to Beth-zur and attacked it for many days. They even used battering rams in the attack, but the Jews bravely ran out of the town and set the battering rams on fire.
Judas and his army left the siege of the citadel in Jerusalem and moved their camp to Beth-zechariah, opposite the camp of the king’s army.
The king rose before daylight and marched his men toward Beth-zechariah, where they prepared for battle and sounded the trumpets.
The elephants were given grape juice and mulberry juice to provoke them to fight.

The elephants were distributed among the ranks of foot soldiers, each elephant to a thousand men, who were dressed in coats of mail and wearing bronze helmets. Five hundred select horsemen were assigned to each elephant.
These horsemen anticipated the moves of the elephants and went with them, never leaving them.
Fastened to each elephant by a harness was a sturdy wooden tower. A team of men fought from each tower while an Indian driver directed the beast.
The rest of the horsemen were placed on either flank of the army to harass the enemy while being protected by the ranks of foot soldiers.
When the sun reflected from the shields of gold and bronze, the hills caught the glare and gleamed as if on fire.
Part of the king’s army was deployed on the high hills, while the other part was on the plain. The soldiers advanced steadily and in solid formation.
Everyone trembled at the noise of this great multitude, for the powerful and numerous army thundered as it marched in its clanging armor.
Judas and his army marched forward, and six hundred of the king’s men were killed.
Judas’s brother Eleazar, who was called Avaran, saw that one of the elephants was larger than the other beasts and was equipped with royal armor. He thought that the king was on it,
so he sacrificed himself to win the battle and earn everlasting fame.
As Eleazar fought his way boldly through the middle of the enemy ranks, killing men left and right, the troops parted as he came.
He got under the elephant, plunged his sword into it, and killed it; but the elephant collapsed on him and he died.
When the Jews saw the strength and determination of the king’s army, however, they retreated.
The king’s army followed them to Jerusalem, where it set up camp to blockade Judea and Mount Zion.
The king granted terms of peace to the people of Beth-zur, and they evacuated the town. (They had no food to withstand a siege, since it was a Sabbath year for the land.)
So the king captured Beth-zur and stationed a garrison there to hold it.
Then he began a long siege of the Temple. He set up siege weapons, battering rams, machines to hurl fire and stones, machines to shoot arrows, and catapults.
The Jews also constructed weapons of war to match these, and they fought for many days.
But since it was the Sabbath year, there was no food in the town. Those who had sought refuge in Judea from the Gentiles had eaten all the stored food.
Because of the food shortage, only a few men stayed in the Temple; all the others had scattered to their own homes.
Before he died, Antiochus Epiphanes had appointed Philip to raise his son, Antiochus Eupator, and to prepare him to be king. Lysias now heard that Philip
had returned from Persia and Media with the late king’s army and was trying to seize control.

So Lysias gave orders to withdraw from attacking the Temple, and he went to King Antiochus Eupator and told him and his commanders, “We are growing weaker every day, we are short of food, and the place we are attacking is strong. Besides, the other affairs of the kingdom demand urgent attention.
Therefore, let us make a peace treaty with these people and their nation.
Let us agree that they may live according to their own laws once again. It is because we abolished their laws that they became angry and rebelled like this.”
The proposal pleased the king and his commanders. He sent the Jews an offer of peace, and they accepted it.
So the king and his commanders gave their word, and the defenders left the stronghold.
But when the king went up to Mount Zion, he saw that its defenses were very strong, so he broke his word and gave orders to tear down the wall around the Temple.
Then he quickly left and returned to Antioch. There he found Philip in control of the city, so he attacked the city and captured it.
In the one hundred fifty-first year of Greek rule, Demetrius son of Seleucus left Rome with a few men and arrived at a coastal city. There he proclaimed himself king.
As he was entering the royal palace of his ancestors, the armies there captured Antiochus Eupator and Lysias, intending to bring them to him.
When Demetrius heard this, he said, “I don’t even want to see them!”
So the army killed them, and Demetrius assumed the throne of his kingdom.
Then all the ungodly and wicked Israelites came to Demetrius. They were led by Alcimus, who wanted to be made high priest.
They accused their own people, saying, “Judas and his brothers have killed all your favored leaders and have driven us from our land.
Therefore, send someone you trust who can survey all the damage that Judas has caused us and the king’s lands. Let him punish Judas and his men and all who help them.”
So the king chose Bacchides, one of his favored leaders who governed the province west of the Euphrates River. He was a prominent figure in the kingdom and was faithful to King Demetrius.
He sent Bacchides and the wicked Alcimus, whom he made high priest, to take revenge on the Israelites.
They set out and arrived in Judea with a large army. Alcimus sent messengers to Judas and his brothers with deceitful words of peace,
but Judas did not believe them, for he saw that the enemy had come with a large army.
Nevertheless, some teachers of religious law went to Alcimus and Bacchides to inquire about just terms.
These Hasidean teachers were the first to seek peace from the two men.
They reasoned, “A priest of the line of Aaron has come with the army. He will not deceive us.”
Alcimus spoke words of peace and vowed to them, “We will do no harm to you or your friends,”
and they believed him. But he took sixty of them in one day and killed them, as had been written in the Scriptures:
“They have scattered the bodies of your holy ones.
Then all the people became very fearful. They said, “They don’t know what it means to be truthful, for they have broken the agreement that they guaranteed with an oath.”
Bacchides moved the camp from Jerusalem to Beth-zaith. He seized many of those who deserted to him and also some Jews, and he slaughtered them all and threw them into a large pit.
He entrusted the country to Alcimus and left some troops to help him. Then Bacchides went back to the king.
Alcimus continually fought to maintain his position as high priest,
and some Jewish dissenters joined his cause. They took control of Judea and did much harm to Israel.
Judas saw all the evils that Alcimus and his companions did to the Israelites. They were worse than the Gentiles.
So Judas marched throughout the whole territory of Judea, taking revenge on those who had deserted and preventing them from leaving their towns.
Alcimus realized that Judas and his companions were gaining control, and he knew he could not stand against them. So he went back to the king and accused Judas and his men of many serious crimes.
Nicanor, one of the king’s most honored generals, despised Israel, so the king sent him to destroy the people there.
Nicanor came to Jerusalem with a large army, and he sent Judas and his brothers a deceitful message of peace:
“There is no need for us to fight each other. I will come with a few men to speak to you in peace.”
So he came to see Judas, and they greeted each other peaceably. All the while, Nicanor’s men were preparing to kidnap Judas.
But Judas learned of this deceitful plot, so he was cautious and would not meet Nicanor again.
When Nicanor realized his plot had been discovered, he went out to fight against Judas near Caphar-salama.
But about five hundred of Nicanor’s men were killed, and the survivors fled into the City of David.
After this, Nicanor went up to Mount Zion. Some of the priests and elders came out to meet him peaceably. They showed him the burnt offerings that were being offered on behalf of the king.
But he mocked and derided them, cursing and spitting at them as he angrily swore,
“Unless Judas and his army are handed over to me, I will burn this house down when I return.” Then he left in a terrible rage.
The priests went into the Temple and stood facing the altar and the sanctuary. They wept and prayed,
“You have chosen this house to honor your name
Take vengeance on this man and his army;
Nicanor and his army left Jerusalem and set up camp near Beth-horon, where the Syrian army joined him.
Judas and 3,000 of his troops set up camp in Adasa. He prayed,
“When the messengers of King Sennacherib blasphemed you, your angel went out and killed 185,000 of the Assyrians.
In the same way, utterly destroy this army before us today. Let everyone still alive know that Nicanor has blasphemed your sanctuary, and judge him as his wickedness deserves.”
The armies attacked each other on March 8. Nicanor’s army was completely defeated, and he himself was the first to fall in battle.
When Nicanor’s men saw that he was dead, they threw down their weapons and fled.
The Jews chased them for about eighteen miles, from Adasa as far as Gazara, and their trumpets kept sounding the battle call.
People came out of all the towns of Judea and drove the enemy back to the pursuing Jewish army, which killed them all by the sword—not a single one was left alive.

The Jews carried away all the goods, and they cut off Nicanor’s head and his right hand, which he had so arrogantly raised against them. They brought his head and hand to Jerusalem and put them on display for all to see.
The people were overjoyed and spent that day in festive celebration.
Judas decreed that there should be a celebration each spring to commemorate the victory.
So Judea enjoyed peace and quiet for a short time.
Judas had heard of the Romans’ famous reputation, that they were powerful and strong and good to those with whom they held alliances. They promised friendship to any who joined them,
and they were very powerful. Judas had heard of their battles and their heroic deeds against the Gauls—how they had conquered them and forced them to pay a tribute tax.
He had also heard of the great things they had done in Spain—how they had gained control of the silver and gold mines there

and taken possession of the whole region by their wisdom and patience, even though Spain was quite far from them. In every part of the world, kings who opposed the Romans had been overthrown with great losses, while others paid them a tribute tax every year.
Philip and Perseus, kings of the Macedonians, and others who had fought against the Romans had been conquered.
The Romans had also defeated Antiochus the Great, king of Asia, who had fought against them with 120 elephants and with horsemen, chariots, and a very large army.
The Romans took Antiochus alive and ordered that he and those who would reign after him should pay a large tribute tax and give them hostages.
Antiochus was also forced to give them India, Media, and Lydia. These were then given to King Eumenes.
The Greeks planned to attack and destroy the Romans,

but the Romans heard about it and sent a single general to attack them. In the ensuing battle, many Greeks were killed or wounded, and the Romans took their wives and children captive, carried away their possessions, annexed their territory, tore down their fortresses, and made them their slaves, as they are to this day.
They destroyed and enslaved all other kingdoms and islands that resisted them.
The Romans have maintained a firm friendship, however, with all their friends and allies.
They make kings of anyone they wish, and they depose anyone they wish; in this way, they have become very great.
Yet no Roman has ever crowned himself king or displayed his grandeur by wearing purple.
They have formed a senate of 320 people, who meet daily to decide what is best for the people and how to govern them.
Their government is directed by entrusting one man each year to rule over the whole country. They all obey him, and there is no envy or jealousy among them.
Judas chose Eupolemus son of John, son of Accos, and Jason son of Eleazar to go to Rome and establish a friendship and an alliance with the Romans.
Judas did this so the Jews could get out from under oppression, for it was obvious that the Greeks were reducing Israel to slavery.
Eupolemus and Jason traveled to Rome, which was a very long journey. When they arrived, they entered the senate chamber and said,
“Judas Maccabeus, his brothers, and the Jewish people have sent us to establish an alliance and a peace treaty with you. We want to be formally considered your friends and allies.”
The senate was pleased to accept their proposal.
The senate sent a proclamation back to Jerusalem, engraved on bronze tablets so that it might be kept there as a permanent record of their peace treaty and alliance:
“May the Romans and the Jewish nation meet with success forever, both at sea and on land. May sword and enemy be far from them.
If war should come to the Romans or to any of their allies in all their dominion,
the Jewish nation will wholeheartedly act as their allies in whatever way the occasion requires.
If an enemy is at war with the Romans, the Jews will not supply them with grain, arms, money, or ships, just as Rome has decided. They will keep these obligations without any compensation.
Likewise, if war should come to the Jewish nation, the Romans will willingly act as their allies in whatever way the occasion requires.
If the Jews have an enemy, the Romans will not supply them with grain, arms, money, or ships, just as Rome has decided. The Romans will keep these obligations without deception.
On these terms the Romans make an agreement with the Jewish people.
If both parties agree to add or delete anything in this agreement, they may do so, and whatever changes they make will be valid.
“Concerning the wrongs that King Demetrius is committing against the Jews, we have written to him as follows: ‘Why are you making things so hard for our friends and allies the Jews?
If they come to us again and complain about you, we will defend their rights. We will make war against you by sea and on land.’”
Meanwhile, when Demetrius heard that Nicanor and his army had fallen in battle, he sent Bacchides and Alcimus back into Judea, along with the right wing of his army.
They marched along the road that leads to Gilgal and set up camp at the ascent to Arbela. They then captured the town and killed many of its people.
In early spring during the one hundred fifty-second year of Greek rule, they set up camp outside Jerusalem.
Then they marched on to Berea near Jerusalem with twenty thousand foot soldiers and two thousand horsemen.
Now Judas and three thousand of his select troops had set up camp in Elasa.
When they saw the size of the enemy army, they became very frightened. Many deserted the camp until no more than eight hundred men remained.
Seeing that only a fraction of his army was left and that the battle was imminent, Judas became discouraged because he had no time to gather more forces.
But even though he was dismayed, he said to those who remained, “Let us get up and face our enemies. We may still have the strength to fight them.”
His men tried to dissuade him, saying, “We don’t have the strength! We should save our lives and return to fight them with more of our fellow Israelites. There are too few of us now.”
But Judas said, “I would never think of running from them. If our time has come, let us die bravely for our people and leave no blemish on our reputation.”
The army of Bacchides moved out of camp and took positions for combat. The horsemen were divided into two groups, and the slingers and the archers went ahead of the army, as did the best fighters.

The ranks of foot soldiers were flanked by horsemen on either side, and Bacchides was on the right flank. The army advanced as it sounded its trumpets, and Judas’s soldiers sounded their trumpets as well.
The earth shook at the noise of the armies, and the battle continued from morning until evening.
Judas saw that Bacchides and the stronger part of his army was on the right, so Judas led his bravest men
and drove back the right flank, chasing them to Mount Azotus.
The soldiers on the left flank realized that the right flank was beaten, so they turned to chase Judas and those who were with him, attacking them from the rear.
The fighting became very intense, and both sides lost many men.
Then Judas was killed, and the rest of his men fled.
Jonathan and Simon took their brother Judas and buried him in the tomb of their ancestors at Modein.
For many days, all Israel mourned deeply for him, saying,
“The mighty hero—the savior of Israel—has fallen!”
The rest of the deeds of Judas—his battles, his heroic acts, and his great achievements—have not been recorded here, but there were many of them.
After the death of Judas, the ungodly came out of hiding throughout Israel, and evildoers reappeared.
In those days there was a very severe famine, and the country eventually sided with the ungodly.
Bacchides chose wicked men to administer the affairs of the country.
These people searched out Judas’s friends and brought them to Bacchides, who punished and publicly humiliated them.
There had not been such distress in Israel since the day the last prophet was seen in Israel.
All Judas’s friends said to Jonathan,
“Ever since your brother Judas died, there has been no one like him to fight Bacchides and our enemies and to deal with our own people who despise us.
Therefore, we have chosen you today to succeed him as our ruler and commander, so that you can lead us into battle.”
So Jonathan became leader in place of his brother Judas.
When Bacchides heard about this, he tried to kill Jonathan.
But Jonathan and his brother Simon and the others who were with them learned of the plot, and they fled into the wilderness of Tekoa. They set up camp by the pool of Asphar.
Bacchides learned of this on the Sabbath, so he and his army crossed the Jordan.
Jonathan sent his brother John to lead a convoy to ask their friends the Nabateans if they would store the Israelites’ sizable amount of baggage.
The sons of Jambri, however, came from Medeba and seized John and all his possessions and took him away.

Sometime later Jonathan and his brother Simon learned that the sons of Jambri had planned a large wedding. The bride was the daughter of one of the great princes of Canaan, and they were planning to bring her from Nadabath in a splendid procession.
Remembering the bloody death of their brother John, Jonathan and Simon went up and hid themselves in the hills.

As they peered out, they saw a great crowd and a caravan loaded with possessions. The bridegroom came out with his relatives and friends to meet the procession with tambourines and musical instruments and a pompous military display.
Then the Israelites rushed from their ambush and began killing them, and many of them died. The survivors fled into the mountains, leaving all their possessions behind to be captured by the Jews.
So the wedding was turned into an occasion for mourning, and the joyful music into a dirge.
When Jonathan and Simon had taken revenge for the death of their brother, they returned to the marshes of the Jordan.
As soon as Bacchides heard about this, he came on the Sabbath to the banks of the Jordan with a large army.
Jonathan said to his men, “Get up! We must fight for our lives, for this is a new and desperate situation.
The battle is now in front of us, the Jordan River is behind us, and marshes and woods are on either side of us. There is no escape!
Therefore, pray to God that you may be rescued from your enemies.”
Then they began to fight.
Jonathan and his men jumped into the Jordan and swam over to the other side, but the enemy did not follow.
That day a thousand of Bacchides’ men were killed.

After returning to Jerusalem, Bacchides built strongholds throughout Judea. He built fortresses with high walls and gates and bars in Jericho, Emmaus, Beth-horon, Bethel, Timnath, Pharathon, and Tephon.
Bacchides placed garrisons in them to harass the Israelites.
He fortified the towns of Beth-zur and Gazara and also the citadel, and he put troops in them, along with provisions.
He took as hostages the sons of the leading men of the country and imprisoned them in the citadel at Jerusalem.

In midspring of the one hundred fifty-third year of Greek rule, Alcimus ordered that the walls separating the Gentiles from the inner court of the Temple be torn down, thereby destroying the works of the prophets. But he had hardly started this
when he suffered a stroke. Paralyzed and speechless, he could no longer give commands even in his own home, so the work stopped.
Then Alcimus died in great agony.
After he learned that Alcimus had died, Bacchides returned to the king, and Judea had peace for two years.
Then the ungodly began to plot, saying, “Jonathan and those with him live in peace and are full of confidence. Let us bring Bacchides back, and he can capture them all in one night.”
So they went to Bacchides and advised him to carry out this plan.
Bacchides set out with a large army, and he sent secret letters to his military allies in Judea, instructing them to seize Jonathan and his men. But this failed because Jonathan learned of the plot.
His men captured about fifty people in Judea who were the ringleaders of the plot, and they killed them.
Then Jonathan, Simon, and their followers withdrew to Bethbasi in the wilderness, and they rebuilt and fortified it.
When Bacchides found out what they had done, he gathered his entire army and sent word to his allies in Judea.
They set up camp outside Bethbasi, and they made siege weapons and attacked the town for many days.
Jonathan left his brother Simon in the town and went out into the country with a few men.
He struck down Odomera and his family and the sons of Phasiron in their tents. Then he attacked Bacchides’ army.
Simon and his troops rushed out of the town and set the siege weapons on fire.
They fought against Bacchides and overcame him, inflicting great losses on him, and his planning and effort came to nothing.
Bacchides was angry with the renegades who had advised him to come into their country, so he killed many of them. Then he decided to return to his own country.
When Jonathan heard about this retreat, he sent ambassadors to Bacchides to offer peace and obtain release of the captives.
Bacchides accepted the terms and kept his word, swearing that he would do Jonathan no harm as long as he lived.
Bacchides released the prisoners he had taken previously from Judea, returned to his own country, and never again set foot in Judea.
So war ended in Israel, and Jonathan settled in Michmash, where he judged the people and rooted out the wicked from Israel.
In the one hundred sixtieth year of Greek rule, Alexander Epiphanes, the son of Antiochus Epiphanes, arrived and occupied Ptolemais. The people accepted him, and he began his reign there.
When King Demetrius Soter heard of this, he gathered together a very large army and went to fight him.
Demetrius sent Jonathan a letter containing words of peace and promises to honor him.
He reasoned, “We need to make peace with him before he makes an alliance with Alexander against us.
For he will remember all the harm we have done to him, to his brothers, and to his nation.”
So Demetrius gave Jonathan authority to recruit and equip an army, hoping to make him a military ally. He also ordered that the hostages in the citadel should be released to Jonathan.
Jonathan came to Jerusalem and read the letters to all the people and to those in the citadel.
They were greatly alarmed when they heard that the king had given him authority to recruit an army,
but the guards at the citadel released the hostages to Jonathan, and he returned them to their parents.
Thereafter, Jonathan lived in Jerusalem and began to rebuild and repair the city.
He ordered workers to build walls around Mount Zion, using squared stones for better fortification.
The foreigners living in the strongholds built by Bacchides fled,
each one leaving his place and returning to his own country.
Only in Beth-zur did some remain who had forsaken the law of Moses and the commandments, for this was a place of refuge for them.

King Alexander heard of the promises that Demetrius had made to Jonathan. He was told of the battles fought and the brave deeds done by Jonathan and his brothers, as well as the hardships they had endured.
He said, “Could we ever find another man like this? We should make him our friend and our ally.”
So the king sent Jonathan a letter that read:
“This letter is from King Alexander to his brother Jonathan. Greetings.
“We have heard that you are a valiant warrior who is worthy to be our friend.
Therefore, today we make you high priest of your nation, and you will be one of the king’s favored leaders and will promote our interests and keep our friendship.”
So in midautumn of the one hundred sixtieth year of Greek rule, at the Festival of Shelters, Jonathan put on the holy vestments, and he recruited troops and heavily armed them.
When Demetrius heard about this, he was very distressed and said,
“What have we done that Alexander has thwarted our plans? He has gotten ahead of us and strengthened himself by gaining the friendship of the Jews.
I’ll do the same thing; I’ll send a letter of friendship to them and offer them honor and gifts so that they will help me.”
So he sent this letter to them:
“We have heard that you have kept your agreement with us and have continued our friendship and have not sided with our enemies. This makes us glad.
Now continue to keep good faith with us, and we will richly reward you for all your efforts on our behalf.
We will grant you many privileges and give you many gifts.
“I now exempt you and all the Jews from all the tribute taxes. I also release you from the tax on salt and the crown taxes.

And from this day forward, I release you from paying the standard tax of one-third of all grain and half of all fruit that is harvested. I will not collect this from Judea or from the three districts that were added to it from Samaria and Galilee from this day and forever.
Jerusalem and its surrounding towns will be exempted from paying taxes on the tithes and revenues it receives.
I release my control of the citadel in Jerusalem and give it to the high priest so that he can station his own guards in it.
I am setting free, without ransom, every one of the Jews who has been brought captive from Judea into my kingdom, and all their taxes—even on their cattle—are remitted.

“I order that all festivals, Sabbaths, new moon celebrations, and appointed days, along with three days before and after each festival, are days of immunity and freedom for all the Jews in my kingdom.
On these days, no one will have authority to take anything from the Jews or harass them.
“Thirty thousand Jews will be allowed to enroll in the king’s army; provisions will be provided for them as for all the king’s troops.

Some of them will be assigned to the great fortresses of the king. Others will be given positions of trust within the kingdom. I will allow their officers and leaders to be chosen from their own ranks, and I will let them live according to their own laws, just as the king has commanded for those in Judea.
The three districts that have been added to Judea from Samaria will be fully annexed, so that they may answer to only one authority—the high priest.
“I give Ptolemais and its adjoining lands to the Temple in Jerusalem in order to meet the expenses of public worship.
I grant 375 pounds of silver annually from the king’s treasury.
All the additional funds that were denied in previous years will be given from now on for the upkeep of the Temple.
In addition, my officials will no longer collect the tribute tax of 125 pounds of silver from the income of the Temple; it will belong to the priests who minister there.

If anyone flees into the Temple in Jerusalem or into its surrounding territory because of a debt owed to the king or anyone else, that person will be released from the debt and will receive back all property taken as collateral.
The costs for rebuilding and restoring the Temple will be taken from the king’s revenues.
The king will also cover the cost of rebuilding the walls and fortifications of Jerusalem and the rest of Judea.”
When Jonathan and the people heard this message, they did not believe it, because they remembered the tremendous harm that Demetrius had done to Israel and how much he had oppressed the people.
They continued to side with Alexander, because he had been the first to offer them a peace treaty. So they remained his ally as long as he lived.
King Alexander gathered a large army and moved his camp near the army of Demetrius.
Then the armies of the two kings began to fight each other. The army of Demetrius fled, and Alexander’s army pursued them and won the battle.
They continued to pursue them until sundown, and Demetrius was killed that day.
Alexander sent ambassadors to Ptolemy Philometor, king of Egypt, with this message:
“I have returned to my kingdom and regained the throne of my ancestors. I have secured my reign by defeating Demetrius. I have regained control of our country
by destroying Demetrius and his army in battle, and now we have seized the throne of his kingdom.

Therefore, let us make a mutual pact of friendship. Give me your daughter in marriage, and I will become your son-in-law. Then I will give you and your daughter gifts that are worthy of your position.”
King Ptolemy answered,
Now I will do what you asked, but meet me at Ptolemais so that we may see one another. Then I will give you my daughter and become your father-in-law as you requested.”
So Ptolemy left Egypt with his daughter Cleopatra and came to Ptolemais in the one hundred sixty-second year of Greek rule.
King Alexander met him on friendly terms there, and Ptolemy gave Alexander his daughter Cleopatra in marriage. Ptolemy celebrated her marriage at Ptolemais with great and royal splendor.
King Alexander wrote to Jonathan that he should come and meet him.
So Jonathan went in stately ceremony to Ptolemais and met the two kings there. Jonathan gave them and their favored leaders silver, gold, and many other gifts and thereby gained their favor.
Some ungodly troublemakers from Israel gathered together to bring accusations against him, but the king paid no attention to them.
Alexander commanded that Jonathan should be clothed with a royal purple robe instead of his ordinary clothes, and it was done.

Then the king gave him a seat of honor at his side. He said to his officers, “Escort Jonathan to the middle of the city and proclaim that no one is to bring charges against him for any reason, nor should anyone even annoy him.”
When Jonathan’s accusers saw that he was being honored and that he was clothed in a royal purple robe, they all fled.
So the king honored him and declared in writing that he was one of his most favored leaders, and he made him general and governor of Judea.
Then Jonathan returned to Jerusalem with a sense of peace and joy.
In the one hundred sixty-fifth year of Greek rule, Demetrius Nicator, the son of Demetrius Soter, came from Crete to the land of his ancestors.
When King Alexander heard about it, he was very troubled and returned to Antioch.
Demetrius appointed Apollonius governor of Coelesyria. Apollonius then gathered together a large army and set up camp outside Jamnia. He sent this message to Jonathan, the high priest:
“You are the only one who opposes us. People laugh at me and reproach me because of you. Why should you dominate us in the hill country?
If you are so confident in your forces, come down and meet us on the plain. There we can test each other’s strength, for I have the power of the cities behind me.
Ask and learn who I am and who my allies are, and you will find that you cannot stand up to us. After all, your relatives have already been put to flight twice in their own land.
You will not be able to defend yourselves against my horsemen and my army on the plain, where there are no rocks, or even pebbles, to hide behind or any place to which you can escape.”
When Jonathan heard the message from Apollonius, he was stirred to action. He chose ten thousand men and marched out from Jerusalem, and his brother Simon met him to help him.
They set up camp outside Joppa, for the gates of the town had been closed because a garrison of Apollonius was in Joppa. When Jonathan’s army began to attack it,
those in the town became terrified. So they opened the gates to him, and Jonathan captured Joppa.

When Apollonius heard about this, he assembled three thousand horsemen and a large army and marched to Azotus, as though he were going to pass through the area. But immediately he went out on to the plain because he had many horsemen he could rely on.
Jonathan pursued him to Azotus, and they fought there.
Apollonius had secretly left a thousand horsemen behind Jonathan’s army.
Jonathan realized that there was an ambush behind him, for they surrounded his army and shot arrows at his soldiers from morning until evening.
But his men stood firm, as Jonathan had ordered them, while the enemy’s horses grew tired.
Then Simon brought his army forward and attacked the enemy’s ranks of foot soldiers, for their horsemen had become exhausted. He crushed the enemy, and they fled.
The horsemen scattered across the plain and fled to Azotus, where they took refuge in Beth-dagon, the temple of their idol.
But Jonathan set fire to Azotus and the surrounding towns. He carried away their possessions and burned down the temple of Dagon, along with all who had fled into it.
Almost eight thousand people were killed, whether by sword or by fire.
Then Jonathan moved his army and set up camp outside Ashkelon. The people came out of the town to greet him with great ceremony.
After this, Jonathan returned to Jerusalem with his people and a large amount of plunder.
When King Alexander heard about these deeds, he honored Jonathan even more.

He sent him a buckle of gold, a gift that is customarily given only to those whom the king regards as members of the royal family. He also gave Jonathan the town of Ekron and all its surrounding villages.

Then King Ptolemy Philometor of Egypt gathered together an army as innumerable as the sands of the seashore, along with many ships. He planned to seize Alexander’s kingdom by treachery and add it to his own kingdom.

He marched into Syria with peaceful words, and the people opened the gates of their cities and greeted him. They did this because King Alexander had ordered them to welcome him, since Ptolemy was his father-in-law.
As Ptolemy entered each town, he stationed a garrison of soldiers there.

When he approached Azotus, the people showed him the ruins of the temple of Dagon, which Jonathan had destroyed by fire. They also showed him the town and its surroundings, which had been leveled, and the corpses lying about. Lining the road were the charred bodies of those whom Jonathan had burned in the battle, for the people had piled them along Ptolemy’s route in heaps.
They told King Ptolemy that Jonathan had done these things, for they wanted the king to dislike him. But the king said nothing.
Jonathan met Ptolemy at Joppa with great ceremony, and they greeted one another and spent the night there.
Jonathan accompanied the king as far as the Eleutherus River; then he returned to Jerusalem.
Continuing in his plot against Alexander, King Ptolemy gained control of the coastal cities, as far as Seleucia on the coast.
He sent ambassadors to King Demetrius to say, “Come, let us make a pact with each other. I will give you my daughter, who is now married to Alexander, and you will reign over your father’s kingdom.
For I regret that I gave Alexander my daughter, since he has tried to kill me.”
He accused Alexander because he coveted his kingdom.
So he took his daughter from Alexander and gave her to Demetrius, and it was now obvious that Ptolemy and Alexander were enemies.
Then Ptolemy Philometor entered Antioch and crowned himself king of Asia; so now he wore two crowns, that of Egypt and that of Asia.
At this time King Alexander was in Cilicia because there was a rebellion there.
But when Alexander heard what had happened, he marched out to fight against Ptolemy, who met him with a strong force and routed Alexander’s armies.
Alexander fled to Arabia to seek protection. King Ptolemy’s triumph was complete
when Zabdiel the Arab cut off Alexander’s head and sent it back to Ptolemy.
However, King Ptolemy died three days later, and his troops in each of the strongholds were killed by the local residents.
As a result, Demetrius Nicator became king in the one hundred sixty-seventh year of Greek rule.
In those days Jonathan gathered forces from Judea to seize the citadel in Jerusalem. They built many war machines to besiege it.
But some renegades who hated their own nation went to King Demetrius Nicator and told him that Jonathan was attacking the citadel.
When Demetrius heard this, he was angry and set out at once for Ptolemais. He wrote to Jonathan, demanding that he end the siege and meet him for a conference in Ptolemais as soon as possible.
When Jonathan heard this, he ordered the siege to continue. Then, despite the danger, he set out with some of the priests and elders of Israel.
He took gold, silver, rich garments, and many other presents and went to meet the king at Ptolemais, and there he won the king’s favor.
Even though certain renegades of his nation made complaints against Jonathan,
the king treated him as his predecessors had done, and he exalted Jonathan in the sight of all his favored leaders.
The king confirmed Jonathan’s position as high priest and all his previous distinctions, and he declared him to be one of his most favored leaders.
Jonathan requested that the king exempt Judea and the three districts of Samaria from taxes, and he promised the king eleven tons of silver in return.
The king consented and wrote this letter to Jonathan about all these things:
“This letter is from King Demetrius to his brother Jonathan and to the nation of the Jews. Greetings.
“This is a copy of a letter I am sending to our relative Lasthenes concerning you. I am sending it so that you might know the contents of the letter.
“‘This letter is from King Demetrius to his esteemed relative Lasthenes. Greetings.
“‘We are determined to do good to the nation of the Jews, for they show their goodwill toward us by being our friends and keeping their agreements with us.

We have confirmed that they possess all the territory of Judea and the three districts of Aphairema, Lydda, and Ramathaim, which were taken from Samaria and added to Judea. For all who offer sacrifices in Jerusalem, we have granted freedom from the annual royal tax and from taxes on their crops and fruit.
From this moment on, we release them from taxes on tithes, the tax on salt, and the crown tax.
Not a single one of these exemptions will ever be revoked.
See that you make a copy of these instructions and give it to Jonathan. Then post this where people can see it on the holy mountain of Zion.’”

King Demetrius Nicator saw that peace reigned throughout the land and that no one resisted him, so he dismissed all his troops, sending each to his own home. He retained the foreign soldiers, however, whom he had recruited from Gentile islands. As a result, he was hated by all the dismissed troops, who had served under his predecessors.

There was a man named Trypho, who had been one of Alexander’s supporters. When he saw that all the dismissed troops were grumbling against Demetrius, he went to Imalkue the Arab, who was raising Antiochus, Alexander’s young son.

Trypho urged the Arab to let him take Antiochus and make him king in his father’s place. Trypho related to him all that Demetrius had done and how his soldiers hated him. Trypho remained there for many days.

Meanwhile, Jonathan sent word to King Demetrius, asking him to remove the soldiers from the citadel at Jerusalem and from the strongholds, because they were constantly fighting against the Israelites.
Demetrius sent this message back to Jonathan: “I will gladly do this for you and your people, and I will also greatly honor you and your nation when the opportunity arises.
Therefore, please help yourself and me by sending some of your men to support me, because my troops have revolted.”
So Jonathan sent 3,000 seasoned troops to him at Antioch, and the king was glad at their arrival.
Then 120,000 people of the city gathered together to kill the king,
but he fled into his palace. The people seized control of the streets and began to fight,
so the king called the Jewish troops to his aid. They rallied to assist him and spread out through the city. They killed about 100,000 people that day
and set fire to the city. They also seized a large amount of plunder and saved the king’s life.
When the citizens saw that the Jews controlled the city and could do as they pleased, their courage failed, and they cried to the king. They begged him,
“Grant us peace, and make the Jews stop attacking us and our city.”
Then the citizens threw down their arms and made peace. So the Jews were honored by the king and all the people of his kingdom, and they returned to Jerusalem with a large amount of plunder.
But when King Demetrius’s rule was secure and the land was peaceful under his government,
he broke his promises and alienated himself to Jonathan. Instead of repaying Jonathan for the favors he had been given, the king caused him much trouble.
After this, Trypho returned with Antiochus, Alexander’s young son, who was then crowned as king.
All the troops that Demetrius had dismissed joined Antiochus’s forces and fought against Demetrius, who was routed.
Trypho captured the elephants and gained control of Antioch.
Then young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan, saying, “I confirm your position as high priest. I appoint you as ruler over the four districts and confirm you as one of the king’s favored leaders.”
He sent him a gold plate from his table service and gave him permission to drink from a gold cup and to be clothed in purple and wear a gold buckle.
Antiochus appointed Jonathan’s brother Simon to be governor from the borders of Tyre to the borders of Egypt.
Jonathan left and visited cities west of the Euphrates River, and all the armies of Syria joined forces with him. When he came to Ashkelon, the people came out to honor him.
He went from there to Gaza, where he was denied admission, so he attacked it and burned its surrounding towns and carried away their possessions.
The people of Gaza pleaded with Jonathan, and he made peace with them. But he took the sons of their rulers as hostages and sent them to Jerusalem. Then he continued northward as far as Damascus.
Jonathan heard that the officers of Demetrius had come to Kadesh in Galilee with a large army, intending to remove him from power.
Jonathan went to fight them, leaving his brother Simon in Judea.
Simon set up camp outside Beth-zur, surrounded it, and besieged it for many days.
The people asked for terms of peace, and he granted them. But he removed the people from the town, took control of it, and placed a garrison in it.
Jonathan and his army set up camp by the Sea of Galilee. Early in the morning they marched on to the plain of Hazor.
The army of foreigners hid a contingent of soldiers in the mountains. Then they met Jonathan’s army face to face on the plain.
When the soldiers in the mountains came out of hiding and joined the battle,
everyone on Jonathan’s side fled. The only ones who remained were Mattathias son of Absalom and Judas son of Chalphi, commanders of the army.
Jonathan tore his clothes in grief and put dust upon his head and prayed.
Then he returned to the battle and sent the enemy running.

When Jonathan’s soldiers who were fleeing saw this, they returned to the battle to help him, and together they chased the enemy all the way to the enemy camp at Kadesh. There Jonathan and his men set up their camp as well.
That day about three thousand enemy soldiers were killed. Then Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.
Jonathan saw that the time was right to confirm his friendship with the Romans, so he chose certain men and sent them to Rome with this mission.
He also sent letters to the Spartans and to other places for the same purpose.
When the men arrived in Rome, they entered the senate chamber and said, “Jonathan the high priest and the Jewish nation have sent us to renew our former friendship and alliance.”
So the Romans provided these men with letters addressed to the authorities of each place, instructing them to provide safe conduct for them as they made their way back to Judea.
This is a copy of the letter Jonathan wrote to the Spartans:
“This letter is from Jonathan the high priest, the high council, the priests, and the rest of the Jewish people. It is addressed to our brothers the Spartans. Greetings.
“Long ago your king Arius sent a letter to our high priest Onias, stating that you are our brothers, as the attached copy shows.
Onias received your ambassador with honor and accepted the letter, which declared our alliance and friendship.
We do not need such alliances, since we find encouragement in our sacred books.
Nevertheless, we have chosen to renew our family ties and friendship with you so that we don’t become strangers to you, for a long time has passed since you wrote to us.
We think of you on every special occasion. At our festivals and on other special days we remember you as we offer sacrifices and prayers, for it is fitting to remember brothers at these times.
We rejoice at your fame.
“We have had many troubles and wars on every side because the neighboring kings have attacked us.
We did not want to trouble you or our allies and friends during these wars,
for our help comes from God. We have been rescued from our enemies, and they have been humbled.
Nevertheless, we have selected Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason and have sent them to Rome to renew our former friendship and alliance with the Romans.
We have also instructed them to visit you and bring our greetings and to give you this letter concerning the renewal of our family ties.
We will be grateful for your response to it.”
Following is a copy of the letter the Spartans had previously sent to Onias:
“This letter is from Arius, king of the Spartans, to Onias the high priest. Greetings.
“We have discovered a document that states that the Spartans and the Jews are brothers and that they are all descendants of Abraham.
Now that we have learned this, write to us and let us know how you are doing.
For our part, we declare to you that what is yours—your cattle and your possessions—is ours, and what is ours is yours. This is what we have ordered our envoys to report to you.”
Jonathan then heard that Demetrius’s commanders had returned with an even larger army than before to wage war against him.
So Jonathan marched out from Jerusalem and met them in the region of Hamath, for he did not want to give them a chance to invade his own country.
He sent scouts into their camp, who returned and reported that the enemy was preparing to attack that night.
When the sun set, Jonathan commanded his men to be on guard all night and to keep their weapons at hand, and he posted sentries around the camp.
When the enemy learned that Jonathan and his men were ready for battle, they were filled with dread. They lit fires in their camp and then retreated.
But Jonathan and his army did not know until morning that the enemy had retreated, because they had seen their campfires burning.
Jonathan chased them but did not catch them because they had crossed the Eleutherus River.
Jonathan then went after the Arabs called Zabadeans. He defeated them and carried away their possessions.
He marched on and came to Damascus and passed through all that country.
Simon also marched out and went as far as Ashkelon and the neighboring fortresses. Then he turned to Joppa and took possession of it,
for he heard that the people were planning to hand their stronghold over to the supporters of Demetrius. Simon then stationed a garrison there to guard it.
When Jonathan returned, he officially called together the high council and made plans with them to build fortresses in Judea.
They planned to heighten the walls of Jerusalem and erect a barrier to separate the citadel from the city, so that the soldiers in the citadel could neither buy nor sell.

So the people worked together to rebuild the city. They repaired a collapsed section of the wall that bordered the Kidron Valley on the east side of the city. Jonathan also repaired the section called Chaphenatha.
Simon built Adida in the western foothills; he fortified it and erected gates that locked with bars.
Trypho was determined to make himself king of Asia and to assume the crown and overthrow King Antiochus.
But he was afraid that Jonathan would prevent him and fight against him, so he marched out to Beth-shan looking for some way to capture Jonathan and kill him.
Jonathan went with forty thousand select troops to meet Trypho in battle at Beth-shan.
When Trypho saw that Jonathan had come with a large army, he was afraid to fight against him.
So he received him with honor, commended him to all his favored leaders, and gave him presents. Trypho ordered his favored leaders and his troops to obey him as they would himself.
He said to Jonathan, “Why have you troubled all these people when you and I are not at war?

Choose a few men to stay with you and send the rest home, and then come with me to Ptolemais. I will give you that city and the rest of the fortresses, along with their garrisons and officials. Then I will go home, for that is why I came here.”
Jonathan believed him and did as he had suggested. He sent most of his army back to Judea,
keeping three thousand men with him. Then he sent two thousand of them into Galilee and kept only one thousand for himself.
But as soon as Jonathan entered Ptolemais, the people of the city shut the gates and captured him; then they killed everyone who had entered with him.
Trypho dispatched foot soldiers and horsemen to Galilee and the great plain of Esdraelon to destroy all of Jonathan’s soldiers.
After Jonathan’s soldiers concluded that Jonathan and his troops had been captured and killed, they encouraged one another and marched in close formation, ready for battle.
When Trypho’s troops realized that Jonathan’s men were ready to fight for their lives, they turned back.
So Jonathan’s men returned safely to Judea. They mourned for Jonathan and those who died with him, and all Israel grieved deeply.

Then all the nations surrounding them sought to destroy them. They said, “Israel has no leader and no one to help them. Now is the time to fight against them and blot out all memory of them from the world.”
Simon heard that Trypho was assembling a very large army to invade Judea and destroy it.
Seeing that the people were trembling with fear, Simon went up to Jerusalem and assembled the people.

He encouraged them, saying, “You know what great things my brothers and my father’s family and I have done for the laws and the Temple. You know the wars we have waged and the hardships we have experienced.
For this cause—for the sake of Israel—all my brothers have lost their lives, and I alone am left.
Far be it from me to spare my own life in time of trouble, for I am no better than my brothers.
Nevertheless, I will avenge my nation and the Temple and your wives and children, for all the Gentiles have gathered together in hatred to destroy us.”
The people were inspired once again when they heard these words.
They cried out to Simon, “You are our leader in place of your brothers Judas and Jonathan.
Lead us in battle, and we will obey your every word.”
So Simon assembled the army and hurried to complete the walls of Jerusalem, fortifying it on all sides.
He sent a large force to Joppa under the command of Jonathan son of Absalom, and they drove out the residents and remained there.
Trypho and his large army left Ptolemais to invade Judea, and they took Jonathan along under guard.
Simon set up camp in Adida, facing the plain.
When Trypho learned that Simon had taken the place of his brother Jonathan and was preparing to fight against him, he sent envoys to Simon with this message:
“We have detained your brother Jonathan for the money that he owed the king’s treasury when he was managing the king’s affairs in Judea.
Send 7,500 pounds of silver and two of his sons as hostages, so that when he is set free, he will not revolt against us. Then we will release him.”
Although Simon did not believe that Trypho could be trusted, he ordered the money and the children to be sent. He did not want the people of Israel to hate him and say,
“Jonathan died because Simon did not send the money and the children.”
So he sent the children and the 7,500 pounds of silver. But Trypho broke his word and did not release Jonathan.
After this, Trypho entered the country to destroy it. His troops took a detour along the road that leads to Adora, but Simon and his army countered them wherever they went.
The soldiers in the citadel sent envoys to Trypho, asking him to hurry to them through the wilderness to bring them food.
So Trypho got all his horsemen ready to leave; but that night a very heavy snow fell, and he could not go. Instead he went into Gilead.
As he neared Baskama, he killed Jonathan and buried him there.
Then Trypho changed course and returned to his own country.
Simon sent for the remains of his brother Jonathan and buried him in Modein, the town of his ancestors.
All Israel wept loudly for him, and they mourned for him many days.
Over the tomb of his father and his brothers, Simon built a tall monument with polished stone at the front and back.
He also erected seven pyramids facing each other for his father, his mother, and his four brothers.
He surrounded these with an elaborate arrangement of large pillars, upon which he hung armor as an eternal memorial. Beside the armor he carved ships large enough to be visible to those at sea.
This tomb remains in Modein even to this day.
Trypho conspired against young King Antiochus and killed him.
He became king in his place, assuming the crown of Asia, and brought great evils upon the kingdom.
But Simon strengthened the strongholds of Judea, fortifying them with high towers, massive walls, and gates locked with bars. He also stored food in the strongholds.
Simon selected ambassadors and sent them to King Demetrius Nicator, hoping to gain relief from taxes for his nation, since Trypho had plundered the land.
King Demetrius answered this request with the following letter:
“This letter is from King Demetrius to Simon, the high priest and favored leader of kings, and to the high council and the Jewish nation. Greetings.

“We have received the gold crown and the palm branch that you sent. We are ready to establish a lasting peace with you and to write to our officials, instructing them to release you from the tribute tax.
All that was previously agreed upon remains in force, and the fortresses you have built are yours to keep.
We forgive any oversights or faults you have committed to this day, and we cancel the crown tax that you owe. If there are any other taxes in Jerusalem, they are now canceled.
If any of you are qualified to join the royal guard, you will be allowed to enroll. Let there be peace between us.”
In the one hundred seventieth year of Greek rule, the yoke of the Gentiles was removed from Israel.
At that time the people of Israel began to date their documents and public records in this way: “In the first year of Simon the great high priest, the commander and leader of the Jews.”
In those days Simon set up camp outside Gazara and surrounded it with troops. He constructed a siege machine and directed it against the town. He attacked one tower and captured it.
The soldiers inside the siege machine entered the town, creating a great uproar.
The men in the town, together with their wives and children, went up to the wall, tore their clothes, and cried out with a loud voice, asking Simon to grant them terms of peace.
They said, “Do not treat us as our evil deeds deserve but according to your mercy.”

So Simon reached an agreement with them. He did not destroy them, but he expelled them from the town and purified the houses where there had been idols. Then he entered the town, singing hymns of praise.
Having cleansed the town of all impurity, Simon appointed people to live there who would observe the law of Moses. He also fortified the town and built a house for himself there.
Then Simon prevented those who were in the citadel at Jerusalem from going in and out and from buying and selling in the countryside. So they became very hungry, and many of them died from famine.
They begged Simon for terms of peace, which he granted. Then he expelled them from the citadel and cleansed it from impurity.

On June 3 in the one hundred seventy-first year of Greek rule, the Jews entered the citadel with thanksgiving, waving palm branches and playing harps and cymbals and stringed instruments. They sang hymns and songs, because Israel’s great enemy had finally been destroyed.
Simon decreed that this occasion should be celebrated every year with gladness. He strengthened the fortifications of the Temple hill near the citadel, and he and his men lived there.
Since Simon’s son John had now reached manhood, Simon made him commander of all the armies. John kept his residence in Gazara.
In the one hundred seventy-second year of Greek rule, King Demetrius assembled his army and marched into Media. He was hoping to gain support for a war against Trypho.
When Arsaces, king of Persia and Media, heard that Demetrius had invaded his territory, he sent one of his commanders to capture him alive and bring him to him.
The commander defeated the army of Demetrius, captured him, and brought him to Arsaces, who kept him prisoner.
Judea was at rest as long as Simon ruled,
To crown his glory, he captured Joppa for a seaport
He extended the borders of his nation
Simon captured many prisoners of war
The people farmed the land in peace.
Old men sat in the squares and talked of good times,
Simon provided food for the towns
He established peace in the land,
The people relaxed under their own vines and fig trees.
No enemy remained in the land to fight them;
Simon strengthened the lowly
He made the sanctuary glorious
News of Jonathan’s death reached as far as Rome and Sparta, and they were deeply grieved.
They heard that his brother Simon had become high priest in his place and was ruling over the nation and the cities there.
So they wrote to Simon on bronze tablets to renew the friendship and alliance they had made with his brothers Judas and Jonathan.
The letter from the Spartans was presented to the high council in Jerusalem. It read as follows:
“This letter is from the rulers and the people of Sparta to the high priest Simon, the high council, the priests, and the rest of the Jewish people, our brothers and sisters. Greetings.
“The ambassadors you sent to us have told us of your glory and honor, and we have enjoyed their visit.
We have recorded their message in our public archives as follows: ‘Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason, ambassadors of the Jews, have come to us to renew their friendship with us.

Our people were pleased to receive the men with honor and to put a copy of their message in the public archives as a record for the Spartan people. We have also sent a copy of their message to Simon the high priest.’”
After this, Simon confirmed the alliance with the Romans by sending Numenius to Rome with a large gold shield weighing 1,250 pounds.
When the people of Israel heard about all this, they said, “How can we thank Simon and his sons?
For he and his brothers and his father’s family have stood firm; they have repelled the enemies of Israel and established freedom for the nation.”
So they made an inscription on bronze tablets and mounted them on pillars on Mount Zion. This is a copy of what they wrote:
in Asaramel, the following proclamations were made in the high council of the priests, the people, the rulers of the nation, and the elders of the country:

“‘Because of the constant warfare in our country, Simon and his brothers, sons of Mattathias, a priest in the line of Joarib, have become great leaders among us. They have put themselves in danger and resisted the enemies of their nation in order to preserve the Temple and the law of Moses. They have brought great glory to their nation.
“‘Jonathan rallied his nation together and became the high priest; now he is dead.
When the enemies of Israel decided to invade the country and capture the Temple,
Simon came forward to fight for his nation. He spent much of his own money to arm the soldiers of his nation and pay them wages.

He fortified the towns of Judea, including Beth-zur, which lies on the border of Judea. At one time, the weapons of the enemies were stored there, but he defeated the enemy troops and replaced them with a garrison of Jews.

Simon fortified the coastal town of Joppa and also Gazara, which borders upon Azotus, where the enemy formerly lived. He settled Jews there and furnished those towns with everything needed to restore them.

“‘When the people saw Simon’s faithfulness and his determination to win glory for his nation, they made him their leader and high priest. They did this in return for all the things he had done and because of the justice and loyalty he showed his nation. In every way he sought to enhance his people’s power.

“‘During Simon’s reign, the country prospered under his guidance. He drove the Gentiles from the land, and he also drove them from the City of David in Jerusalem. From this citadel they had gone out to defile the Temple, ruining its purity.
But Simon settled Jews in the citadel and fortified it for the safety of the country and the city. He also heightened the walls of Jerusalem.
“‘Because of these things, King Demetrius confirmed Simon’s position as high priest,
made him one of his favored leaders, and granted him great honor.
For Demetrius had heard that the Romans regarded the Jews as their friends, military allies, and brothers, and that the Romans had received Simon’s ambassadors with honor.
“‘The Jews and their priests have decided that Simon should remain their leader and high priest until a true prophet should arise.
Simon should be their governor and take charge of the Temple. He should appoint officials over the Temple duties and over the country, the weapons, and the fortresses.
He should be obeyed by all, and all official documents in the country should be made in his name. And he should be clothed with purple and wear gold.

“‘None of the people or priests may nullify any of these decisions, nor may they oppose Simon’s orders. They may not gather an assembly in the country without his permission, nor may they be clothed in purple or wear a gold buckle.
Whoever violates or rejects any of these decisions will be liable to punishment.’”
All the people agreed to allow Simon to act in accordance with these decisions.
Simon accepted this and agreed to be high priest, commander, and leader of the Jews and priests, and to exercise supreme authority over them all.
The people ordered that this proclamation be engraved on bronze tablets and set up where people could see it in the Temple area.
They also ordered that copies be deposited in the treasury so that Simon and his sons could access them.
Antiochus Sidetes, the son of King Demetrius Soter, sent a letter from the Mediterranean islands to Simon, the priest and leader of the Jews, and to all the people.
