The letter read as follows:

“Certain rebels have seized control of the kingdom of our ancestors, but I intend to reclaim it and restore it to its former state. I have recruited a large army of foreign troops and have built warships,
and I plan to arrive in my country and take revenge on those who have destroyed our country and devastated many cities in my kingdom.
Therefore, I confirm all tax exemptions that the kings before me granted you, along with any other promises of release from payments.
I give you permission to mint your own coins in your country.
I declare Jerusalem and the Temple to be free. All the weapons you have made and the fortresses you have built and occupy are to remain yours.
Any debts owed to the king, including future obligations, are canceled from this moment and for all time.
When we regain control of our kingdom, we will highly honor you, your nation, and your Temple, so that your glory may be known throughout the world.”
In the one hundred seventy-fourth year of Greek rule, Antiochus Sidetes entered the land of his ancestors. All the troops rallied to his support so that only a few people supported Trypho.
King Antiochus pursued him, and Trypho fled to the coastal town of Dor.
Antiochus realized that Trypho was in deep trouble and that his troops had deserted him,
so Antiochus set up camp near Dor with 120,000 soldiers and 8,000 horsemen.
He surrounded the town, and his ships took up positions offshore. Antiochus shut off the town by land and sea so that no one could go in or out.
Meanwhile, Numenius and his companions arrived from Rome with letters to various kings and countries. The letters read as follows:
“This letter is from Lucius, consul of the Romans, to King Ptolemy Physcon. Greetings.
“Ambassadors of the Jews have come to us as friends and allies, and they wanted to renew our former friendship and alliance. They had been sent by the high priest Simon and by the Jewish people.
They also brought a gold shield weighing 1,250 pounds.

Therefore, we have decided without hesitation to send these instructions to many kings and countries: Do not harm the Jews or attack their cities or their land. Do not make alliances with anyone who wages war against the Jews.
As a token of our friendship, we have decided to accept the shield from them.
Therefore, if any troublemakers have fled to you from Judea, return them to the high priest Simon, so that he may punish them according to their law.”
This same message was sent to King Demetrius, Attalus, Ariarathes, and Arsaces
and to all the countries, including Sampsames, Sparta, Delos, Myndos, Sicyon, Caria, Samos, Pamphylia, Lycia, Halicarnassus, Rhodes, Phaselis, Cos, Side, Aradus, Gortyna, Cnidus, Cyprus, and Cyrene.
A copy of the letter was also sent to Simon the high priest.
King Antiochus Sidetes continued in his siege of Dor, assaulting it continually and building war machines to use against it. He trapped Trypho inside, and he could not escape.
Simon sent Antiochus two thousand select troops to help him, along with silver, gold, and a large amount of military equipment.
But Antiochus refused to receive them. Instead, he renounced all agreements he had made with Simon and alienated himself from him.
He sent Athenobius, one of his favored leaders, to meet with Simon and say, “You are occupying Joppa, Gazara, and the citadel in Jerusalem, which are cities of my kingdom.
You have devastated their territories, inflicted great damage on the land, and taken control of many places in my kingdom.
Therefore, give back the cities you have taken and the tribute taxes from the places you control beyond the borders of Judea.

Otherwise, give me nineteen tons of silver for the destruction that you have caused, along with nineteen tons more to reimburse me for the tribute taxes of the cities. If you fail to do this, we will come and attack you.”

So Athenobius, the king’s favored leader, came to Jerusalem. He was astonished when he saw Simon’s splendor—his cabinet with the gold and silver plate and his great magnificence. Then he delivered the king’s message.
Simon responded, “We have not taken anyone else’s land or property. Rather, we have taken what is the inheritance of our ancestors, which had been unjustly occupied by our enemies.
Now that we have the opportunity, we are merely recovering this inheritance.
Joppa and Gazara inflicted great harm on our people and our land, but we will give you 7,500 pounds of silver for them.”
Athenobius did not answer a single word in reply. He returned angrily to the king with this message and told him about Simon’s great splendor. The king was enraged.
Meanwhile, Trypho escaped by ship to Orthosia.
The king appointed Cendebeus commander of the coastal areas and gave him an army of foot soldiers and horsemen.
The king ordered him to set up camp outside Judea. He ordered him to build up Kedron, to fortify its gates, and to attack the Jews. But the king himself pursued Trypho.
So Cendebeus came to Jamnia and began to harass the people by raiding Judea, taking prisoners, and then killing them.
He built up Kedron and stationed horsemen and foot soldiers there so that they might make raids along the highways of Judea, as the king had commanded him.
Simon’s son John came up from Gazara and told his father what Cendebeus had done.

Simon called for his two eldest sons, Judas and John, and said to them, “My brothers and my father’s family and I have spent our whole lives fighting Israel’s battles. Things have gone well under our leadership, for we have rescued Israel many times.
Now I am old, but by God’s grace you have matured to manhood. You must replace me and my brother and continue fighting for our nation. May God help you.”
John chose twenty thousand soldiers and horsemen from Judea, and they marched out to fight Cendebeus. They camped for the night in Modein.
Then they got up early in the morning and moved out on to the plain, where they faced a large army of foot soldiers and horsemen. A stream separated the two armies.
As John and his troops lined up against the enemy, he saw that his troops were afraid to cross the stream. So he went over first. When his men saw him lead the way, they crossed over behind him.
John divided his army, positioning the horsemen in the center of the foot soldiers, for the enemy also had a large cavalry.
John’s men sounded the trumpets and attacked, and Cendebeus and his army fled. Many of the enemy were wounded and fell, and the rest fled into the fortress.
At the same time, John’s brother Judas was wounded, but John chased the enemy as far as Kedron, which Cendebeus had built up.
Some also fled into the towers in the fields of Azotus, but John burned these down. About two thousand enemy soldiers were killed, and John returned safely to Judea.
Ptolemy son of Abubus had been appointed governor over the plain of Jericho. He had a large amount of silver and gold,
for he was a son-in-law of Simon the high priest.
He became overly ambitious and wanted to gain control of the whole country. So he plotted against Simon and his sons to get rid of them by treachery.

As Simon was going through the towns of Judea and attending to their needs, he and his sons Mattathias and Judas went down to Jericho in late winter of the one hundred seventy-seventh year of Greek rule.
At Dok, a small fortress he had built, Ptolemy welcomed them with a deceptive display of friendliness. He invited them to a great banquet, but he hid his men in the fortress.
When Simon and his sons were drunk, Ptolemy and his men jumped up, grabbed their weapons, and rushed into the banquet hall, killing Simon and his two sons and some of his servants.
In this way, Ptolemy committed an act of great treachery, repaying evil for good.
Ptolemy wrote a report of his actions and sent it to King Antiochus Sidetes, asking him to send soldiers to help him. He also asked the king to place the towns and the country under his authority.
Ptolemy also sent soldiers to Gazara to kill Simon’s son John, and he sent letters to the army officers, asking them to come to him so he could give them silver and gold and gifts.
He sent other soldiers to capture Jerusalem and the Temple mount as well.
But someone ran ahead to Gazara and told John that his father and his brothers were dead and that Ptolemy had sent men to kill him, too.
When John heard this, he was astounded. He captured the men that came to kill him, and he killed them instead, for he knew their intentions.
The rest of John’s deeds, his battles, his brave accomplishments, his rebuilding of the walls, and his achievements,
are all recorded in the history of his high priesthood, beginning from the time he succeeded his father as high priest.
“This letter is from the Jews in Jerusalem and Judea to their fellow Jews in Egypt. Greetings and true peace to you.
“May God be good to you and remember the covenant he made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants.
May God give you a desire to worship him and to do his will with a loving heart and a generous spirit.
May he open your heart to his law and his commandments, and may he grant you peace.
May he hear your prayers and be reconciled to you, and may he never forsake you in the time of evil.
We are now praying for you here.

“When Demetrius Nicator reigned in the one hundred sixty-ninth year of Greek rule, we wrote to you of the trouble and intense conflict we experienced in the years after Jason defected from the holy land and from the kingdom.

He burned the Temple gate and killed innocent people. So we prayed to the Lord, and our prayers were answered. We offered sacrifices and fine flour, and we lit the lamps and set the Bread of the Presence on the table.
We are writing to remind you to commemorate this event by celebrating a second Festival of Shelters each year in the month of Kislev.

“This letter is from the people of Jerusalem and Judea, from the high council, and from Judas. It is written to Aristobulus, a member of the family of anointed priests and a teacher of King Ptolemy Physcon. This letter is also written to the Jews in Egypt. Greetings and good health to you.
“Having been rescued by God from dangerous times, we give him great thanks for championing our cause against the king.
God was the one who drove out those who fought against the holy city.
When their leader, Antiochus, was in Persia with what seemed to be an invincible army, he and his men were killed in the temple of the goddess Nanea, for he was deceived by her priests.
Hoping to secure large sums of money as a dowry, Antiochus led everyone to believe that he was going to marry Nanea. When he and his men arrived in Persia
and the priests of Nanea set out the treasure, Antiochus and a few men entered the interior of the temple. The priests closed the door, trapping them inside.

Then, opening a secret trapdoor in the ceiling, the priests threw stones down on Antiochus and his men, killing them. The priests then dismembered them, cutting off their heads and throwing the body parts outside.
May God, who has judged the wicked, be blessed in all things!

“Therefore, since we will be commemorating the purification of the Temple on the twenty-fifth day of the month of Kislev, we thought we should remind you also to celebrate this second Festival of Shelters, which also commemorates the day when the fire was given to Nehemiah to offer sacrifices. This fire was given to Nehemiah after he rebuilt the Temple and the altar.

“When our ancestors were taken captive into Persia, the devout priests at that time secretly took the live coals from the altar and hid them deep in a dry cistern. There they kept the holy fire safe in a place unknown to anyone.

When many years had passed, it pleased God to send Nehemiah back to Israel by order of the king of Persia. Nehemiah sent some of the descendants of those priests who had previously hidden the fire to look for it. They reported that they found no fire but instead found a thick liquid in the cistern. Nehemiah told them to draw it up and bring it to him.
Then he commanded the priests to pour this liquid over the wood and sacrifices placed on the wood.
This was done and sometime later, when the sun came out from behind a cloud, and a great fire broke out on the altar. Everyone was amazed,
and all the priests and the people prayed while the sacrifice was burning. Jonathan took the lead, and the others joined Nehemiah in a response.
“Their prayer went like this: ‘O Lord, Lord God, Creator of all things, you are awesome and strong, just and merciful. You alone are king, and you are kind;
you alone are gracious; you alone are just and almighty and eternal. It was you who saved Israel from all evil and chose our ancestors, setting them apart.
Accept this sacrifice for all your people Israel, and preserve your own inheritance and make it holy.
Gather together our scattered people. Free those who are slaves to the Gentiles. Look favorably on those who are despised and rejected, and let the Gentiles know that you are our God.
Torment our insolent oppressors.
Firmly plant your people in your Holy Place, as Moses said.’
“Then the priests sang hymns.
When the sacrifice was fully burned, Nehemiah ordered the remaining liquid to be poured over large stones.
When this was done, flames burst forth on them, but the light that blazed from the altar was even brighter.

“This became a well-known event. The king of Persia heard that a thick liquid had appeared in the place where the exiled priests had hidden the fire and that Nehemiah and those with him had used the liquid to burn the sacrifices.
The king verified the matter and then enclosed the place, declaring it sacred.
The king gained a great deal of revenue from the place, and he used this money to give gifts to people he favored.
Nehemiah and his people called this liquid nephthar, which means ‘purification,’ but many call it naphtha.
“The records show that it was Jeremiah the prophet who commanded those who went into captivity to hide some of the fire of the altar.
He also ordered them not to forget the commandments of the Lord and warned them not to be deceived in their thinking when they saw the gold and silver idols with their ornaments.
With similar speeches he told them to keep the law of Moses in their hearts.

“The same records tell us how God told the prophet to take the Tabernacle and the Ark with him until he came to the mountain where Moses had looked out over the land God had promised to give his people.
When Jeremiah arrived there, he found an empty cave into which he carried the Tabernacle, the Ark, and the altar of incense. Then he blocked the entrance.
Some of those who followed him wanted to mark the place, but they could not find it.
When Jeremiah heard this, he rebuked them, saying, ‘The place will be hidden until God gathers his people together again and shows them his mercy.
Then the Lord will reveal these things, and the glory of the Lord will appear in a cloud, as in the days of Moses and again when Solomon prayed that the Temple might be specially set apart for God.’
“It is also recorded how Solomon in his wisdom offered sacrifices for the dedication and completion of the Temple.
Just as Moses prayed to the Lord and fire came down from heaven and consumed the sacrifice, so also Solomon prayed and fire came down from heaven and consumed the sacrifice.
And Moses said, ‘Because the sin offering was not eaten, it was consumed.’
Solomon also celebrated the dedication for eight days.

“These same things were written in the records and in the memoirs of Nehemiah. It is recorded that Nehemiah established a library by collecting the books about the kings and the prophets, the writings of David, and the letters of the kings concerning offerings to fulfill vows.
Likewise, Judas collected all the books that were lost in our war, and now they are in our possession.
If you need these things, send someone to get them for you.
“We are writing to you because we are about to celebrate the purification of the Temple, and we would like you to celebrate this same festival.
It is God who has saved his people and returned to us our inheritance, our kingdom, our priesthood, and our holiness,

as he promised in the law of Moses. We trust that God will soon have mercy on us and gather us together from every land under heaven to the Holy Place. For he has saved us from great dangers and purified the Temple.”
This is the story of Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, including an account of the purification of the great Temple and the dedication of the altar.
This story recounts the wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator
and the heavenly apparitions seen by those heroes who fought bravely for Judaism. These heroes, though few in number, took the whole land and routed the barbarian hordes.
They regained the Temple renowned in all the world, liberated the city, and restored the laws of Moses, which were nearly abolished. The Lord showed great kindness and mercy to them.
All these things were recorded in five books by Jason of Cyrene, but we will attempt to condense them into one.
There are so many statistics—a veritable flood of material—that anyone who wants to study the narratives of history has a difficult job.
Therefore, our goal has been to make it easy for those who simply wish to read about these things and to help the studious to memorize more easily. We want all who read these things to profit.
As for ourselves, this work of condensing the records is a difficult task, yes, one of hard work and loss of sleep,
much like it is for those who prepare a banquet and try to please others. Yet we willingly undertake this labor for the sake of many.
We leave to compilers the exact handling of every detail, intending here to outline a brief digest.
The contractor of a new house must take care of the whole building, while the painter is concerned only with its decoration. So I think it is with us.
It is the historian’s duty to collect all that is known, to put the events in order, and to search out and discuss every detail.
But one who makes a digest is allowed to pursue brevity of speech and avoid lengthy explanations.
So let us begin the narrative without adding any further comment, for it would be foolish to make a long preface and then cut short the story itself!
In the days of Onias the high priest, the holy city of Jerusalem was at peace, and the laws of Moses were diligently observed, because Onias obeyed God and hated evil.
So even the kings honored the sanctuary and embellished the Temple with wonderful gifts.
Even Seleucus, king of Asia, paid from his own revenues all the expenses connected with offering the sacrifices.
But a man named Simon from the tribe of Benjamin opposed the high priest because he disagreed about how the city markets should be administered. Simon had been appointed manager of the Temple.
When he could not win his dispute with Onias, he went to Apollonius of Tarsus, who was governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia.

Simon told him that the treasury in Jerusalem was so full of wealth that it couldn’t be counted. Since this money did not belong to the account set aside for the sacrifices, Simon suggested that this money be brought under the king’s control.
When Apollonius saw the king, he told him about this money. Then the king called Heliodorus, who was in charge of his affairs, and ordered him to bring it back to him.
So Heliodorus immediately set out on his journey, under the guise of visiting the cities of Coelesyria and Phoenicia. But his real purpose was to fulfill the king’s order.
When Heliodorus came to Jerusalem, the high priest received him courteously. Heliodorus told him what he had heard about this large sum of money and asked if it was true.
The high priest told him that there were sums deposited to provide for widows and orphans.

He also stated that the rest belonged to Hyrcanus son of Tobiah, a man of prominent position. Contrary to what the wicked Simon had reported, the total amount was fifteen tons of silver and seven and a half tons of gold.
The high priest said he could not touch these deposits, for they had been brought for safekeeping to the Temple—the holy and sacred place that is honored throughout the whole world.
But because of the orders he had received from the king, Heliodorus said he had no choice but to take the money for the royal treasury.
So he set a day and entered the treasury to take inventory.

and the priests, dressed in their special clothing, threw themselves face down before the altar. They called upon God in heaven, who had given the law concerning the deposits, asking him to preserve the money for those who had deposited it.
Everyone who saw the high priest became heartbroken, for his face showed the inward anguish of his soul.
His body trembled with horror, making the sorrow in his heart clear to all who saw him.
Many of the people hurried from their homes to join in corporate prayer because the sanctuary was about to be defiled.
The women, dressed in sackcloth, gathered in the streets. The young women ran from their homes—some to the gates and some to the walls—while others peered out of windows.
All of them stretched their hands toward heaven in prayer.
It was pitiful to see everyone lying face down in anguish and to see the high priest in his agony.
While the people were calling to the almighty Lord to keep the deposits safe and secure for those who had given them,
Heliodorus went on with his plan.

But as he arrived at the treasury with his guard, the Lord of all spirits and all authority caused such an awesome heavenly apparition that all who had boldly accompanied Heliodorus collapsed in terror, overwhelmed by God’s power.
Before them appeared a horse splendidly decorated, and on the horse sat a fearsome rider clad in gold armor. The horse charged and reared fiercely, striking Heliodorus with its front hooves.

At the same time, two young men of amazing strength and striking beauty, dressed in magnificent clothing, appeared to Heliodorus. They stood on either side of him and whipped him continuously, striking him with blow after blow.
Heliodorus suddenly fell to the ground, overwhelmed by a deep darkness. His men came to his rescue. They picked him up, put him on a stretcher,
and carried him away. He had come into that treasury with a large retinue of servants and all his guard, but now he was carried away helpless. He had experienced the power of God.
Indeed, because of God’s intervention, he lay speechless and without hope of recovery.

The people praised the Lord because he had marvelously honored his sanctuary. And the Temple, which a short time before had been full of fear and commotion, was filled with joy and gladness because of the almighty Lord’s appearance.
Because Heliodorus was dying, some of his friends urged Onias to call upon the Most High to spare his life.
So the high priest, fearing that the king would suspect the Jews of foul play, offered a sacrifice for Heliodorus’s recovery.

While the high priest was making a sacrifice for atonement, the same young men, dressed in the same clothing, appeared to Heliodorus once again. They stood before him and said, “Give thanks to Onias the high priest, because for his sake the Lord has spared your life.
And you, having been whipped by God, should tell everyone of the great works and power of God.” Then they vanished.
Heliodorus offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made great vows to him, for he had spared his life. Then he said good-bye to Onias, and he and his troops returned to the king.
He told everyone about the works of the supreme God, whom he had seen with his own eyes.
Then the king asked Heliodorus what kind of person he should send to Jerusalem. Heliodorus replied,
“If you have any enemy or conspirator in your country, send him there. He will return to you whipped, if he survives at all, for there is undoubtedly a certain power of God in that place.
For the one who dwells in heaven is the guardian and protector of that place, and he strikes and destroys those who come to harm it.”
This is the story about Heliodorus and how the treasury was saved.

Previously we told the story about Simon, who betrayed his country by informing about the money in the sanctuary. Then he blamed Onias for what had happened to Heliodorus, as if he had caused all the trouble.

Simon even dared to accuse Onias of being a conspirator against the government, despite the fact that he was the benefactor of Jerusalem, the defender of his people, and a man zealous for the laws of Moses.
When Simon’s hatred got to such a point that his followers even committed murders,
Onias realized the danger of this rivalry. He also could see that Apollonius son of Menestheus, governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, was encouraging Simon in his hatred.
So Onias appealed to the king, not to accuse any of his own people, but with their good in mind, both as individuals and as a nation.
He saw that unless the king intervened, conditions would go from bad to worse because Simon would not stop his foolish actions.
When Seleucus died and Antiochus Epiphanes became king, Onias’s brother Jason became the high priest by corrupt means.
He went to the king, promising him thirteen and a half tons of silver immediately and another three tons from future revenue.

Besides this, he promised another five and a half tons of silver if the king would grant him a license to set up a school to promote Greek culture and a youth center and allow him to enroll people from Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch.
When the king approved this and Jason took office, he immediately began to force the Greek lifestyle on his people.

Jason rescinded the freedoms that the kings had granted the Jews through the mediation of John, the father of Eupolemus. (Eupolemus later went to Rome as ambassador to make a treaty of peace and alliance.) Jason also prohibited the people from keeping the law of Moses and introduced customs that were contrary to God’s law.
He went so far as to build a Greek school near the citadel, and he made the most outstanding young men wear hats that were usually worn by Greek students.
Jason was extremely successful in his efforts to introduce foreign and pagan customs, for he was a man of incredible evil who lacked every virtue to be a true high priest.

The priests were no longer concerned with the duties of the altar. Despising the Temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hurried off to take part in the sinful athletic events whenever there was a call for the games to begin.
Looking down on the values of their ancestors, they held Greek customs in the highest regard.
But disaster overtook them in the end, and the very ones whose values they desired and whose lifestyles they imitated were to become their enemies and tormentors.
For contempt for the laws of God does not go unpunished, a fact that time would prove.
Now when the games that were held every four years took place at Tyre in the king’s presence,

the evil Jason sent Hellenized citizens from Jerusalem to carry three hundred silver coins for the sacrifice to Hercules. But even the envoys considered it inappropriate to use the money for the sacrifice and decided it should be used for something else.
So the money intended by Jason for the sacrifice to Hercules was contributed by the envoys for the construction of some ships.

Apollonius son of Menestheus went to Egypt as an ambassador to attend the coronation of Ptolemy Philometor. Antiochus Epiphanes heard from Apollonius that Ptolemy was hostile toward him, so he took measures for the king’s security, going first to Joppa and then on to Jerusalem.
In Jerusalem, Jason and the people received him in magnificent style, welcoming him with torchlights and shouts of praise. From there, Antiochus returned with his army to Phoenicia.
Three years later Jason sent Menelaus, brother of the previously mentioned Simon, to carry money to the king and bring back the king’s decisions regarding certain important affairs.
But when Menelaus met with the king, he exaggerated his own authority and obtained the high priesthood for himself by offering eleven and a half tons of silver more than Jason paid.
Having received the king’s authorization, Menelaus returned home, but he was not worthy to be high priest. He had the hot temper of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast.
So Jason, who had undermined his own brother Onias, was undermined himself. He fled as a fugitive into the land of Ammon.
Menelaus continued to hold the position of high priest, but he did not send the king any of the payments he had promised.
He repeatedly ignored the requests for payment made by Sostratus, the commander of the citadel and the one in charge of collecting the king’s revenues. So both men were summoned by the king.
Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus as deputy high priest, and Sostratus left Crates as commander of the troops from Cyprus.
Meanwhile, a revolt broke out in Tarsus and Mallus because those areas had been given as a gift to Antiochis, the king’s concubine.
The king went immediately to settle the problem, leaving Andronicus, one of his nobles, to act in his place.

Menelaus saw an opportunity to strengthen his position, so he presented Andronicus with some gold vessels he had stolen from the Temple. He also sold some other vessels in Tyre and the surrounding towns.
When Onias became aware of what Menelaus was doing, he publicly exposed him, but he did it from the safety of the temple of Daphne near Antioch.

So Menelaus took Andronicus aside and urged him to kill Onias. Andronicus went to Onias and deceitfully offered him his right hand as a pledge that he would not kill him. Onias had some suspicions, but Andronicus persuaded him to leave the sanctuary. Then he immediately killed Onias without any regard to justice.
Both the Jews and the other nations were angry and very saddened by the unjust murder.
When King Antiochus Epiphanes returned from Cilicia, the Jews at Antioch went to him and complained about the unjust murder of Onias. The Greeks shared the Jews’ anger over this crime,
and Antiochus was deeply saddened by the news of Onias’s death. He even shed tears, remembering the wisdom and noble character of the dead man.

Inflamed with anger at the injustice, Antiochus commanded that Andronicus be stripped of his purple robe and be led naked through the city to the very place he had so shamelessly murdered Onias. There the wicked murderer was put to death. In this way the Lord repaid him with the punishment he deserved.

In Jerusalem, Lysimachus, the deputy high priest, committed many sacrilegious acts, which were planned by Menelaus. Reports of his actions spread abroad, and the people turned against Lysimachus, who had already stolen many gold items from the Temple.

Because the people were angry and ready to riot, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and launched an unjust attack under the command of Auranus, a man as advanced in foolishness as he was in age.
When the Jews saw what was happening, they attacked Lysimachus and his men with stones and blocks of wood. In wild confusion they threw ashes at the men to blind them.
As a result, many of Lysimachus’s men were wounded, some were killed, and the rest fled for their lives. As for the Temple robber himself, he was killed outside the treasury.
Charges about this affair were filed against Menelaus, the high priest.
When the king came to Tyre, the Jewish high council sent three men to plead their cause.
Menelaus, knowing he would be defeated, promised Ptolemy Macron son of Dorymenes a large bribe if he would persuade the king to favor him.
So Ptolemy, as though to get a breath of fresh air, took the king aside in a colonnade and persuaded him to change his mind.

Because of this, Menelaus, who was guilty of all this evil, was acquitted by the king, and those poor souls who had brought the charges were condemned to death. It was so obvious that the three men were right, however, that even barbarian Scythians would have acquitted them.
So those who argued the cause for Jerusalem, for the Jewish people, and for the sacred vessels suffered unjust punishment.
Even some people from Tyre were indignant over the deed and buried the three men with great ceremony.
But Menelaus, through the greed of those in power, remained the high priest and grew even more wicked. He became the chief conspirator against his own people.
About this time Antiochus Epiphanes prepared for his second invasion of Egypt.
For nearly forty days, apparitions were seen in the sky over Jerusalem. Horsemen in gold armor charged through the air, armed with lances and swords.
Ranks of horsemen were seen with swords drawn—attacking and counterattacking, with flashing shields and numerous spears and flying arrows and shining gold armor of every sort.
All the people prayed that this amazing apparition might be a good sign.

A false rumor began to circulate that Antiochus had died in Egypt, so Jason returned and assaulted Jerusalem with a force of no less than a thousand men. As the defenders on the wall were being defeated and the city was open to attack, Menelaus took refuge in the citadel.

Jason killed his own people in Jerusalem without mercy, not realizing that success at the expense of relatives is the greatest of failures. He imagined that he was winning victories over his enemies rather than over his own people.
But he did not gain control of the government, and in the end he was disgraced as the reward for his treachery. He was forced to flee again into the land of the Ammonites.

Jason’s life had a miserable end. After being imprisoned for a time by Aretas, king of the Arabians, he fled from town to town. He was pursued and hated by everyone as a despicable betrayer of the laws of Moses, a butcher of his own country and people. Finally, he was driven into Egypt.
From there he went to live with the Spartans, hoping they would give him refuge because of their family ties with the Jews. Then Jason, who had exiled so many others, died in a foreign land.
The man who had thrown out so many corpses to lie unburied had no one to mourn his death, no funeral, and no place in the tomb of his ancestors.

When the news of fighting between Jason and the Jews in Jerusalem reached King Antiochus, he suspected that the Jews had revolted. So he left Egypt in a furious state of mind and took Jerusalem back by force.
He commanded the soldiers to kill everyone they met and even to hunt down people hiding in their houses and kill them.
They slaughtered young and old, women and children, young girls and infants.
Within three days, there were eighty thousand victims—forty thousand killed and forty thousand sold into slavery.
But this was not enough for Antiochus. He dared to enter the Temple, the most holy place in all the world. Menelaus, a traitor to the laws of Moses and to his country, was his guide.
That filthy Antiochus seized the holy vessels; with defiled hands he took the ornaments that had been given as offerings by other kings to glorify and honor the Temple.

Deluded by his pride, Antiochus did not realize he was successful only because the Lord was angry for a time with the sinful residents of Jerusalem. It was the Lord who permitted this contempt for the Holy Place.

If the Jews had not been involved in many sins, Antiochus would have been immediately whipped for his presumption and turned back—as Heliodorus was when King Seleucus sent him to inspect the treasury.
But the Lord did not choose the nation for the sake of the Holy Place; rather, he chose the Holy Place for the sake of the nation.

So the Holy Place itself suffered evils inflicted on the people, just as later it participated in their good fortune. As it was forsaken by the Almighty in his anger, so it would be restored again with great glory when the people were reconciled to the great Lord.
After Antiochus had taken at least sixty-eight tons of silver from the Temple, he hurried back to Antioch. Carried away with pride, he believed he could sail on the land and walk on the sea.
He left governors to oppress the people. He left Philip, a Phrygian by birth, at Jerusalem. But Philip was even more barbaric than the one who appointed him.
Antiochus left Andronicus at Mount Gerizim. And Menelaus remained high priest, oppressing his own people even more than the others did.
Antiochus sent Apollonius, the captain of the Mysians, with an army of twenty-two thousand men and commanded him to kill all the grown men and to sell the women and children into slavery.

Apollonius came to Jerusalem under the pretense of peace and waited until the holy day of the Sabbath. Then, as the Jews observed the holy day of rest, he ordered his men to parade around fully armed.
After a crowd had gathered to watch them, he killed everyone who had come there. Dashing through the city with his armed men, he destroyed many others as well.

But Judas Maccabeus and nine others escaped into the wilderness. They stayed in the hills, where they lived off the land like wild animals. They ate nothing but wild plants to avoid defiling themselves by eating forbidden animals.
Not long afterward the king sent an influential Athenian citizen to force the Jews to abandon the laws of God and their ancestors

and to defile the Temple in Jerusalem. They were to call it the temple of Olympian Zeus, and the temple on Mount Gerizim was to be called the temple of Zeus the Hospitable, just as it was by those who lived there.
This intensification of evil was hard for everyone to bear.

The Temple was filled with Gentiles getting drunk at wild parties. They took their pleasure in prostitutes and had intercourse with women in the sacred Temple area. And for sacrifices they brought in things that were prohibited by the law of Moses.
The altar was covered with offerings that were strictly forbidden by the laws.

The Sabbath was not allowed to be kept as a holy day, and the people were prohibited from celebrating the festivals instituted by their ancestors. They were not even allowed to identify themselves as Jews.

Each month at the king’s birthday celebration, they were forced to participate in the pagan sacrifices. And when the festival of Dionysus was celebrated, they were forced to wear ivy wreaths in honor of the pagan god.
At the suggestion of the people of Ptolemais, a decree was sent to neighboring Greek cities that all Jews should be forced to participate in the sacrifices
and that anyone who refused to conform to Gentile customs should be executed. The misery of the Jews was obvious.

For example, two women were accused of having circumcised their children. They were seized and paraded through the city, clutching their infants to their breasts. Then they were thrown down from the city walls.

Others who met secretly in nearby caves to keep the Sabbath day were betrayed to Philip. Then, because it was the holy Sabbath, they refused to resist their attackers, and they were all burned to death.
Now, I urge those who read this book not to be disheartened by these calamities. Look at these, not as being for the destruction, but for the correction of our people.
For it is a sign of great kindness when sinners are not allowed to continue in their sin for a long time but are immediately punished.
In the case of other nations, the Lord waits patiently to judge them so that their punishment will be based on the full measure of their sins.
But that’s not how he deals with us. He punishes us before our sins reach their limit.
That way he never withdraws his mercy from us. Although he chastises his people with adversity, he never abandons them.
But let these words be sufficient warning to the readers. Now we must go on with the story.
Eleazar, one of the leading teachers of religious law and an elderly man of noble appearance, was being forced to eat pork.
But he preferred an honorable death to a defiled life, so he spit out the pork and went voluntarily to be beaten and tortured.
He acted as all people should who have the courage to refuse to eat forbidden food, even if it means ignoring their natural instincts for staying alive.

The officials in charge of the pagan sacrificial meal were old friends of Eleazar. In private they urged him to secretly bring meat he was allowed to eat by the law of Moses and only pretend to eat the pork from the king’s sacrificial meal.
In this way they were trying to be kind to Eleazar and help him save himself from death.

But Eleazar had firmly decided to do otherwise. He was a gray-haired old man, who had lived an honorable life since childhood. He was worthy of the distinction that comes with such age and reputation, and he wanted to obey God’s holy law. So he answered immediately that they should send him to his death.
“It is not right to pretend at my age,” he said. “And I don’t want to give young people the idea that Eleazar, at the age of ninety, has converted to a foreign religion.
I could gain a few more days of life by pretending to eat the pork, but I would also lead young people astray and defile and disgrace my old age.
For even if I should escape human punishment, whether I live or die, I will not escape the hands of the Almighty.
Therefore, by giving up my life bravely, I show myself worthy of my old age.
I also will give the young people a good example of how to die an honorable death willingly and bravely for the revered and holy laws of Moses.” Then he was immediately taken to be tortured to death.
Those who had just acted kindly toward Eleazar suddenly turned on him because what he had said seemed to them to be utter madness.

When he was about to die from the blows, he moaned, “The Lord knows all things. He knows I could have saved my life, but instead I suffer this agonizing pain. He also knows I am happy to suffer these things because I worship and fear him.”
So this was how Eleazar died, leaving a memorial of virtue and courage not only for the young but also for the greater part of the nation.
Another time seven brothers, together with their mother, were arrested by the king. They were tortured with whips to make them violate the law of Moses by eating pork.
One of them, speaking for all of them, asked, “What are you trying to find out from us? We are ready to die rather than sin against the laws of our ancestors.”
The king became enraged, and he ordered that pans and cauldrons be heated.
When they were hot, he ordered that the tongue of the spokesman be cut out, that he be scalped, and that his hands and feet be cut off. His brothers and his mother were forced to watch all this.

When the young man was completely helpless, the king commanded that he should be fried alive in the pan. As smoke rose from the sizzling pan, his brothers and his mother strongly urged each other to die bravely.
They said, “The Lord God is watching over us, and he will surely have compassion on us. As Moses declared in the hymn that he sang before the people, ‘He will have compassion on his servants.’”

After the first brother died this way, they brought forward the second to continue their cruel sport. When they had scalped him, they asked him, “Will you eat pork, or do we have to tear you apart limb from limb?”
He replied in Hebrew, the language of his ancestors, “Never!” So he suffered the same torment as his brother.

And with his last breath, he said, “You wicked tormentor! You may be sending us from this present life, but the King of the world will raise us up again to live forever because we have died for his laws.”
After him the third brother was sent to the same torture. When he was ordered to do so, he quickly stuck out his tongue and courageously stretched out his hands.
Then he said with boldness, “I received these hands from God, but for his laws I will gladly give them up, for I hope to receive them again from him.”
The king and his men were amazed at the young man’s courage because he regarded his suffering as nothing.
After he was dead, they tortured the fourth brother in the same way.
When he was near death, he said, “It is better to die by human hands while clinging to the hope that God will raise us up again. But for you, there will be no resurrection to life!”
Then they brought the fifth brother and tortured him as well. But he looked at the king
and said, “You have power among mortals, even though you are also mortal, so do whatever you want. But do not think that God has forsaken our people.
Wait, and you will see how his great power will torment you and your descendants.”

After him they brought the sixth brother. Just before he died, he declared, “Do not deceive yourself. It is our own fault that we suffer these things, for we have sinned against our God. Appalling things have happened to us.
But do not think that you will escape unpunished for trying to fight against God.”
The mother was particularly admirable and worthy of honorable memory. Although she saw her seven sons killed in the space of one day, she bore it with great courage because of her hope in the Lord.
She bravely encouraged each of them in Hebrew, the language of their ancestors. Joining a man’s courage to a woman’s insight, she said to them,
“I do not know how you were formed in my womb. I wasn’t the one who gave you breath and life, nor did I shape any part of you.

But the Creator of the world, who formed the human race, devised the origin of us all. In his mercy, he will restore both breath and life to you because you are obeying his laws and showing no concern for yourselves.”

Antiochus, suspecting insult in her tone of voice, thought she was mocking him. The youngest brother was still alive, so Antiochus assured him with an oath that he would make him a rich and happy man if he would abandon the traditions of his ancestors. Antiochus said he would make him one of his favored leaders and give him a high office.
But the young man was not moved by these offers, so the king called for the mother and told her to persuade the youth to save his life.
After Antiochus had argued with her for a long time, she said that she would try to persuade her son.

Then, bending over him, she made a fool of the cruel tyrant and spoke to her son in their native language. “My son, have pity on me. I carried you nine months in my womb, nursed you three years, nourished you, and raised you to this age.
I urge you, my child, look at heaven and earth and all that is in them, and remember that God made them out of nothing. He made all human beings in this way as well.
So do not fear this butcher, but show yourself worthy of your brothers. Accept death, so that by God’s mercy I may receive you back again along with your brothers.”
While the mother was still speaking, the young man said to his tormentors, “What are you waiting for? I will not obey the king’s command but only the law that was given to our ancestors by Moses.
Antiochus, you have contrived all sorts of evil against the Hebrews, but you will never escape the hand of God.
We are suffering for our own sins.
Though the living Lord is angry with us for a little while and punishes us, we, his servants, will be reconciled to him in the end.
But you are wicked and most unmerciful. Do not let your vain hopes make you proud because you have the power to torture God’s people,
for you have not yet escaped the judgment of the sovereign God who sees all things.
My brothers suffered briefly for the sake of the covenant, and now they have drunk of eternal life. But God will justly punish you for your arrogance.

But I, like my brothers, offer my body and my life for the laws of our ancestors. And I call upon God to show mercy to our nation quickly. And may you be tormented and filled with pain until you confess that he alone is God.
Perhaps because of my brothers and myself, the just wrath of the Almighty against our nation will cease.”
This made the king extremely angry, and he tortured him more cruelly than he had the others, for he bitterly resented his ridicule.
So the youth died without being defiled, trusting wholly in the Lord.
Last of all, after her sons, the mother died.
But this is enough about the eating of pagan sacrifices and of the extreme cruelties.

Meanwhile, Judas Maccabeus and those who were with him went secretly through the towns, calling together their relatives and friends and enlisting those who continued in the Jewish faith. They gathered six thousand men.
Then they called on the Lord to look down upon his oppressed people and to have pity on the Temple, which had been defiled by wicked men.
They asked the Lord to have mercy on Jerusalem, which was being destroyed and was soon to be leveled to the ground, and to listen to the blood crying out to him.
They begged him to remember the wicked slaughter of innocent children and the blasphemies spoken against his name and to show his hatred for evil.
Once Maccabeus had organized his army, the Gentiles could not stand against him because the anger of the Lord was turned to mercy.
So Maccabeus took the towns and villages by surprise and set them on fire. He captured strategic places and sent many enemies fleeing,
usually making his strikes during the night. The reports of his bravery spread far and wide.

Philip could see that Maccabeus was gaining ground little by little and that his victories were becoming more frequent, making him a real threat. So he wrote to Ptolemy Macron, the governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, asking him to send aid to the king’s garrisons.

Immediately Ptolemy sent Nicanor son of Patroclus, one of the king’s most favored leaders, giving him no less than twenty thousand Gentile troops from different nations to wipe out the whole Jewish race. He also sent Gorgias, a general who was very experienced in matters of war.
The king owed a large sum of money to the Romans, so Nicanor proposed to raise seventy-five tons of silver by selling captured Jews into slavery.

So he sent invitations to dealers in the coastal cities, offering to sell Jewish slaves at the price of ninety slaves for seventy-five pounds of silver. Little did he know that the vengeance of the Almighty was about to catch up to him.
When Judas learned that Nicanor was invading, he told those who were with him that the enemy was near.
Some of them were afraid and did not trust the justice of God, so they ran away.
Others sold all their possessions and prayed to the Lord that he would save them from the wicked Nicanor, who had already sold them even before meeting them.

They asked the Lord to do this, if not for their own sakes, then for the sake of the covenant he had made with their ancestors and for the honor of his holy and glorious name, by which they were called.

Maccabeus called together the six thousand that were now with him, encouraging them to fight bravely and not to be afraid of the enemy or discouraged at the vast horde of Gentiles who were wickedly advancing against them.
He vividly reminded them of the sinful and outrageous acts done to the Holy Place and of the way Jerusalem had been attacked and humiliated, not to mention the destruction of the ancestral customs.
“They trust in their weapons and their boldness,” Maccabeus said, “but we trust in almighty God, who with a single nod can completely destroy both those that fight against us and the whole world.”
He also reminded them of the help their ancestors had received from God. Once in the days of Sennacherib, 185,000 enemy soldiers were destroyed.

Maccabeus also recalled the battle when 8,000 Jews and 4,000 Macedonians fought against the Galatians in Babylonia. When the Macedonians were in danger, the Jews received help from God and killed 120,000 of the enemy. Then they carried off many of the Galatians’ possessions.
The soldiers were greatly encouraged by these words and resolved even to die for their laws and country.
and appointed his brothers—Simon, Joseph, and Jonathan—to be captains over three of the divisions. Maccabeus assigned fifteen hundred men to each division.

He instructed Eleazar, another one of his brothers, to read to them from the holy book, and then he gave them their battle cry: “God is our help!” Then Maccabeus himself led the first division in an attack against Nicanor.
With the Almighty as their helper, they killed more than nine thousand of the enemy. They also wounded and disabled the greater part of Nicanor’s army and forced them to flee.
They seized the money of those who had come to buy them as slaves. They also pursued the enemy for a considerable distance, but they had to call off the chase because it was getting late.
The Sabbath would begin that evening, and for that reason, they could not continue in pursuit.

When they had gathered together the weapons and captured the spoils of their enemy, they observed the Sabbath. They greatly praised and thanked the Lord, who had saved them that day and had chosen to begin showing his mercy to them.
After the Sabbath, they gave some of the spoils to those who had been tortured and to orphans and widows. The rest they took for themselves and their children.
When this was done, they all prayed together, asking the merciful Lord to be fully reconciled to his servants, the Jews.

In confrontations with Timothy and Bacchides, the Jews killed more than twenty thousand of the enemy. They captured the high strongholds, and then they divided a great amount of plunder among those who had been tortured and to orphans and widows and the elderly.
When they had carefully gathered together the enemy’s weapons, they stored them in strategic places. They carried the rest of the plunder to Jerusalem.
They also killed the commander of Timothy’s forces, a wicked man who had harmed the Jews in many ways.

As they celebrated the victory in Jerusalem, the city of their ancestors, they burned Callisthenes and some others who had been hiding in a certain house. These men had set fire to the sacred gates of the Temple, so they were justly repaid for their sacrilege.
But Nicanor—that most hated man, who had brought a thousand merchants to buy the Jews as slaves—

was humiliated, with the Lord’s help, by the very ones he considered insignificant. He took off his brilliant uniform and fled like a runaway slave through the open country. He was fortunate to even arrive at Antioch, for his entire army had been destroyed.

He had promised to raise the tribute money for the Romans by capturing people from Jerusalem, but now he proclaimed that the Jews had a Defender and that they could not be harmed, for they were following the laws God had given them.
About that time Antiochus Epiphanes returned from Persia with his armies in disarray.

He had entered the city of Persepolis and attempted to plunder its temples and bring the town under his control. However, the people there had rushed to arms and routed the invaders, forcing them into a humiliating defeat.
When Antiochus arrived at Ecbatana, he received the news of what had happened to Nicanor and to Timothy’s forces.

He became furious and decided to make the Jews pay for the humiliation he had just suffered. So he commanded his chariot driver to take him to Jerusalem without stopping. But God’s judgment went with him because in his arrogance he had said, “When I get to Jerusalem, I will make it a mass grave for the Jews!”

But the Lord, the God of Israel who sees all things, struck Antiochus with an incurable and mysterious disease. For as soon as he had said these words, a dreadful pain seized his intestines—an excruciating intestinal torture that could not be stopped.
This was a very just punishment indeed, considering he had tormented the intestines of others with many barbaric tortures.

But not even this stopped his arrogance; he was still filled with pride. Breathing fire in his rage against the Jews, he commanded the driver to go even faster. But as they were hurrying along, he was thrown from the chariot and fell so hard that his every limb was in agony.

In his superhuman arrogance, he had thought he could command the waves of the sea and weigh tall mountains on a scale, but now he was thrown to the ground and had to be carried on a stretcher. This was a clear manifestation of God’s power.
Maggots swarmed out of the wicked man’s body, and while he still lived in grief and pain, his flesh rotted away. The stench of his decaying flesh made his army sick.
No one could stand to carry the stretcher of this man who had thought only a little while earlier that he could touch the stars of heaven.
As a result of God’s curse, Antiochus was humbled and began to come to his senses, for his agony grew by the minute.
When he himself could no longer stand his own stench, he said, “It is right to be subject to God, and mere humans should not think they are equal to God.”
Then this wicked man vowed to the Lord (who would not show him any mercy)
that he would set Jerusalem free rather than level it and make it a mass grave.

He had previously said that the Jews and their children were not worthy to be buried but only to have their bodies thrown out to be eaten by wild animals and vultures. But now he promised to grant them rights equaling those of the Athenians.

He had previously desecrated the holy Temple, but now he promised to decorate it with the finest gifts, to lavishly replace the holy vessels in it, and to pay from his own resources all the expenses connected with offering the sacrifices.
He even said that he would become a Jew himself and go throughout the earth declaring the power of God.
But his agony continued, for the just judgment of God had come upon him. Then, realizing he was going to die, he wrote a letter of request to the Jews:
“Antiochus, king and commander, sends hearty greetings to his excellent citizens, the Jews, and wishes them health and prosperity.
If you and your children are well and everything is going as you wish, I am thankful, for my hope is in God.
“As for me, I have fond memories of you. When I returned from the regions of Persia, I became seriously ill and thought it necessary to make plans for everybody’s welfare.
Not that I despair of my health, for I have every expectation of recovering from my illness.
But I noticed that my father always appointed a successor whenever he led an army into the upper provinces.
He wanted to leave everything in order in case anything unexpected happened to him. That way the kingdom would not degenerate into chaos because the people would know who was to lead the government.

And I know that the rulers of the neighboring nations watch for opportunities to take advantage of us, so I have appointed my son Antiochus Eupator to succeed me as king. When traveling in the upper provinces, I have often left him in charge. I have sent him a copy of what I have written here.
So I urge and beg you to recall the public and private favors given to you and to continue to be faithful to me and to my son.
For I am confident that he will follow my instructions to be fair and kind to you.”
So the murderer and blasphemer suffered terribly, much as he had made others suffer. And he died a miserable death in the mountains of a foreign country.
Philip, his close friend, carried his body home. Then, fearing the son of Antiochus, Philip went to stay with King Ptolemy Philometor in Egypt.
Now Maccabeus and those who were with him, by the protection of the Lord, recovered the Temple and Jerusalem.
They tore down the altars the Gentiles had set up in the public square and destroyed their pagan shrines.

After they had purified the Temple, they made another altar. Striking new fire from flint, they offered the first sacrifice in two years. They burned incense, lit the lamps, and set out the Bread of the Presence.

When they had done all these things, they fell face down on the ground and asked the Lord to keep them safe from any further disasters. They also asked that he punish them more gently if they did sin again and that he not hand them over to barbarians and blasphemous people.
The purification of the Temple occurred on the anniversary of the day it had been polluted by foreigners—that is, on the twenty-fifth day of the month of Kislev.

They celebrated with joy for eight days, as is the custom for the Festival of Shelters. They remembered how they had recently kept the Festival of Shelters when they were living in caves in the mountains like wild animals.
So they carried garlanded wands, green branches, and palm branches and sang hymns to the one who had given them success in purifying his Holy Place.
They voted to pass a public decree that the entire Jewish nation should observe these days every year.
We have finished recounting the death of Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes.
We will now relate the events that took place during the reign of Antiochus Eupator, the son of that wicked man. We will give a brief summary of the evils brought about by his wars.
When Eupator became king, he appointed a man named Lysias to administer the affairs of his kingdom. Before this, Lysias had succeeded Ptolemy Macron as governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia.
Ptolemy was determined to act justly toward the Jews and to deal with them peacefully, especially because of the wrongs that had been done to them.

But the king’s favored leaders came and accused Ptolemy Macron because of his policy toward the Jews. On every side he was called a traitor because he had also left Cyprus, where King Ptolemy Philometor had put him in charge, and had defected to Antiochus Epiphanes. Since Ptolemy Macron had no support, he committed suicide by taking poison.
When Gorgias replaced Lysias as governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, he hired mercenaries and continually fought the Jews.
At the same time, the Idumeans, who controlled important fortified strongholds, were also harassing the Jews. They welcomed renegade Jews from Jerusalem and did everything to keep the war going.
After seeking God’s help through prayer, Maccabeus and his troops launched an assault against the Idumean strongholds.
They attacked vigorously and captured them, driving back those who fought on the walls and slaughtering everyone they encountered. They killed at least twenty thousand men.
At least nine thousand men took refuge in two very strong towers with plenty of food and weapons to withstand a siege.
So Maccabeus left Simon and Joseph, along with Zacchaeus and his troops, to command an army that was large enough to besiege them. Then he left to take care of more urgent matters.
But some of Simon’s men were greedy, and they accepted a bribe of seventy thousand silver coins to let the men in the tower escape.
When Maccabeus was told what had happened, he gathered the leaders of the people and accused them of selling out their fellow Jews for money by letting their enemies escape.
Then he put those traitors to death and quickly captured the two towers.
He was successful in battle and in everything else he did, and he killed more than twenty thousand men in the two fortresses.
Timothy, who had already been defeated once by the Jews, gathered a large army of mercenaries and assembled many horsemen from Asia. He approached Judea, intending to take it by force.
But Maccabeus and his men prayed to God as Timothy drew near. To show their humility, they sprinkled dust on their heads and wore sackcloth.
They lay face down at the foot of the altar and asked God to be merciful to them and to be an enemy to their enemies, an opponent to their opponents, as the law of Moses says.
After they had prayed, they took up their weapons and marched from the town until they came near their enemies.

As soon as the sun came up, the two forces attacked each other. One army had not only courage but also confidence in the Lord as its guarantee for victory and success; the other army made rage its leader in the battle.
When they were in the heat of battle, the enemy saw five men from heaven riding on brilliant horses with golden bridles. These heavenly horsemen were leading the Jews.

Two of them stood on either side of Maccabeus, shielding him with their armor and keeping him safe. They shot arrows and thunderbolts at the enemy, making them blind and confused and throwing them into chaos.
The Jews killed 20,500 troops and 600 horsemen.
Timothy fled to Gazara, a heavily guarded stronghold where Chaereas was governor.
Maccabeus and his army eagerly laid siege to the fortress for four days.
Those who were inside, trusting in the strength of the place, kept shouting blasphemies and profanities.
On the morning of the fifth day, twenty young men who were with Maccabeus became furious because of the blasphemy. They bravely stormed the wall and fiercely cut down the enemy.
Then others followed them and set fire to the towers, burning the blasphemers alive. Still others broke open the gates and let in the rest of the army so they could capture the town.
They killed Timothy, who was found hiding in a cistern, his brother Chaereas, and Apollophanes.
After their victory, they sang hymns of thanksgiving, praising the Lord who had shown great kindness to Israel and given them the victory.
A short time after this, Lysias became very displeased with what had happened. Lysias was the king’s guardian and second-in-command, and he was a member of the royal family.
He gathered eighty thousand soldiers and all his horsemen with the intention of capturing Jerusalem and making it a Greek settlement.
He intended to tax the Temple, as he did the shrines of other nations, and to auction off the office of high priest every year.
He had no regard for the power of God but proudly trusted in his numerous foot soldiers, thousands of horsemen, and eighty elephants.
He came into Judea and approached Beth-zur, a fortified place about twenty miles from Jerusalem. He began to vigorously attack it.
When Maccabeus and his men learned that the strongholds were under siege, everyone cried out to the Lord. With tears they begged him to send a good angel to rescue Israel.
Maccabeus himself was the first to take up arms, and he urged the others to follow him into battle in order to help their fellow Jews. So they rushed out together.
While they were still near Jerusalem, a horseman in white clothing appeared to them brandishing gold weapons.
Together they praised the merciful God and took such courage that they were ready to assault not only the men but also the fiercest beasts and walls of iron.
So they advanced in battle formation, having a heavenly ally, the merciful Lord.
Like lions they leaped on the enemy, killing eleven thousand foot soldiers and sixteen hundred horsemen and sending all the rest fleeing for their lives.
Most of those who fled were wounded and without weapons. Even Lysias was forced to flee in shame.
But Lysias was not stupid. He saw the loss he had suffered and realized that the Hebrews could not be overcome, because the mighty God fought along with them. So Lysias sent a message to them,
urging them to settle everything on just terms and promising to make the king their friend.
Maccabeus thought about what would be best for everyone, so he accepted Lysias’s offer. The king, in turn, consented to all the Jews’ requests, which Maccabeus had submitted in writing to Lysias.
Lysias wrote the following letter to the Jews:
“John and Absalom, your messengers, have delivered your written terms and requested that I grant them.
I have reported all the necessary details to the king, and he has granted as much as he can.
If, therefore, you will remain loyal to the government, I will endeavor to help you from now on.
I have given verbal orders that my officials and your messengers should talk with you about the details.
“Farewell. This letter was written on April 20 in the one hundred forty-eighth year of Greek rule.”
The king had written this letter to Lysias:
“Now that our father has taken his place among the gods, we desire that those in our realm should be left undisturbed in caring for their own affairs.
We understand that the Jews will not accept the Greek customs of our father. They prefer to keep their own ways and have asked us to allow them to follow their own customs.
Since we desire that this nation should be at peace, we have decided that their Temple should be restored to them and that they may live according to the custom of their ancestors.
You will do well, therefore, to write to them and pledge them your friendship. When they have heard this decision, they will be able to rest easy and take care of their own business.”
The king’s letter to the Jews was as follows:
“We hope you are well, as we ourselves are well.
Menelaus told us that you wish to return home and care for your own affairs.
We therefore grant safe conduct to all who go home by April 26.
We also decree that the Jews may follow their own food laws, as they did before, and that none of them will be harassed in any way for things they may have done in ignorance.
I have sent Menelaus to reassure you.
“Farewell. This letter was written on April 11 in the one hundred forty-eighth year of Greek rule.”
The Romans also sent a letter to the Jews, which reads as follows:
“Whatever Lysias, a member of the royal family, has granted you, we also grant.

But he thought some things should be referred to the king. So confer among yourselves on these issues, and then send someone with a message. That way we can make good proposals on your behalf, for we are going to Antioch.
Write back immediately so that we may know what you are thinking.
“Farewell. This letter was written on April 11 in the one hundred forty-eighth year.”
When these agreements were made, Lysias returned to the king and the Jews turned their attention to farming.
However, some of the governors would not let them live in peace. These governors were Timothy, Apollonius son of Genneus, Hieronymus, Demophon, and Nicanor the governor of Cyprus.

The people of Joppa also committed an evil deed. They invited the Jews who lived among them (men, women, and children) to go for a boat ride. Since this was an obvious sign of friendship, the Jews publicly voted to accept the offer.
They did not suspect a thing and wanted to be on friendly terms. But when the boats were some distance from the shore, the people of Joppa drowned at least two hundred of the Jews.
As soon as Judas heard about this cruelty to his fellow Jews, he assembled his men for action.

After calling upon God, the just Judge, he attacked those murderers of his fellow Jews. He set the port on fire in the night, burned the boats, and killed with the sword those who had taken refuge there.
Then he left, since the town’s gates were closed. But he planned to return again to completely destroy all the people of Joppa.
When he learned that the people of Jamnia also planned to wipe out the Jews who lived among them,
he attacked Jamnia at night and set the port and its ships on fire. The light of the blaze was seen in Jerusalem twenty-eight miles away.
When they had gone about a mile from Jamnia and were marching toward Timothy, over five thousand Arabian foot soldiers and more than five hundred horsemen attacked them.

After a hard fight and with the help of God, Judas and his men won the victory. The defeated nomads asked Judas for a peace treaty, promising to give him livestock and to help the Jews in every other way.
Thinking that they might indeed be useful in many ways, Judas promised them peace. After an exchange of pledges, the Arabians returned to their tents.
Judas also attacked Caspin, a certain town that was surrounded by fortifications and walls and inhabited by all sorts of Gentiles.
Confident in the strength of the walls and their supply of food, the people there became insolent, and they taunted Judas with mockery, blasphemy, and all sorts of evil words.

But Judas and his men called upon the great Ruler of the world, for in the time of Joshua, the Lord had crumbled the walls of Jericho without the use of battering rams or war machines. Then Judas fiercely assaulted the walls.
By God’s will Judas and his men captured the town. They slaughtered so many people—a countless number—that a nearby lake that was about a quarter of a mile wide seemed to overflow with blood.
From there they marched eighty-seven miles to Charax, to the Jews living in the land of Tob.
But they did not find Timothy there, for he had left the area without doing anything, except that he left a very strong garrison in a certain fortress.
Dositheus and Sosipater, who were captains under Maccabeus, went and killed the men Timothy had left in the fortress—over ten thousand in all.
Maccabeus separated his men into divisions and appointed officers over them. He hurried after Timothy, who had with him 120,000 foot soldiers and 2,500 horsemen.

When Timothy learned that Judas was coming after him, he sent the women and children and also the baggage to a fortress called Karnaim. This fortress was hard to besiege or attack because all the approaches were so narrow.

But when Judas’s first band of soldiers came into sight, their enemies were struck with fear because of an apparition sent by the All-Seeing One. The enemies fled in such confusion that many of them were injured by their own companions and wounded with their own swords.
Judas went after them vigorously, killing the sinners by the sword, and he destroyed about 30,000 men.

Timothy himself was captured by the soldiers of Dositheus and Sosipater. With great cunning, he begged them to let him live, for he held the parents and brothers of many of them, and if he died, they would also perish.
When he had solemnly promised to return them unharmed, they released him in order to save their relatives.
Judas then went to Karnaim and the temple of Atargatis. There he killed twenty-five thousand people.

After he had destroyed these and put the rest to flight, Judas led his army to Ephron, a fortified town where Lysias and many people from various nations lived. Strong young men guarding the walls made a vigorous resistance, and they had many catapults and plenty of ammunition.
But when the Jews invoked the name of the Sovereign One, whose power breaks the strength of his enemies, they captured the town and killed twenty-five thousand of those who were inside.
From there they pressed on to Scythopolis, which lies seventy miles from Jerusalem.
But the Jews who lived in Scythopolis testified that the people of the town were kind to them, especially during times of adversity.
So Judas thanked the people, strongly urging them to remain friendly to Jews in the future. They arrived back at Jerusalem just before the Festival of Pentecost.
After the Festival of Pentecost, Judas and his men marched out to attack Gorgias, the governor of Idumea.
Gorgias met them with three thousand foot soldiers and four hundred horsemen.
When the battle began, a few of the Jews were killed.

Then a certain Dositheus, one of Bacenor’s men and a strong horseman, caught hold of Gorgias and began to drag him by his cloak. Dositheus would have taken the accursed man alive, but a Thracian horseman rushed at him and cut off his arm, and so Gorgias escaped to Marisa.
Meanwhile, since Esdris and his men had fought a long time and were weary, Judas called upon the Lord to be their helper and their leader in battle.
After he chanted the battle cry in Hebrew, the language of their ancestors, accompanied by hymns, they made a surprise attack on Gorgias’s troops and caused them to flee.
Judas then assembled his army and went to the town of Adullam. Since the seventh day was approaching, they remained there to purify themselves according to custom and to keep the Sabbath.

By the day after the Sabbath, it had become urgent that the bodies of the Jews who had been killed be removed, so Judas and his men went to bury them with their relatives in the tombs of their ancestors.
But under the clothing of the dead they found some sacred amulets of the idols of Jamnia. The law forbids Jews to wear such things, so it was obvious to all that this was why these men had died.
Then they all blessed the ways of the Lord, the just Judge, who reveals things that are hidden.

They spent time in prayer, asking the Lord to completely forgive the sin that had been committed. Then the noble Judas strongly urged the people to keep themselves free from sin, since they saw with their own eyes what happens to people who sin in the same way as those who had died.

Taking up a collection from each person, Judas sent two thousand silver coins to Jerusalem for a sacrifice to be offered for the sins of those who had died. In so doing he acted well and honorably, for he kept the resurrection in mind.
If he had not expected that those who had died would rise again, it would have been useless and foolish to pray for the dead.

But since he had in mind the splendid reward that awaits those who die a godly death, his thought in doing this was holy and devout. Therefore, he made this atoning sacrifice for the dead so that they might be released from their sin.
In the one hundred forty-ninth year of Greek rule, Judas learned that Antiochus Eupator was marching with a great army toward Judea.

He had with him Lysias, his guardian and second-in-command, and each had an army of 110,000 foot soldiers, 5,300 horsemen, 22 elephants, and 300 chariots armed with deadly blades to cut down foot soldiers.
Menelaus joined them, and with great pretense he urged Antiochus on. But he was not really looking out for the welfare of his country; he simply hoped to strengthen his political position.

The King of kings caused Antiochus to become angry at the wicked man. So when Lysias suggested that Menelaus was the cause of all their trouble, Antiochus commanded that Menelaus be taken to Berea in Syria and executed according to their local custom.
For in Berea there was a tower seventy-five feet high, with sides steeply sloping down to piles of ashes all around it.
Anyone guilty of sacrilege or notorious for other crimes is taken to the top of the tower and thrown down into the ashes to die.
That was the fate of sinful Menelaus, and he was not even given a decent burial.
It was only fitting that he die in ashes because he had committed many sins against the altar of the Temple, the fire and ashes of which are holy.
The king was consumed with savage arrogance, and he had plans, even worse than his father’s, to devastate the Jews.

When Judas learned of these plans, he ordered the people to pray to the Lord day and night, asking him to help them now more than ever. For they feared that they would be deprived of the law of Moses, their land, and the holy Temple.
They prayed that God would not let his people be overtaken again by blasphemous Gentiles, for they were only now recovering from past troubles.

They all joined in this prayer and begged the Lord to be merciful. For three days they continually wept, fasted, and lay face down before the Lord, and then Judas encouraged them and ordered them to stand ready.

After consulting with the high council, Judas decided not to wait for the king to lead his army into Judea to make himself master of the city. Judas decided instead to rely on the Lord to help them defeat the king’s army in open warfare.

So Judas committed everything to the Creator of the world and encouraged his troops to fight bravely, even to death, in defense of the laws of Moses, the Temple, the city of Jerusalem, and their country and its citizens. Judas set up camp near Modein,

and he gave his soldiers their battle cry, “God brings us victory!” Then, with a select contingent of brave young men, he attacked the king’s camp at night and killed as many as two thousand men in the camp. He also killed the lead elephant with its driver.
Having created great fear and confusion in the enemy camp, they left with great success
just as dawn was breaking. This all happened because the Lord helped and protected them.
